div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 6, 1914.

div.head: ENGLAND'S PERNICIOUS LAND SYSTEM.
div.p: ENGLAND'S PERNICIOUS LAND SYSTEM.
MR. & MRS. GROSFIELDYS LEAD.

Mr. Aaron Israel presided at the well-attended meeting held in Liverpool-road on Friday even- ing last week, when Mr. Crosfield and Mr. E. Enerer Todd (of Manchester) were the speakers. At the outset, on the proposition of the CHAIR- mot, a vote of sympathy and regret was passed in connection with the wreck of the Empress of Ireta,nd.

MR. CROSFIELD'S CLAIMS UPON WARRINGTON. An exceedingly well-attended and successful meeting was held at the corner, of Catherine-. street on Satiirday evenifig, when Mr. Crosfield and Mr. Todd were the principal .speakers, Councillor Gough presiding. The CHAIRMAN referred to the splendid pro- gress made by the Liberal party under its able and gifted leaders. Mr. Asquith had made a name for himself that would last as long as English history. Mr. Lloyd George had also become famous for the excellent prinzmpies which were embodied j, his Widgets ellear, hear.) He had the democracy AL heart, for he placed the burden on the right shohidEt.s. Brains, and not land, were ;;oing to govern the people. Mr. Harold Smith's return at the last election was a fluke, but that would be redressed at the next election. They were more determined than ever to return Mr. Crosfield. If ever there was a man who had stuck to the people, both in and out of Parliament, it was Mr. Crosfield, and it was a shame that a stranger should have been sent to the House of Commons. What had Mr. Smith done for democracy since be represented Warrington? tA Voice: "Nothiti.T.") IN hat did Mr. Crosfield do? He supported the founda- tion of all social government—the Parliament Bill. (Applause.) 'FIIE LABOURER WORTIIY OF lIIS lIIRE. Mr. TODD said that one of the reforms. they were out to accomplish was to make sure that for the future, when the wealth and prosperity of the country was increasing by leaps and bounds, the lowest paid and unorganised worker would receive higher pay and have a fair share of the increasing prosperity of the country. (Hear, hear.) They could not retain their industrial position unless they saw to it that there was not one of the workers paid a wage so low that lie could not provide the minimum of good food for physical efficiency. The Liberal Government were going to see to that, and the land campaign was a big step in that direction. The Liberal Government had shown that wages could he forced up without putting people out of their jobs, and without increasing the price of the necessaries of life. The payment of higher wages would in itself do something to solve the housing question. ENGLAND AN INSPIRATION FOR THE WORLD. If they could solve the evils to which they were going to devote their labours they would keep England as the leader of the world, not only in industry, but also as an inspiration to all the other working-class nations of the earth. That was true patriotism. It was a fine thing to think that the English, Scotch and Irish ideas were having their influence over the whole globe. That was a fine type of patriotism, but there was a finer, and that was to feel that in England the people had greater comfort and greater happiness than anywhere else in the world; not because they did not want other people to be happy, but because they wanted to show them the way. (Hear, hear.) It was a great thin.' to think that the people of this country had got the finest living conditions on God's earth. (Applause.) MR. CROSFIELD'S POLICY OF HELPING TIIE "UNDER DOG." Mr. CROSFIELD, who was accorded a hearty reception, said: Mr. Todd has made a speech saturated with knowledge and based on solid facts and justice, without one trace of bunkum in it. I want to thank the Chairman for what he said about myself. He said that all my life I had stuck to the democratic cause. (Hear, hear, and a Voice: "Quite right, too.") Well, I can assure you, fellow-towns- men—l don't want to boast—but I can tell you in all sincerity that what the Chairman has said is quite true. I was brought up from a little lad to be a democrat and to look forward to the progress of the whole of our people. I was not brought up to be content with the condition of things that you find in slumdom— I have hated it all my life. (Applause.) It is now 30 years—a good long slice out of one's life— since I first began to have the privilege of ex- changing political opinions and ideas with you, and I well remember how, in those early days, and since, there were three things we often talked about; and well the Chairman will re- member it, too. There is not a Liberal amongst us, however old, who can remember the time when Liberals did not look forward to land reform. (Hear, hear.) That is one of the three things that we have talked about most of all. The other two were qualified individualism and graduated taxation. In these days we have got qualified individualism, and that is what Mr. Lloyd George—(applause.) I like to see the way his name is received. When a man fights so earnestly and with such sincerity—and I speak from personal knowledge, because he is a personal friend Of mine—(applause)—and places his genius at your service, it is time for Lancashire lads to take off their coats and say they will see him through. (A Voice: "And they will do.") You have only got to make up your minds to do it, and you can do it. (A Voice: " That is all.") Never forget a saying of which we in Lancashire have every reason to be proud—" What Lancashire thinks to-day England will think to-morrow." (Applause.) I am glad to see that you are in that frame of mind about as gifted and as earnest a democratic leader as we have ever had to be the pioneer in these great reforms. I quoted his name just now, because I was going to quote you what he sags in summing up all the work upon which he is engaged. Speaking of his job, Mr. Lloyd George says: "I am out to help the under dog " —(applause)—and if you like that is a homely way of expressing qualified individualism. (Hear, hear.) The Chairman spoke of the way in which taxation, in these modern days, has been laid heavily upon the shoulders that are capable of bearing it—a matter of enormous im- portance to the whole nation; of importance to every householder in Warrington, Tory as well as Liberal, of benefit to the whole lot of us—in a a e Mr. ago. B accordance with the great doctrine laid down, by t. thantaxation, a century marvellous economist, Adam Smith, more adjustingeorg ehasof tlte done bur n burden Lloyyd G these last two great Budgets—that is qualified individualism and it is also graduated taxa- on. The Chairman knows as well as I do that iwhen we talked over these tl • iings 20 or 30 years ago we w • etc, in a mighty different position—in a position of impotence. Twenty or thirty years ago we were in a far different " posi- tion, in fact, of importance. position a TI days when wc, talked lose were the sands; the days when nd fabout ploughing the reformers might sow as much good seed as the liked, but a great deal of it fell upon stony andy 11) not so to-day. Now our ar,leground. It is falls Iron fertile .) soil. (Hear, hear, and cheers Why is that? Well, for one thing we have to large extent made that fine, memorable al' very phrase of the great American's, "Government f o the people, by the people, and for the people," a reality in our land, and we are going to still further im- prove upon what has been done by very shortly abolishing plural voting. (Loud cheers.)
Reforms that will Banish Slums, lll.health and Inequalities.
With a rest on Whit-Monday, the Land Campaign has been conducted incessantly through the present week.

Mr. Crosfield and a clever band of speakers, IN ell versed in their subjects, have spoken in many parts of the Borough, and an intricate subject has been explained fully and satisfactorily. It has been made clear that there is no question of attacking a class. Landowners, as land- owners, have been shown every consideration.

But the pernicious land system, under which the many suffer for the supposed benefit of the few, has been ruthlessly assailed and exposed. as our reports will show. A feature of the week was Thursday's special ladies' afternoon, at which Mrs. A. 11. Crosfield , presided, and fittingly introduced the speakers by showing how seriously the land question, by its bearing upon the rates, and its perpetuation of slum, affects the women of .the land.

The campaign Is to be continued next week till Wednesday. when the final mass meeting will be held at Bridge Foot, or, if wet. In the Co-operative Hall. To-night's meeting is at Town's End; Monday's at Bridge Foot; Tuesday's in Ellesmere-street.

this self-government is the best earnest of per- manent progress and develops at the same time a spirit of enterprise on the one hand, and on the other a sober, solid sense of responsibility and spirit of self-control. Yes, and what has become a reality in this country we are going to make a reality over the water—(cheers)--so that Ireland may share in those advantages. And then besides this we are now feeling the effect of our national system of education—a notable work that spread of education. (Cheers.) Our democracy is to-day possessed of knowledge far more than was ever the case formerly, and knowledge is based upon science, and part of it. Although I have not time to-night to dwell upon it, let us always, all of us who love human progress, first amongst our own folk, and afterwards amongst all other peoples, let us, who hold that noble faith, never forget to take off our hats to science. (Applause.)

div.head: EVILS OF INSANITARY
div.p: THE EVILS OF INSANITARY
DWELLINGS.

Mt. TODD said that already the Govbrnment had started a scheme whioh was in actual work- ing order for the treatment of consumptives. There were, at the present time, something like 8,000 to 10,000 consumptives who were getting proper medical treatment solely as a result of the action of the Liberal Government. Although that was highly satisfactory, one point that was very unsatisfactory was that as yet hardly any- thing at all had been done to prevent the spread of consumption through the bad housing, which waa the chief agency in the spread. (Hear, hear.) From two of the wealthy parts of Lon- don they had striking examples. In Kensington , Dispensary, out of 7,000 patients treated, only 150 slept in separate rooms, all the rest were sleep- ing in the same room and the majority of them in the same bed as other members of the family. ("shame.") All that was due to overcrowding, which existed in the district. In a report for the same district it was stated that badly ventil- ated, over-crowded bedrooms, and the frequent use of the same bed by a consumptive patient and other members of the family, were respon- sible for more consumption than any other ageiry.

div.head: CONSUMPTION A CERTAINTY.
div.p: CONSUMPTION A CERTAINTY.

Tbe Medical Officer of Health for the district reported that there were 600 people who were known to be living with consumptive patients in tenen:ients so small and crowded as to render their ultimate death from consumption a mat- ter of certainty. He (the speaker) took it that if they were going to deal adequately with that scourge of consumption they must essentially deal with the problem of housing, and one of the principal land reform proposals of the Liberal Government was to make it a duty on local authorities to provide adequate and sani- tary houses for the people. They would have to prepare schemes for the clearing out of slums and insanitary dwellings and to see that there were a proper water supply and proper sanitary arrangements to every house. They would be able, through the land proposals, to effect those necessary changes more easily and cheaply. (Applause.) The Liberal party were out to get justice, where, obviously to everyone, justice existed, and the unjust privileges of the few would be regarded as mere dust in the balance when compared with the prosperity, efficiency, happiness and security of the nation at large. (Applause.)

div.head: "TIME IS NOW RIPE FOR LAND
div.p: "TIME IS NOW RIPE FOR LAND
REFORM."

Mr. CROSFIELD said that the Liberal party had always striven for rational land reform, but the results bad hitherto been disappointing. In his opinion the reason was that it was largely a question of the time not being ripe for carrying the reform through. They had been making sure of their foundations and the time was now ripe, and they were going forward. The ques- tion had been thoroughly studied throughout the length and breadth of the land. Men were now coming to realise that there were very few social evils which in a greater or lesser degree were not to be traced to the question of land. (Hear, hear.) They were going to have decent wages and better houses for the agricultural labourer, and the houses would be erected on an economic basis. They were not going to have any element of misplaced charity entering into the proposition.

div.head: STARTING POINT.
div.p: THE STARTING POINT.

In far too many counties in England the agri- cultural labourers were not receiving a fair and rational wage for a fair day's work. That was the starting point. The agricultural labourer would be put in a position that he could pay an economic rent for his cottage. His whole conditions of life would be transformed, and they all knew the influence that would have on conditions of life in the towns. clfear, hear.) Better conditions in the country would tend to bring down rents in the towns. As long as there was any man in England who was not get- ting a fair wage on which to bring up his family in decency and comfort there was work left for that great Progressive party to do. They were easing a bit now. By passing the Home Rule Bill they had, got rid of some of the congestion at Westminster which made it so difficult for them to go on with their reforms. In dealing with their great proposals they were not taking up a mean and selfish attitude, for all would re- ceive the benefits of the Liberal legislation.

div.head: CO-OPERATION TO REPLACE INTERNATIONAL HATRED.
div.p: CO-OPERATION TO REPLACE INTER- NATIONAL HATRED.

Appealing for a little bit of international co- operation, Mr. Crosfield said they had had eofnotnhe opinionghofint that we were ehrae tred He was firmly within a measurable distance of the time wheinn,dthrough the indirect co-operationandhatef hateful influence and effect oft we might see a check in the heavy expenditure on armaments Inter- national Association for Lhe aboTr towards ds tion had done good work i wLegisla- that end. Only a few years age England France hated each other like poisaTirld They were good friends now, and we were fast ap- proaching the day when we would be go, friends with Germany. (Hear, hear.) He knew they had friends in Warrington who frightened the old ladies very much by making them think they would wake up one morning to the tune of a German brass band in their garden. (Laughter.) The relations between Germany . and England were steadily improving. (Hear, hear.) The great difficulty in the European situation was the question of Alsace-Lorraine. If once the differences between France and Ger- many were adjusted, they would see an enormous slump in the expenditure on armaments, and there were plenty of good purposes to which the money could be devoted instead in old England. (Hear, hear.) During the last eight years every- one had benefited by Liberal legislation. They were going on in their great work of bettering the conditions of the people; one thing they must do was to settle that question in support of which they were there that night. (Cheers.) Mr. SANDERS proposed a hearty vote of thanks to the speakers and Chairman, and said they could not get a better man than Mr. Crosfield, and so long as he would give them his word that .he would stand they would all work for him in Warrington. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: LIVING WAGE FOR ALL.
div.p: A LIVING WAGE FOR ALL.

One thing that makes me, in a special degree, hopeful for the future success of this great land campaign—which has been expounded in prin- ciple and in detail night after night with such striking ability by Mr. Todd nay, not only hopeful, but dead certain of our success, is the fact that the eminent band of expert and able men who have investigated the question exhaustively, and in town, city and country district have gone to work scientifically. They have gone to the root of the whole question, and have given us a good bird's-eye view of it in all its complexity, yet in all its simplicity. I ask you to put your shoulders to this work and help to make life a fair thing for the agricultural labourer. (Ap- plause.) It is a good thing in itself to help the other man independent of your own interests, but by helping the agricultural labourer, in all conscience you help the town labourer, too. This great and progressive Government, fighting for your interests, begins with a minimum wage for the agricultural labourer. We are going to apply the principle of a minimum wage to every section of workers in England—men and women who are not strong enough through their own organisations to do their own collective bar- gaining. (Applause.) HUNGRY 'FORTIES LEFT BEHIND. Let me go back to the hungry 'Forties. The Tories are fond of talking about the good old days. I wonder if anyone in Warrington, whose father or relatives can tell them of the hungry 'Forties, will call them good old days. I have heard a good deal about those hungry 'Forties. What did some persons preach in those days, when men and women were sunk in adversity under that evil system of taxation of food, clothing and everything you got? Under that evil regime of scarcity, men and women were advised to reconcile themselves to the hardships of this world by the prospect of a bright here-. after. ("Shame.") That is not our view of , things in these days. The Progressive party, to which you and I belong, will never rest until we see that every man in the land has as fair a chance, to begin with, as the agricultural lab- ourer is going to have. After him the town labourer shall have—what? (A Voice: "A minimum wage.") A reasonable wage, with which he can afford to pay an economic rent for a decent home. (Hear, hear.) We cannot give them all palaces, and we do not profess to, but we shall never rest until all our people are living in decent and sanitary houses. (Applause.) Give tho agricultural labourer his minimum wage with which to go and live in decent comfort in his cottage see to it that he gets the chance of an allotment A Voice: " And not take his common right from him either.") I quite agree: that is an infamous thing. I speak of the chance which the agricultural labourer will surely get, of a little allotment, and the other advantages he will get if he stays in the country. (Ap- plause.) Let him have his prospect before him of becoming a smallholder. (Hear, hear.) Yes, let him have the further prospect of advancing himself until he may become a small farmer— it is an enormous thing. (Hear, hear.) If you treat the agricultural man fairly it will be an enormous national gain to have a strong, healthy country population rooted in the soil of the want t better And w abouthwaatges? A rthese t in h these ee wages who IN depressed when you get men flocking in from the country to towns already congested? It is dead against hear.) Your interests to have it so. (Hear,

HOUSE SHORTAGE INFAMY. Mention has been made of housing accommo- dation. It is estimated that we are 120,000 cot- tages short in the country, and that is an infamy. (Hear, hear.) The population of the United Kingdom is 44,000,000; the population of Great Britain will be about 40,000,000. Out of that population you have half a million of our people who have not got decent accommodation. Land reform spells the abolition of all these icongs. rhave not preached absolute equality, but of the extremes of inequality we must get rid, and I say emphatically we will. (Applause.) The uplifting of our people is the finest and noblest work to which any man can set his hand. NO RED RUIN, BUT ORDERLY PROGRESS. Let me say how glad I was to hear Mr. Todd strike the international note. While I like to think of our industrial prosperity,' like, above all, to think of the gradual rising of the level of well-being all over Europe. In the days to come, as I have other opportunities of speaking to my fellow-men in Warrington, I am going to have more to say on that question, and what can be achieved in.lielping to raise the general level of common well-being by a little bit of sane international co-operation. I thank you all, in conclusion, for your great kindness in listen- ing to me for so long. (A Voice: "Go on a lot longer.") Well, I thank you for your kindness and your encouragement. (A Voice: "You are worth a thousand times more than Harold Smith.") I again thank you very warmly, and I wish you were a little warmer, too. (A Voice: "We will be warm at the next election.")

There are people wile—fraTe—ibeinienCe and the audacity to adopt violent tactics, and I hope we in Warrington will give a pretty warm time to anyone who comes preaching violence against the State. (Hear, hear.) - You and I are out for progress. We believe in pro- gress as the noblest of causes, and we believe it is best achieved /IS orderly progress. We do not believe in and won't tolerate what Lord Tenny- son referred to as "red ruin and the breaking up of law." We will not tolerate such things, but strengthen the hands of those who are working for orderly progress and the well-being of every household in the land. (Cheers.) A FOUR-FIGURE MAJORITY.

Mr. SANDERS proposed a hearty vote of thanks and said a man had come forward and announced that he had been converted by Mr. Todd's speeches. On the bowling green he had said he did not have much to do with politics, hut since he heard Mr. Todd's remarks on housing, &c., he had decided he had made a mistake and offered to become a worker for the Liberal party. (Applause.) Councillor GOUGH said he would like Mr. Cros- field's majority to be a thousand. (Applause.) Mr, CROSKELD : Well, four figures will be very bood.

div.head: MASSES NOT CLASSES.
div.p: MASSES NOT CLASSES.
Fixing the Medium Between Two
Extremes.
CAPRICIOUS LANDLORDS,
The well-attended meeting at Orford Village on Wednesday night was presided over by Mr. P. 11. Brown and addressed by Mr. Crosfield and Mr. W. Lyon Blease.

div.head: TO BRING ABOUT THE HAPPY MEDIUM.
div.p: TO BRING ABOUT THE HAPPY MEDIUM.

The CHAIRMAN said they had had a great fight from 1900, and he was of the opinion that they had been conquerors. They had won in their battle against the House of Lords. Measureswhicli were of great benefit to the working classes had , been passed, but there was one great thing they were going to tackle—the poverty question. In England they had, on one hand, the extremes in poverty; and on the other hand extremes of luxury and riches. They were of the opinion that there was a happy medium, and that was what they were going to bring about, by first of all tackling the land question. (Applause.)

div.head: DENOUNCING A SYSTEM; NOT A
div.p: DENOUNCING A SYSTEM; NOT A
CLASS.

Mr. BLEASE said they were there to talk about land and not landlords. They were denouncing a system and not people. They were not want- ing to call people robbers and grinders of the face of the poor, but to criticise the system which enabled a selfish landlord to act in a tyrannical and unjust way to the people work- ing on his land. They wanted to criticise, land , because it was a natural monopoly. If a man needed a certain piece of land in a particular part of the town, the landlord could demand his own price for it, for he knew that the prospective purchaser must have that particular piece of land for a particular pur- pose. By their industry and enterprise the people had created the value of land, and put streams of money in the pockets of the land- lords. That monopoly nature of land gave money to the landowners in an—well, not im- moral—unfair way. Other injustices would be swept away. The landowner would not have to discuss as a landlord, but as an employer, with the. farmers on his estate. In NorthamPtuu- shire, Lord Lilford had said that no labourer on his estate should join an agricultural trade union. About 20 labourers contended that they were free men in a free country, and had a right to protect their interests. Lord Lilford said, "Out of my cottages you go," and a County Court judge had held that the notices were valid. Those men were turned out. Liberals, as a party, said that no man should have that power to turn a man out of his home just be- cause he did not satisfy a whim or a caprice of the landlord, or for reasons that had no con- nection with the man's tenancy. (Hear, hear.) ' such iniquities would be swept away by the Liberal land proposals, and the people of the country would be free to live and express their own opinions. (Applause.)

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD AND NARROWING
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD AND NARROWING
TIIE CLASS GULF.

Mr. CROSFIELD said that in days gone by the old chieftain, Mr. Gladstone, had to fight t great battle of emancipation. (Bear, h e hear.) They were now approaching the completion of that battle. Reference had been made to the abolition of plural voting; that was part of the work that brought them near the completion of that gospel of emancipation preached and fought for so splendidly by Bright, Cobden and Gladstone. Now they were in the thick of constructive work, which was full of hope for everyone who believed in the future of human- ity at large. By graduated taxation and quali- fied individualism they were gradually narrow- ing the gulf between the two extremes in this country—great affluence and extreme poverty. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: CLASS LEGISLATION UNDESIRABLE.
div.p: CLASS LEGISLATION UNDESIRABLE.

The question of land reform was also part of that great constructive work, and he might say that if they had failed in the past to accomplish the reforms they desired it was largely due to the fact that they had been faced with landlord Parliaments. Perhaps if they had had Parlia- ments of employers Of labour or manned by the modern syndicalist, they, too, would have been biased in favour of their own particular class, and it was not a healthy thing for one section of the community to have a free hand in man- aging things for the benefit only of their own class. They said it was not fair for the owner of the soil calmly to confiscate the improvements of industrious men. It was not fair, but abso- lutely indefensible. They were now in a posi- tion to accomplish remedies, cwing largely to the passing of the Parliament Act. If they studied the land reform they would find that the case was so strong that it would carry in support of it every Progressive, Radical, Liberal, Socialist, or any section of the community.

div.head: PEOPLE'S BATTLE.
div.p: THE PEOPLE'S BATTLE.

- -- - -- - In the matter of land reform they were fight- ing the people's battle just as surely as they had fought their battle in making a reality of graduated taxation. Just as in the great Insur- ance scheme, in the Old-Age Pensions Act, and the multitude of other things they had done, they were not going on the old principle of an Open field, and no favour and Devil take the him:lmost. They were going on the principle so significantly and strikingly illustrated in the principle of the minimum wage, that where people were not strong enough theriselves or collectively they should be helped by He had never argued from any Warrington Platform that where they had strong trade 7t he. State. unions i the State should step in and inter- fere with the rate of wages which those n the trade unions had arrived at by their collective bargaining, and the result of their negotiations with the employers of labour. He would say that there were great masses of workers who f , so powerful and so beneficent in were not strong enough to keep their end up, and the Government had done, and would still further look after them. (Applause.) The work done by the Liberal party had been so far-reaching, its effect that already they had begun to lift III) the general level of comfort and well-being of many of the people in the country. They were, however, only at the beginning of the journey, and Progressives had a long way to travel yet.

div.head: HOPE OF THE FUTURE.
div.p: THE HOPE OF THE FUTURE.

- - - -•- - Be that as it might let them never minimise the work that had been done in those very memorable years. There were great periods in English history—the times of the Magna Charta, the Charleses, Oliver Cromwell, of the inven- tions of printing and steam—epochs when the country made important steps forward in poli- tical and industrial advantages, but he felt certain that when the future historian came to chronicle the events he would not find the last eight years, and the memorable work accom- plished- in that period, the least full of signifi- cance an the race. (Cheers.) d hopefulness for the whole future of

div.head: LAND -NATIONALISATION TOO
div.p: LAND -NATIONALISATION TOO
DIFFICULT.

A questioner asked if Mr. Blease thought that the land reform scheme, as advocated by the Liberal party, would be of more benefit to the country than the nationalisation of land? Mr. BLEASE said he thought the Liberal pro- posals were easier of execution than nationalis- ing the land, which meant the expenditure of an enormous sum of money. They were aiming at modifying the existing system. He was in ,favour of the nationalisation of land, but if they could not get a majority to agree upon it they had to do, as the Liberal party were doing, the best they could. (Applause.) Mr. SANDERS, proposing a hearty vote of thanks to the speakers, said the Liberal party had al- ways got a programme. They would knock Mr. Smith out at the next election, and he would have to find fresh lodgings. (Laughter.) They should return Mr. Crosfield, who was not only a Liberal, but an advanced Liberal. (Ap- plause.)

div.head: MRS. CROSFIELD SPEAKS OF THE DISGRACE OF OVERCROWDING.
div.p: MRS. CROSFIELD SPEAKS OF THE DISGRACE OF OVERCROWDING.
Support the Government,

The great land question has a particular interest for women, as many of the defects of the present system directly affect the home, and in order to put the points of the proposals before the ladies, a special meeting was held for them in the Co-operative Hall on Thursday afternoon. Mrs. Crosfield presided, and there were present Mr. A. 11. Crosfield, Mr. J. S. Devine (the speaker), Mrs. Osborne, and Miss Booth. MRS. CROSFIELD AND THE ATTACK UPON SLUMS.

Mrs. Caosiann was heartily cheered on rising to open the proceedings. She said the land question was even more important to women than to men. The healthy condition of the home, the need for plenty of air space, the desire to have a little garden in which the children could play, were essentially women's questions. That was why she hoped that when the Government put its proposals before the House of Commons, and before the nation, they would back the Government up for all they were worth. (Applause.) The proposals were so many and varied that she would only touch upon some of the most important. One was that for raising the wages of the agricultural labourer and fixing a minimum wage for him. At present in England agricultural labourers were badly paid, 60 per cent. of them only get- ting 18s. per week or less. No man could live decently, keep his family in comfort, pay a rent for a nice sanitary house, and buy food and clothing on such a wage. (Hear, hear.) The result was that it did not pay landlords to build decent cottages, and -so a large number of the people were living in habitations not fit for human beings. The Liberal party were going to give the agricultural labourer a minimum wage. Some people said it was not the business of Parliament to meddle with wages, but the Liberal Government had " meddled"; they had fixed a minimum wage in some trades, and were going to do more. (Hear, hear.) The Liberal party intended that the labourers should have decent wages, and that they should get decent housing accommodation. There were 2,000,000 people living in slums to-day. At the last census it was shown that one-tenth of the popu- lation of England and Wales were living under conditions of overcrowding—that was to say, , more than two people were living in every room, Which was a shameful state of affairs for ' England. It meant that there were homes which were not homes, and houses in which it was not fit to live. It did not need much imagination to picture what misery, degradation and dirt existed in those houses. She was sorry to say that slums were not unknown in Warrington, although she thought there was less overcrowding here than in other places such as London. One day during the Whitsuntide holi- days there was not much sunshine and people were depressed. Could they imagine what it must be like to live in dark alleys and streets where the people never got a single ray of sun, where houses were damp, dismal and miserable, where children could not go out in the fields to gather flowers, or even play in open spaces? It _ _

was terrible that in thousands of cases they had the aged man and the feeble grandmother living together with the mother and the new-born babe. She was glad to see the Government pro- posals were directed against such evils as slums. One of the ways in which they would deal with the question was by making land cheaper. That was one of the most important proposals the Government was going to make.
That was where the solution of the land ques- tion would have very great effect.

In the past manY, -Commissions had saf to deal with the land, but not until the recent in- quiry had evidence been taken from any class except the wealthy people and landowners. The recent land inquiry was objected to because it was secret, but could they have got the great mass of information by other means?

One prominent fact brought out by that in- quiry was the awful conditions that prevailed in the rural districts—bad housing, bad health. That was due to the fact that wages were low. An average was 15s. per week. Deduct 2s. for a cottage, 2s. for clothes, and they would find that an agricultural labourer could not feed on a basis which was given to the beasts in the field. Bad feeding, bad housing drove the people into the towns and into the colonies, with the result that the feeble were left behind. Lord Roberts‘was carrying on a campaign to improve the national physique, but he began at the wrong end. The only way was to improve the conditions of the land workers, and they would be able as a nation to defy the assembled world in arms. (Applause.)

div.head: WHY THE LAND SYSTEM IS UNJUST.
div.p: WHY THE LAND SYSTEM IS UNJUST.

There was no greater obstacle to the improve- ment of houses than the high prices that were demanded for land. Land was required every (lay for housing accommodation, street widen- ing, institutions such as hospitals and schools. As soon as it was known that a public authority required land the owner immediately put a prohibitive price upon it. Such unjust demands were checking public improvements and the industry of the people. Why was the land sys- tem so unjust? Simply because it was made by the landlord and was consequently one-sided and unfair. The landlord paid practically nothing in rates for the land. It was rated really at prairie value, but if he sold it it was at a price that would pave it with gold and silver. (Hear, hear.) The landlord should be forced to contribute something to the rates. In future the price of land would be fixed by the County or Town Councils, and it was hoped in that way more land would be brought in the market at a cheaper price.

div.head: MODEL VILLAGES.
div.p: MODEL VILLAGES.

There would be a town planning scheme, which meant plenty of decent houses, places where the children could play, streets made wide, houses airy, comfortable, and built according to sani- tary conditions, and there would be none of the overcrowding, darkness and misery of the slums. She had this week seen an instance of town planning by a private individual at Port Sun- light, where Sir-William Lever had carried out a great scheme for his workers. It was a beautiful little village, the houses were pictures in themselves, each having its garden, three rooms and a bathroom. But she must not tell them any more about Sir Wiriiam Lever's vil- lage, because they in Warrington would want a " Perfection" village, like that at Port Sun- light. (Laughter.) If the Government could get land cheaper and more of it into the market, villages would be planned on such lines. That was only part of a great scheme that touched the lives of the men, women and, children in such a direct way. The scheme was put for- ward by men who had set themselves out to better the conditions of the workers; and she hoped that the Liberal women of Warrington, who were so deeply interested in the matter, would see that the Government were properly backed up in their fight for liberty, equality and the improvement of the general conditions of the people. (Cheers.) -

div.head: TO EQUALISE THE DISTRIBUTION OF WEALTH..
div.p: TO EQUALISE THE DISTRIBUTION OF WEALTH..

Mr. DEVINE, the speaker, said there was no question which was purely a man or woman's question, but one that interested both of them. This land question was ode for both sexes. They were told that government was to be made impossible. Was that to be the effect in free England? They were told of former Liberal Governments that were in power, but a Liberal Government was never in power in the history of the country until the passing of the Parlia- mentary Act. It was not perfect, but would be amended, and one amendment would be to make a perfect House of Lords, whith would be per- fectly neutral to both parties. (Hear, hear.) There had been some Bills before them which they looked upon as very old friends—Welsh Disestablishment and Home Rule. Taking the , case of the Church in Wales, he said if that ' Church showed that by being established and endowed it forwarded the cause of religion, they would have let her stay. Did she forward the cause of religion? The Church in Ireland, which had points in common with the Church in Wales—the Church of the minority and aris- tocracy—had been disestablished, and before that event took place 200,000 Orangemen sealed their hearts' blood to die in the last—not first —ditch. When the Church was disestablished, where were the 200,000 Orange martyrs? They were not to be found, and the Irish Church was disestablished. Possibly the same thing would happen in connection with‘the present threats in Ulster. The Church had risen after disestab- Bailment to become a real power in the land, which it was not before, and so would it happen in connection with the Church in Wales.

div.head: WEALTH AND POVERTY CONTRASTS.
div.p: WEALTH AND POVERTY CONTRASTS.

The land question was the great question now before the people. This was a year of an enor- mous Budget, and yet in a year of a 200 million Budget they found ill was not well with the country. There was an immense wealth in the ship of State, but the cargo had got shifted—a danger to the State—and the wealth was found in one place. They had great wealth in one part of the State, and great poverty in the other, and now the time had come to equalise matters.

div.head: PROTESTANT AND HOME RULE
div.p: PROTESTANT AND HOME RULE

Home Rule, they were told by Unionists, was never debated. What had they been doing for 30 years? They were told that the Catholics oppressed Protestants. As a Protestant he had lived in one of the most Catholic counties, and had received nothing but kindness from the Catholics. In his home they never ate fish on 1 Friday, but in an Orange family near at hand they always fried steak and onions on that day, and half the parish smelt it. (Laughter.) They were told that when Home Rule came the Orangemen were to set up a provisional Government, and the first thing they would do was to refuse to pay the income tax. Doubtless many Orangemen would be glad to do that. (Laughter.) There was talk about shooting, but if the Ulstermen shot down innocent people it would be the duty of the nation to protect these people. He was told that the provisional Government had set up Courts, and amongst them was a Bankruptcy Court. That Court would do good business if the Ulstermen tried to fight the British Empire. (llear, hear.) The Orangemen said they loved England with an undying love, and would not be parted from her. They also said the 80 Nationalist Members hated England, and that the Liberal party was absolutely controlled by the Irish party. It was true, except where there was a large major- ity, the Irish party held the balance of power, , but had they ever sought to damage England or stop Acts for her benefit?

_ If the Ulstermen loved England with an un- dying love why should they not try to keep the Irish party in Ireland, where they could do little damage and keep them out of beloved England, where they " might" do a lot of damage? (Laughter.) Home Rule would help the Ulstermen to save England, but they still wanted, despite their undying love for England, to keep the Irish Nationalists there. (Laughter and applause.)

div.head: WOMAN'S INTEREST.
div.p: WOMAN'S INTEREST.
Concrete Examples of How Towns Are
Plundered.
OVER 1,000 YEARS' PURCHASE.

Mr. A. H. Caosnun, who was cordially re- ceived, jocularly remarked that he did not know whether to begin with "Mr. Chairman or Madame Chairman." Reference had been made to a minimum wage for agricultural labourers. If such a wage was an important thing for the labourers it was still more important to the women of the country, because it was the first guarantee that the people were to have decent housing accommodation in country districts. It was calculated that in the agricultural dis- tricts alone there was a shortage of 120,000 cot- tages, and if they reckoned five to a family they had 600,000 persons who were living in cottages which really were little better than hovels, houses thoroughly insanitary, and very bad from every point of view. (Hear, hear.) Give a labourer a minimum wage and he could afford to pay a decent rent for his cottage; and that would encourage people to build good houses. The Government was going to see to it that the shortage of cottage accommodation was ended, and that, either directly through the Government, or by action taken through the local authorities, decent cottages would be built. He could not imagine anything—not even Free Trade—which must appeal so forcibly or vitally to women as this great question. They could not have health in such hovels as many people had to live in; it was in these places they got the plague of tuberculosis, and all sorts of disease were produced by these insanitary dwel- lings. By getting the reform carried they would get healthy homes, get rid of the dis- eases, and have healthy and thriving families. After all, it was the women who were .most concerned with the homes, and the health of the families, and so he put to them as women that this vast undertaking of the Govern ment Woman's was in a very special degree a ques- tion. (Applause.)

WOMEN'S REFORM. It was not the first time he had had to point out that the Government's work during the past few years had been of special interest to the women, and had been in a special degree a women's question and therefore women must assist in the social reforms upon which the Government was at present engaged. At first it might appear as if it was for the men, but it was of vital interest to the women, and there- fore they, as Liberals, felt they had a perfect right to think that, given a good backing by the women, they would be in an infinitely stronger position, and now they asked the women to give them that backing. (Hear, hear.) The Government's case was very strong, and he thought it should have the special and vig- orous and enthusiastic support of all. He could not imagine how any of their Conserva- tive or Tory friends could make out a case against it; he thought they were in a very strong position when they could appeal not only to Liberals and Radicals, but to Conservative friends to come out and, in their own interest, take up the reform for which the Liberal Gov- ernment was working. (Applause.) They were not workers only for the benefit of _Liberals, Radicals and Socialists, but for the Tory work- ing men, for the Conservative middle-class voter who benefited as much as the Liberal and Radical and Socialist. Everybody would stand to benefit immensely for that great and magpi- ficent reform, and soon all would be asking themselves why on earth the reform was not brought in before. (Hear, hear.) To illustrate one of the grossest pieces of injustice under the present land laws, he might say that land was now rated at one value for one purpose and another value for other pur- poses. He would give some illustrations of that mysterious position. If land was required by a local authority it became rated at an infinitely higher price,than formerly. Hastings Corpora- tion had to buy land which was rated at £3 per acre. The price was £2,000, which worked out at 6,677 years' purchase. A 25 years' pur- chase was a fair price. Birmingham wanted land for a school site and paid £4,750 for 10,000 square yards, or 1,020 years' purchase of the rateable value. Sheffield Corporation required land for a housing scheme, and the area required was just under two acres and rated at £3 10s., and that was in respect of an advertising hoard- ing, as the land was then vacant. The price was £5,993, and therefore the number of years' purchase was 1,712. The consequence of paying an absolutely ex- orbitant price was simply to place a higher burden upon the ratepayers—he did not know who thought more about the question of rates than the women—but now the Government were going to take steps that wherever land was wanted for building schools or to put baths upon or used for any public purpose, if there was any

div.head: tettrrs to the (Etritor
div.p: tettrrs to the (Etritor

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. TEE EDITou of "The Examiner" invites corre- spondence on all subjects of public interest. LETTERS should be brief and pointed. Their object must be to impart or seek information. not abuse. Lamas must in all cases be accompanied by the name and address of the writer, CommuNwArroNs received early in the week— except urgent matters—can always be given the best attention.

div.head: PERAMBULATOR WANTED.
div.p: PERAMBULATOR WANTED.

Sir,—A perambulator is badly needed by a family which is being assisted by the Guild of Help. If one of your readers has a baby car- riage which he requires no longer I should be thankful for such a gift. The family wanting it is large in numbers and young in years, and there is a good deal of sickness in the home, one child being perman- ently crippled. The father is in steady work, but his wages are insufficient to meet his present heavy claims. Convalescent treatment would also be a boon. I should be glad to give fuller particulars to anyone who would care to help such a family financially. WILPRID J. ROWLAND. Guild of Help, Winmarleigh Chambers, June 4th, 1914.

div.head: GUILD OF HELP INQUIRY CARDS.
div.p: GUILD OF HELP INQUIRY CARDS.

Sir,—l fancy many of your readers are not aware that very useful inquiry post cards are supplied by Mr. Rowland, secretary of the Guild of Help, Winmarleigh Chambers, Spring- field-street, Warrington. They are in two parts, one of which is given to the applicant, the other is posted to Mr. Rowland, so that an exact record of them can be kept. This has the effect of greatly diminishing fraudulent applications for help, while those who are really in need of help, encouragement or advice, will be assisted by the voluntary workers of the Guild, and by friends who are prepared to act as standbys.- Mi. Rowland will gladly supply cards to anyone, whether a subscriber to the Guild of Help or not. Personally I have found these cards to be a great boon, and I think they alone justify the existence of the Guild, apart from the other good work it has accomplished. CONSTANCE H. BROADBENT. Latchford, May 29th, 1914.

div.head: SOCIAL TEACHING OF THE BIBLE.
div.p: SOCIAL TEACHING OF THE BIBLE.

Sir,—Returning to Mr. Parker's letter in your last issue on this subject, we agree that the Bible speaks with no uncertain voice on pro- blems affecting the social well-being of the people, but the difficulty is how far can the Methodist Church go in working for social as well as the spiritual salvation of men? Shall we, forinstance, be justified in going to men and saying: 'lt really does not matter whether you believe or not what we have to say about the soul. We are at one in the struggle for exist- ence, so come along with us and we will do you good"? Our point is this: We are hopelessly at variance as to the right remedies for these ills. While prohibition appears to be the watchword of some, the free man in the free State is the ideal for others. If the social service Mr. Par- ker speaks of means the stretching out of help- ing hands to the aged, weak and unfortunate, and if the Methodist Church, or any other of the Churches for the matter of that, could work together over given areas, we agree that it would be a very happy thing; but if, on the other hand, it means that we are meekly to acquiesce and support any and every proposal submitted by a somewhat embarrassed legislature under this heading, then we say that it cannot be done, and those that leave us thinking we are out of touch with things as they are will have to leave us, that's all. They will never shake off our influence, however 1 LATCHFORD WESLEYAN.

div.head: CHILDREN AND THE CINEMA.
div.p: CHILDREN AND THE CINEMA.

Sir,—l read in your paper a little while ago recommendations of the Education Authority with reference to cinema houses and the attend- ance of children at the same, particularly with regard to the eyesight question, and it will pro- bably interest your readers to read the expres- sion of opinion of Dr. Harlan, medical inspector of the State of Maryland. Dr. Harlan said attendance two hours daily at a cinema show was recommended as the best means to strengthen the eyesight. He declared that his researches had sho,nn him that eye affections of all kinds had diminished in all American cities in the ratio to the number of picture palaces they possessed. The rapid succession of differ- ent projections on the screen, it was pointed out, imposed on the organs of the sight a series of slight variations in focussing, which produced a marked benefit on the retina. Further, the changes in optical adjustment acted as a perfect form of massage on the pupils of the eyes, which imparted to them a healthy brilliance and mobility. I notice one usually well posted member of the Education Committee said children were not allowedtln Liverpool cinemas after 4.30. This is incorrect; the time is 6.30.

The family is a numerous one, and one generation follows an- other so rapidly that a slight attack soon de- velops .into a big and troublesome one, unless prompt measures are taken. Plants affected in the.open should be forcibly syringed with clean water one day and sprayed the next with soapy water or quassia mixture. Repeat the doses until the plants are clean. Carrot fly may be kept in check by frequent dustings of soot, or water between the rows with gas liquor diluted with six times its bulk of water. Chrysanthemum rust usually appears towards the end of summer. Spraying with sulphide of potassium—half an ounce in one gallon of water —is an excellent preventive as well as a cure.

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.
MAY RAINS AND FROSTS.

The rains of a week ago were not so effective ' as was expected, says "The Times." Rain fell in almost every county, but in very unequal quantities, and only where the thunderstorms were most severe was there enough to have any lasting effect. The frosts that followed were as widespread as the rains, and in general effect they more than discounted them. The whole country south of the Tyne appears to have been visited. Vegetation of all kinds was checked more or less severely, but the injury can be partially repaired, although the process may mean a later or a lighter harvest. Correspon- dents appear to be most concerned about the effect upon the meadows and pastures. The grass areas are in an extremely unsatisfactory state in the southern, eastern, and Midland counties as far north as the Mersey.

A Moderate Hay Harvest.. June brings .with it the first of the great harvests of the farm. The cutting and making of hay begins early in the month—this year a start was made last week—in the southern and eastern counties with the sainfoin, clovers and mixed seeds, followed in July by the meadows, the latest of which often overlap into the cereal harvest. The aggregate expanse of rotation and permanent hay is greater than that devoted to all three cereals, and the total value of the pro- duce is about equal to that of wheat, barley, and oats combined, exclusive of the straw. Prospects for the approaching harvest are only moderate. The crops that will average better than one and a half tons to the acre will be few.

The meadows had a disappointing appearance in the middle of May, but they benefited con- siderably in some parts by the rains of last week. The result, however, would have been more pronounced had the downpours been fol- lowed by the high temperatures and suo3hine that preceded them.

div.head: COOLING SUMMER MILK. . _ _ _
div.p: COOLING SUMMER MILK. . _ _ _

I am inclined to believe that thoroughness in cooling stands next to cleanliness in the man- agement of milk. Where clean milk is well cooled it will keep in all weathers long enough for all practical purposes. Where milk is un- clean, containing a large number of micro- organisms, it will keep much better if well cooled than cleaner milk badly cooled. The reason is that in badly cooled milk the bacteria increase with enormous rapidity, especially in warm summer weather. Thus effective cooling keeps the bacteria down. Cleanliness, however, can be controlled, but not refrigeration where the water supply is imperfect, and this leads one to suggest the importance of providing for sum- mer work by one of two means—the provision of ice or a cooling plant, where there is power on the farm, or the co-operative establishment of a plant near the station which eight or ten farmers could run with profit to themselves. Milk cooled to 40 deg. or 45 deg. in hot weather is worth a great deal to the trade, where, as sometimes happens, prices rise to half a crown a gallon. In hot summers milk is spoiled in abundance, and I have never once come across a really cold sample, but it can be done, and we are approaching the period. If the cows are milked in the fields during the summer months the milk will be infinitely cleaner than if milked in the foul atmosphere of the cowhouse, which, judged by what a ray of sunlight reveals, reeks with dust and germ life. In the Yorkshire investigation the one good sample of milk among hundreds, containing only 5,000 bacteria per cubic centimeter, was drawn in the open air, while others contained up to a million.--James Long, in "Farm and Home."

div.head: FORMALIN AND THE WART DISEASE OF
div.p: FORMALIN AND THE WART DISEASE OF
POTATOES.

The Board of Agriculture has received a com- munication from Professor Eriksson, of the Central Botanic 'Experimental Station, Stock- holm, relative to a successful experiment in killing the contagious matter in soil infected with wart disease of potatoes. The Professor wishes to bring the method adopted by him to the notice of potato growers, especially in Eng- land. He experimented by treating the soil with a solution of formalin, and he found that soil intentionally infected would then produce clean tubers, while soil not so treated produced tubers more or less infected with the disease. In his opinion, it has been proved by his experi- ment that a dilute solution of formalin, 1 to 100, is capable of killing the infective matter in soil contaminated with the disease, and he proposes that experiments should be arranged in England to test the remedy.

div.head: SYMPTOMS OF FITS" IN PIGS.
div.p: SYMPTOMS OF FITS" IN PIGS.

The pigs, perhaps, look at first to be doing exceptionally well, then one will come up to the trough, put his head down to eat, and fall over on his side struggling convulsively and frothing at the mouth, until he becomes quite insensible. In a few minutes he will get up, looking very dazed and stupid, and go away and lie down in the darkest corner of the stye. One after an- other a whole farrow may be affected, until the owner begins to think it is something "catch- ing"; but this is not so, and the fact of more than one being affected is due simply to the same system of feeding and management being applied to all. I have seen three pigs in a small farrow all kicking and struggling on the ground at once. If no relief is afforded by altered feed- ing and treatment the fits increase in frequencY and intensity until the animals die, while in all cases it causes a check in their growth and development, and time has been lost instead of gained by the over-feeding. When worms are the cause of convulsions they must be expelled; in fact, all treatment must have removal of the cause for its initial step. Change the food to something light and easy of digestion, and do not give too much of anything. Turn the pigs out to exercise, and allow small coal, charcoal or cinders. Turves of grass, with the earth ad- hexing, should be thrown into the stye. When they are in a fit throw cold water on the head, and give an injection of warm soapy water. A full dose of castor oil or Epsom salts should be given, and the bowels kept open by the use of laxatives. Later on it may be useful to give small doses of sulphate of iron in the food, which should be gradually increased in quantity. A run in the orchard or grass plot, or even by the roadside if nothing else is available, is very useful in these cases. Prevention, however, is best, and this is only to be attained by judicious feeding from the beginning.—" Veteran," in "Farm and Home."

div.head: IN THE GARDEN.
div.p: IN THE GARDEN.

As potatoes push through the soil draw a little dry soil over the growths, as previously advised, as night frosts often do some injury at this period of the year. Keep ferns moist from the time the fronds begin to grow until the end of the summer Lime and soot dusted around the young shoots of rambler roses will keep away slugs. Gladioli coming through the soil may also be dusted with soot and lime. Feed carnations, pinks and violas with guano. German irises throwing up their spikes will be improved by a little guano around the roots.
Sow peas and runner beans. Earth up peas. Thin all vegetable. crops needing it.

Sow seeds of wallflowers, forget-me-not, carna- tions, aubretias, pansies, primroses, polyan- thuses and most perennials in a shady spot. Make the soil as fine as possible, and if an inch or more of potting soil can be placed on top, the seeds will germinate quickly. Keep the soil moist. _

Sow seeds of hollyhocks to produce plants for flowering next year. In due course pick off the seedlings and later plant them in their flowering quarters. Many pleasing colours may be raised, and plants raised from seed are not so liable to the fungus.

div.head: GARDEN PESTS.
div.p: GARDEN PESTS.

The various destructive insects which do so much damage to our flowers and vegetable crops are beginning to appear, and if not timely checked will eventually get the upper hand and spoil everything. If the plants are treated in time their depredations can be greatly mini- mised, but once they get a good hold of plants. it is a difficult matter to bring the plants back to a clean and healthy condition. Just as a stitch in time saves nine, so does a canful or so of insecticide used early save dozens later on. Rose growers have two pests to contend with, the greenfly and the maggot. Syringing the trees with a strong solution of soft soap or quassia are good remedies for greenfly, but no amount of syringing touches the maggot, which is curled

As the seasons succeed each other (says a writer in "Farm and Home") it is necessary for the poultry keeper to make some alteration, though it may be but slight, in the food that he is feeding to his stos,k birds. As the warmer weather advances thebest results in the way of egg-production, from the point of view of the strength of the germs contained in the fertile eggs, can only be attained by so adapting the diet to the special needs of the body.

div.head: TWO CLASSES OF STOCK BIROS.
div.p: TWO CLASSES OF STOCK BIROS.

When the object of hatching is to produce birds that are to be reared to maturity for lay- ing purposes, it is advisable to use only hens in their second season, since the eggs coming from these fully-matured fowls are more likely to produce much stronger chickens than if pullets are used. On the other hand, if the eggs are to be used for the production of killing birds, there is no reason why pullets' eggs should employed. Pullets lay earlier a larger number of eggs than do two-year- olds, lu though the germs are never quite so ni a d vigorous, and do not possess the same degree of vitality. This classification must be taken into consideration when we come to deal with the question of feeding. It is possible in the latter case to feed a rather more forcing food than would be suitable under the conditions govern- ing the former. Again, the pullets will have been laying for some mouths, if a a winter. laying breed, and this point must also be taken into account.

div.head: FEEDING FOR STOCK CHICKENS.
div.p: FEEDING FOR STOCK CHICKENS.

Breeders will do well to be content with a smaller number of eggs from each hen when their object is to produce good, sound stock birds in the future. To force feed such stock means that the germs in the eggs will be weak- ened at the outset, and this will consequently have a great influence on the quality of the chickens raised. A smaller number of high vitality birds is preferable to a larger number of fowls having poor stamina and unsound con- stitutions. In making up the diet for our stock we should select those foods that have a large percentage of digestible constituents, but which are not stimulating. We must perforce give the elements required by the body in their correct proportions, but on no account should forcing feeding stuffs be employed.

div.head: ablirdi 0615,
div.p: ablirdi 0615,
WHITSUNTIDE SERVICE.

Whitsuntide was celebrated at the Warring- ton Parish Church on Sunday by means of ser- vices at once joyous and impressive. The choral celebration of the Holy Communion, which was beautifully rendered by thb choir, consisted of the music by Sir, George Martin and Berthold Tours. "Lovely appear," from Gounod's "Redemption," was sung at the even- song, Mr. F. M. Darby accompanying expres- sively. A large quantity of flowers decorated the church for the occasion.

div.head: WYCLIFFE P.S.A.
div.p: WYCLIFFE P.S.A.

The meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society held on Sunday was presided over by the Rev. T. T. James, when Mr. William Beswick gave an address upon "Whitsuntide Thoughts." The speaker referred to.the work of the _Spirit with the descent of the Holy Ghost, and the influence He had exerted over men in all ages. To this influence of the Spirit we owe a great debt. Special hymns and prayers were offered for the victims in the recent St. Lawrence disaster, Miss Eva Tanner appropriately rendering "Nearer, my God, to Thee," and "Lead, kindly light." Mr. Payton presided at the organ. Mr. B. Farrar, the secretary, announced that the Rev. J. G. Gascoigne, of Manchester, would address the National Campaign meeting, to be held in the Wycliffe Memorial Hall on June 11.

div.head: ELMWOOD-AVENUE CHURCH.
div.p: ELMWOOD-AVENUE CHURCH.
Appointment of New Congregational Pastor.

Mr. C. P. Pitt has accepted an invitation for- warded to him a fortnight ago to become the assistant minister at Wycliffe Congregational Church, Warrington, with particular supervi- sion of the work at Elmwood-avenue Church, the new branch opened last September and situated in the growing neighbourhood of Pad- gate-lane. _ . .

Mr. Pitt has been trained for the ministry at the Lancashire Independent College, Manches- ter, where he has had a very successful course. He is a Bachelor of Arts of the University of Manchester,. having taken his degree in 1913. He will commence his work in Warrington on Sunday, August 23rd. It is confidently anticipated that the work at the new branch church will prosper under his ministry.

div.head: RELIGIOUS ATMOSPHERE.
div.p: RELIGIOUS ATMOSPHERE.
The Rev. 11. Ogden_ on Whilsun and
National Morals.

The Rev. 11. Ogden preached at the Golborne- street Baptist Church on Sunday evening upon the subject " Whit-Sunday : Its Relation to National Morals," basing his remarks upon the text, Acts ii. 2: "And suddenly there came a sound from Heaven as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled all the house where they were sit- ting." The preacher said there are moments in the life of every religious man—certainly weak moments, but none the less they come—when he pines for a visible manifestation of the Deity. In the Acts of the Apostles we read that the Holy Spirit appeared as cloven tongues. That night they were not concerned with the phenomenon, whether visible tut invisible. But were it a visible phenomeflofl lii our Weak moments, we pine for its repetition. What a revelation to some gaping crowd, struck dumb with awe and fear, if the actual Spirit could be seen by them! What a triumph over those who tell us that religion is a pious hallucination, and that all religious efforts are as "love's labour lost " ! But no such experience as a visible spirit, descending as a dove, or as cloven tongues like as of fire, is felt to-day. If man could only be converted by outward display; there will never be any inward reality. And yet contact with the Holy Spirit of God is real and certain, and has a definite effect 'upon the life of a man or woman, and leads them to develop a deep concern for national well-being. The Spirit is as a mighty wind, and fills all the house where men are sitting. It creates an atmosphere in which the good and the pure can thrive. Physical atmosphere is a matter of the deepest concern to health authorities and education boards. One has but to follow a ruddy-faced boy to some unhealthy Occupation to discover the necessity for health vigilance. The ruddy boy in two decades, and probably less, becomes wan and attenuated, and is being expeditiously prepared for the grave by unhealthy occupation. The girl, who might have been one of the beauties of her day, is robbed of one of Nature's choicest gifts by labouring in polluted atmosphere. Atmosphere means either life or death. Ten years ago "Religious atmosphere" was one of the terms of hot debate. Anglicans have striven for, and have financed schemes to keep their religious atmosphere. Even a writer in the `)Baptist Times" suggests that Baptists should build and endow day schools to ensure a Baptist atmos- phere.
A Miracle Involved.

What an effect upon English life would be ' wrought; what a miracle would be accomplished in the moral realm, if a tithe of the nation were conscious of a living, real fellowship with God! It would affect all branches of our life. Henry Ward Beecher, in his lectures to young men— and one would suggest to those who are troubled with the problem of adolescence to place this book in the hands of young men—sketches for us a suburban garden. The fruit trees within it are full and ripe: the hedges and palings are neatly trimmed and tended. Some vandal tears down the hedges, and helps himself to the fruit. All the country is scoured to find the culprit, and when found all the resources of the law are employed to convict. And yet, says Henry Ward Beecher, the choicest fences are torn down, the richest fruit is pillaged, and there is hardly a protest. Men, for their own gain, are permitted to raid our Sunday schools, and to place in the way of our young dangerous temPtations; and it is permitted almost unchallenged. There is no surer way for a man to learn that lie is his brother's keeper than by the Spirit of God. If his life is filled with the Spirit which is like the wind, he will crowd his life not merely with good thoughts, but with noble deeds. Not only is the Holy Spirit as the wind, but, like all pure atmosphere, it quickens into life and power. The garden in winter is a grave- yard of buried roots. One would hardly dream that beneath its grey surface there is such a mass of insipient life. Springtime, and the action of the sun, makes the wilderness to blos- som as a rose. The whole concealed life is revealed, and Spring moves over the surface of the earth with a magician's wand. And that is how the Spirit acts on the souls of men. There are moments when the crowd is gayest, when a thinking man is saddest. There are times when the crowd is full of mirth, and yet it is most like winter. There is no soul in all the mirth and laughter and gaiety; and one wonders if the crowd has a soul. Beneath the crust of human life, and beyond the reach of man's eyes, in every man and in every woman there is soul; and it but needs the action of God's spirit upon it, and the wilderness will blossom as the rose, and speedily, answer the perpetual questions about the life we now live, and solve the national problems that are our deepest concern.

Infantile Mortality. Recently a circular was issued by our local Guild of Help. The worthy Secretary and his colleagues, naturally alarmed that the infantile death-rate of our town was so high, sent out a circular asking ministers and all interested in social welfare to answer certain questions: how to rectify maternal carelessness, how to avoid malnutrition, how to guarantee cleanliness for a baby. These are the types of questions that concern all who love our nation; and yet one felt convinced that their only permanent answer was to be found in the acknowledged sway of the Holy Spirit. Nobody is more anxious for the social uplifting in these days than the Church. Every man should have-the luxury of his own bathroom, and every cottager should have his strip of garden in which lie. can breathe; but there is no guarantee that if all that were to come to-morrow, we are not on the verge of a national disaster, unless there were some moral authority and some spiritual power which the people -would acknowledge. Whitsuntide has a real relation to national well-being, and may the day be hastened when all people shall give themselves time to reflect that there are greater powers than those we see with our eyes, and that there is a • mightier strength than that we can touch with our hands.

div.head: LATE MR. H. FERGUSON. Interment at the Warrington Cemetery.
div.p: THE LATE MR. H. FERGUSON. Interment at the Warrington Cemetery.

On Behalf of" Brother Ass." Ascetics have frequently referred to the body as "Brother Ass." They spoke of it as an en- cumbrance with a tendency to weigh down the soul and the higher emotions. Let us to our own selves be true, and acknowledge that bodily comforts are essential to happiness. Diet, of course, is an essential to health. Foods that nourish the body, and are easy of digestion, must at all times be chosen; and of those the most efficacious is the little Greek Currant. The highest medical testimony has been voluntarily given, with the object of inducing people to eat plenty of Currants. The late Sir Francis Laking, the physician of Kings, urged us to eat Currants, not on occasions, but daily. When arranging the meals for the day, let the first consideration be in what way Currants are to be used. For to-day, try this excellent recipe specially prepared by an eminent chef. CURRANT CARES.

lb. Currants, 1 lb. flour, 1 lb. castor sugar, teaspoonful bicarbonate of soda, 1 teaspoon- ful cream of tartar, 1 oz. candied peel, 4 lb. butter, 3 eggs, pinch of salt. Method: Sift the flour, soda and cream of tartar, also the salt. Cream the butter and sugar in a basin; when well beaten, add the eggs one at a time. Mix thoroughly, and lastly work in the fruit—the peel to be cut in fine shreds or chopped very small. If found too stiff add a little milk. Bake in a buttered cake tin, in square frame, or in round hoops, for about 40 minutes.

Quinine Useless for Colds. The old idea that quinine would cure a cold has been exploded. It used to be supposed that quinine checked fever; it is now known that the only fever it has any effect on is malaria. Colds are treated in many ways, but all depend upon one principle—that of opening up all the organs of elimination. Anything that will make the kidneys, bowels and lungs work and will open the pores of the skin and cause profuse perspiration is good for a cold. A hot bath, fol- lowed by a hot drink and rest under blankets, is the best and simplest of home treatment. Hot milk or hot lemonade is far better than hot whisky. There is no need to take an alco- holic drink, but if this must be taken gin is the least injurious, as it has a stimulating effect upon the kidneys. But a far better way to use alcohol is to rub it over the body immediately after the hot bath.

div.head: UNION JACK HYSTERICS.
div.p: UNION JACK HYSTERICS.
Adult School Lecture on Real Loyalty and Responsibility.

At Sankey Bridges Men's Class on Sunday morning Mr. George Shaw gave an. instructive lecturette on "Loyalty." Mr. Shaw said we were living in an age of institutions and societ- ies, the main of which was progress. It seemed to him, however, that there was more than an element of doubt as to whether we were making. headway. If we admitted we were not pro- gressing as rapidly as we ought, could we had the cause? At the base it would be found that want of loyalty to ideals was one great reason of so much failure: Defining loyalty, the speaker said that to many people "Empire Day" was an expression of its essence. This was a mistake. Whilst every man loved his country the idea underlying Empire Day was erroneous and mischievous. It gave children, in particu- lar, a bias which had evil consequences in after- life. The nation and national life were impor- tant, but deeper still, and of more vital importance, was the individual and individual life.

MORE IMPORTANT THAN FLAG-WAGGING Before a man can be, in a lasting sense, loyal to anything he must learn to be loyal to him- self. This was more difficult than flag-wagging or shouting, but of more importance to the race. The result of this loyalty would be a deepening of our sense of responsibility. Those who are periodically afflicted with Union Jack hysterics clo not always make the best type of citizen. True loyalty produces true comrade- ship and brotherhood, national and inter- national, and is based on intelligence and an appreciation of the good qualities of our fellows. A mere petty nationalism is too limited, and its outlook too narrow to produce any lasting loyalty between men and men, or nations and_ nations. When we have learned to be loyal to ourselves, said the lecturer, we begin to understand that our brethren in other countries are flesh of our flesh and bone of our bone. The same idea when applied to industry brings about a better state of things in our workshops, be- tween men and men, and between masters and men. When a man has learnt to be loyal to himself he will give of his best during his work- ing hours, and will try to produce his best under his limited conditions. Neither failure nor 'prosperity matters: the glory of life cornea not from what we do, but what we are.
The subject was well discussed from many points of view.
