div.head: TO A FINISH.
div.p: TO A FINISH.

Mr. LLOYD GEORGE, in a speech at Criccieth, on Tuesday, to the delegates of the Bristol Radical Operatives' Asso- ciation, made it clear that the Govern- ment have no intention of leaving unfinished the task they undertook when for the third time the Liberal policy received a vote of confidence at a General Election in December, 1910. "The Parliament Act was planted in British soil three years ago," Mr. LLOYD GEORGE said, "and we are not going to dissolve Parliament until we have gath- ered in the fruit that is ripening on that tree." The Parliament Act has rendered the veto of the House of Lords upon democratic legislation, while still a very unfair handicap, impotent for pur- poses of destruction against fixed resolve and long-continued effort. But the party of privileges and vested _interests still has a tremendous advan- tage in electoral conflicts through the extra votes given to property. Thc Plural V ote, some Tories have them- selvef. crlmputed, means about forty seats for the Tory party at a General Election. In by-elections the out-voter weights the electoral scales still more unfairly. From time to time the Tory party, by demanding a referendum, or, as Mr. BALFOUR would say, a poll of the

people, m which one man would have one vote and no more, has made the •admission that the plural vote is incom- patible with democratic institutions. But the Tory .party is now clamouring for an early General Election in order to prevent the Plural Voting Bill being passed under the Parliament Act. When the Tory party assert that there is no alternative in the Irish question—if Ulster is not to be abso- lutely excluded from Home Rule—but either a General Election or Civil War, they fall into an interminable morass of inconsistencies. Can the Tory Leaders switch Civil War off and on in
--- Ulster at their pleasure and their tactical convenience? If not, how would a General Election, in which the electors declared for the Home Rule . _

Bill, avert Civil War in Ulster? But are the Tories honestly alarmed at the prospect of Civil War? If they are, surely they should have made Home Rule; and not the Insurance Act, the dominant issue at every by-election in the last two years. Again, if the Tories were really -obsessed by a sense of horror at imminent Civil War, they would not, as they appear to have done, recently raised their demands to a claim for the exclusion of the whole of Ulster if amajorityvote for this could be obtained by a poll through the whole province. They know that the counties in which the Nationalist element enor- mously, almost exclusively, prevails, would, if anything, feel exclusion more keenly than the North-East counties would feel inclusion.

• Any Government which was willing or was obliged to submit to the dicta Hort of its opponents as to when it should dissolve, so long as it had a sub- stantial majority in the House of Com- mons, would be liable to lose the enthu- siasm of its followers in Parliament, and the support of its following in the country. Liberal Governments in the past have been impaled on the cruel dilemma of ploughing the legislative sands or of dissolving, owing to the power of the Lords' veto. At the cost of tremendous efforts and of two General Elections in one year, the pre- sent Government rescued the Liberal party from this dilemma. And now the Tories cannot understand why the Liberal Government does not behave as if the two General Elections of 1910 meant and had achieved nothing at all. The Government, they say, ought to dissolve at one. Why? Primarily, and for the most important reason, that the Tory Oovernment saystso. In the I

second place, because some seats have been lost at by-elections. No Govern- ment has ever been known not to shed some of its majority at by-elections. But why has the Government lost seats? Mr. LLOYD GEORGE did not exaggerate in the least in his Criccieth speech, when he declared that the pre- sent Government has hardly lost a seat at by-elections except through dissen- sion between Liberalism and Labour. And this dissension means, not that the electors are growing tired of a too rapid advance, but that they cannot appreciate the strength of the obstacles which the Government have encoun- tered in their advance. If the Govern- ment felt it necessary to put on the drag, if their sympathies were with re-action rather than with progress, then, and only then, would the lesson of the by-elections inculcate the duty of a speedy dissolution.

div.head: EVERYWHERE.
div.p: EVERYWHERE.
The man who measures success by inches doesn't get very far.
It always seems much easier to forget our friends than our enemies.
It's the easiest thing in the world to know how to succeed after you have failed.
The man who starts to ride a hobby should at once equip himself with an emergency brake.
The reason the guess of a woman is so often right is she backs it against her husband's judgment.
Shortly after a woman gets norried she gives up the role of guardian angZl and assumes that of detective.
We can all be thankful for what we have, but few of us consider that we also ought to be thankful for what we haven't.
The cross was formerly a part of all signatures, made as an evidence of the subscriber's faith and not of inability to write, as it is now.
Atlanta is to have a club house exclusively for women if all the feminine organisations of the city can be got to co-operate and to agree on plans.

The town of Eccles, Norfolk, was overwhelmed by the sea in 1604 and all the inhabitants were drowned. Now, after more than 300 years, the sea has receded, disclosing the ancient ohurch and churchyard.
Not So Bad As He Looked. A small boy's essay on Oliver Cromwell: " Cromwell had an iron will, an unsightly wart, and a large red nose, but underneath were deep feelings."

Can't Say What Any More. " The gentleman farmer is now teaching the other kind of farmer," says a Westerner. " The other kind of farmer can no longer say with a grin: " 'A gentleman farmer is a man with science enough to run a farm as it should be run, and with money enough to stand the loss."

div.head: Futile Plea.
div.p: Futile Plea.

A prisoner, charged at the local Police Court on Monday with having gone beyond the bounds of temperance, said he had never touched beer since he signed the pledge." The Chief Con- stable retorted: "We don't suggest it was beer."

A Fourteen Days' Birthday. "I was only keeping my birthday up," was the explanation given by a prisoner at the local Court on Saturday, when he was charged with being drunk. "The police regret they cannot help to keep it up for more than 14 days," re- plied the Chief Constable.

A Late Discovery. After fumbling with his keys for several minutes the other day, the manager of a local picture house succeeded in unlocking the door with difficulty, whereupon he discovered the door in immediate proximity to it to be vide open!

div.head: WHITSUNTIDE TRAFFIC.
div.p: WHITSUNTIDE TRAFFIC.
Trams Have a Profitable Time.

The Whitsuntide traffic this year has been quite up to the usual standard in Warrington. The takings of the Corporation trams were as follow: Saturday, ..tlOB 7s. 11d.; Sunday, .C4O Bs. hid.; Monday, £7B 2s. sd. The motor omni- buses took: Saturday, £l4 10s. 7d.; Sunday, £5 10s. 31d.; Monday £lO ss. 51d. Last year the Cheshire Lines Railway had an excellent Whitsuntide, and this year shows no decrease. The principal bookings were for I Liverpool, Manchester, Belle Vue, Buxton, Douglas, Matlock, New Brighton, and North Wales.

The London and North-Western Railway was Patronised well over the average, the traffic being mostly local. Saturday's bookings were chiefly for the usual seaside resorts, and we understand that the Whit Monday bookings were " abnormal—certainly a great increase l" How WHIT MONDAY WAS SPENT. Although the weather during the first part of Monday was a little doubtful, the forecast in "The Examiner" last week of fine weather for the holidays proved correct. Brilliant sunshine brought forth gay crowds of pleasure-seekers from all parts of the borough. Many picnic parties left early in the afternoon, spending several happy hours in the various Cheshire beauty spots. Others visited the seaside resorts of their own comity, whilst those who remained in town thoroughly enjoyed themselves at the various places of entertainment. All day the roads swarmed with motorists and cyclists.

div.head: riliE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 6, 1914.
div.p: riliE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 6, 1914.
pAssING-WEEK.
OUR HIGII DEATH-RATE.

Dr. G. W. N. Joseph's first annual report as medical officer of health is a masterly arrange- ment of-facts, and a fine record of what he and his committee are doing in the interests of the health of the community. But the somewhat disconcerting fact comes out prominently above all the other facts that in 1913 our general death-rate increased to 17.2 per 1,000 from 15.7 in 1912; and that our infantile death-rate in- creased to 131 from 92 in the preceding year. In the 96 great towns with which Warrington is grouped the advance in the general death- rate was but a fraction—from 14.6 to 14.7 and the advance of the infantile death-rate was from 101 to 117; so that our general death-rate which was already worse than the average has become still worse by comparison; while in the infantile rate, where we were much better than the average, we are now much worse. Bron- chitis, pneumonia, consumption and the in- creased deaths of children under one year of age are responsible for this slide backward. It is clear from the Doctor's report that, he holds our laCk of proper sewerage arranjements to be responsible for much of the mischief. "Un- doubtedly," he says "the time has come for a discussion of the question" of re-sewering the borough with a view to the abolition of the pail system. We have only to screw our courage to the sticking point of spending quarter of a million, and the thing will be done.

div.head: LAND CAMPAIGN.
div.p: THE LAND CAMPAIGN.

Large audiences have assembled throughout the week to hear a systematic explanation of the principles underlying the great land cam- paign upon which the Liberal party have entered with all the enthusiasm and determina- tion that properly pertains to the Progressive side in politics. Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield have been most energetic in the fight that promises to bring better times and more agreeable con- ditions for the toilets in town cod country. There is no doubt that the people will give that support to the Government which is the only thing necessary to the achievement of a tre- mendous social reform. Ttie facts are collected, the scheme is formulated—and the people will supply the motive power to carry it through.

div.head: DRUIDS HONOUR WARRINGTON.
div.p: DRUIDS HONOUR WARRINGTON.

Mr. Edwin Allen, paint merchant, Butter- market-street, was paid a signal compliment this week by the Druids, who, at their Sheffield "delegation" " unanimously elected him as the Grand Master of their Order. It is a recognition of services, long and true, but unostentatiously given, in the cause of friendly societies in general, and his Order in particular, and some of the glory is reflected upon the place of which he is so worthy a citizen. Next year's confer- ence will be held at Warrflieton, which was further noticed by the election of Mr. John aby on the Board of Management.

div.head: PLEASURE AND BUSINESS.
div.p: PLEASURE AND BUSINESS.

We do not know whether it was the experi- ence the delegates had had in Sheffield, or the prospect of what they may expect next year when the conference will be held in Warring- ton, that induced one, of the delegates to ask whether it was possible to hold the conferences in seaside places instead of in towns similar to those from which' many of the members came. He pleaded for change of air and recreation. As it was decided to come to Warrington and then consider the question, we shall not be accused of being an interested party when we say that delegates are not necessarily elected in order that they may go away and enjoy them- selves in a holiday sense. The "Sheffield Tele- graph," wlifch feels acutely the reflection cast upon a city that has made great efforts to let in the sun upon itself, rend the slanderous dele- gate a serious lesson. As a matter of plain fact, says our contemporary, delegates "are much more likely to do their business as it ought to be done in a city like Sheffield than in a popular seaside town, where their main anxiety would be to get down to the beach, or out on the sea. If the delegates want a holi- day, by all means let them go to the seaside. But they should be honest enough to tell the mern.bers they represent that it is a toliday they are after. If the Sheffield Druids are doing their duty they are letting the visitors know that there is plenty of lovely scenery just outside the city, where they can spend delightful even- ings when their Conference work is over." If the Warrington delegates do their duty next year they may show them what we possess in the way of lovely scenery. Whether it will stop their friends pining for sand and ozone, we will not venture to say.

div.head: HORN IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: HORN IN WARRINGTON.

A neatly printed account of the achievements of the late Dr. Arthur Ellson Davies, a former president and editor of the Edinburgh .Field Naturalists and Microsclopical Society, has just come to hand. In it we learn Dr. Davies was born near Warrington, and passed his youth in the town, where his father, Dr. John Davies, carried on a consulting practice. He became a Fellow of the Chemical Society in 1866, and was distinguished in many branches of learning. He remembered Warrington to the end, for to ' our Field Club he bequeathed a valuable copy of the first edition of Sowerby's " English Botany."

div.head: TIIE SUNKEN LINER.
div.p: TIIE SUNKEN LINER.

• Information is gradually leaking out which shows that Warrington suffered more by the sinking of the Empress of Ireland than was at first known. Probably we shall learn even worse news U.S time goes on, but the facts we print in another column seem to point to at least two local families having been severely striken by the great calamity. It is a sadly interesting fact that Laurence Irving and Mabel Hackney played "Margaret Catchpole" at the Royal Court Theatre, War- rington, in August, 1910, and at the•same time rehearsed daily Mr. Irving's great success, "The Unwritten Law." Before entering the profession, Mr. Irving was preparing for the Diplomatic Service, being engaged for a time at the British Embassy at St. Petersburg, a sojourn which led, most likely, to his writing, in after days a play on "Peter the Great," for his father, and his „recently produced adaption of "Crime and Punishment," the Unwritten Law.

Mr. Harold Neville, Mr. Irving's manager, and his wife, Miss Elsie Vron Neville, also among the missing, last appeared at the Royal Court Theatre some six years ago with The Ryder Boys Season. Mr. Neville contemplated sending out two companies in the autumn, "The Honeymoon" and "The Passing of the 3rd Floor Back." The latter play was booked to appear at the Roxal Court Theatre.

div.head: PRESTATYN SUMMER CAMP.
div.p: PRESTATYN SUMMER CAMP.

From now till the school holidays begin and from the end of the school holidays to the end of the summer, the resources of the Children's Summer Camp—and those resources are many —are placed at the disposal Of approved visitors at rates which will allow people of slender means to enjoy a restful holiday by the sea. Over thirty people availed themselves of this privilege during Whitsuntide, and the pleasures of the place only need to be known to put it in greater demand. Those who have visited Prestatyn in previous years will, be pleased to know that Mr. Bodgers, the experi- enced and Capable caretaker, is again in charge. Mr. Ernest Bradshaw, Egypt:street, the acting hon. secretary, will be pleased to give every itiformation to intending visitors. .

div.head: Facts the Warrington Deputations knew
div.p: Facts the Warrington Deputations knew
not of.
BELFAST A DISGRACE TO CIVILISATION.
Mr. Harold Begbie Presents an Old Sub- ject in a New Light.
BY C. E.

Who is not bored with reading d'ry facts and ingenious falsehoods about the various phases of the Irish question in political speeches and factioneering pamphlets? Hence it is a pleasure to find on a bookstall and get for a shilling a book that goes • below' the surface, gets to the heart of the Irish people, and therefore to the heart of the Irish question. The book is Harold Begbie's " The Lady Next Door." Whatever be the political leaningsiof the reader, no one can fail to be charmed with t the writer's vivid glimpses into Irish life and character—into the soul of a people. Only incidentally is the \book a plea for Home Rule, or, if it is a plea, it is made on grounds widely differing from those we usually hear; the emphasis is laid elsewhere. Harold Begbie is a poet, an enthusiast, a seer. It is not the possible greater prosperity of Ire- land in a material sense that appeals to him in her demand for freedom. "What shall it profit a nation," he asks, "if it becomes the clearing house of the world and miss the way to pea"? What ehall it nrofit a democracy if it gain the , 4 whole wages of mannriOn sad lose the Joy of Life?" Begbie's picture of the lady next door is that of "a young and capable matron seated at her fireside, who raises her grey eyes to the visitor, and says without apology, but with a whimsical and ingratiating play of laughter at her lips, I wish to do my own housekeeping; I think I can do it in a better way, and more cheaply, than other people can do it for me. I have no desire to fall out with iny neighbours, no inclination to remember old scores against them. I simply want to be left alone to attend to my own business, and bring up by own family in my own way.' "The old gentleman. next door may be alarmed by this ambition, but the lady has really no more evil intent against his prosperity than to sell him the surplus of her butter and eggs." The key to this book is in the questions What is life? What is the object of existence? From this view-point (whether we adopt it or no) we can understand the writer when he says "The industrial North filled me with depres- sion. I can think of few sharper contrasts in the world than to go from some beautiful village on the coast of Donegal straight to the squalor and poverty of Belfast." Of course, one might suggest that in this same beautiful village there is Probably as great poverty as in the Belfast slums. But Begbie would claim that it was a different kind of poverty, not one that debases, brutalises and takes away the Joy of Life. With this new point of view we eagerly scan Mr. Beg- bie's presentation of his case. Happily he lets the Irish peasant, priest, doctor, lawyer, all sorts and conditions of men and women, do most of the talking.

England and Ireland in Contrast. There is a very interesting chapter entitled " The Bishop's Dream," which contains a sum- mary of conversations which Begbie had with a Roman Catholic bishop in the South. Begbie puts down what he recalls of what he character- ises as the soul of what the Bishop said. This Bishop has a remarkable power of expressing himself, or he owes a good deal to the genius of the man who reports his talks. The following is very suggestive, and I never felt the force of this line of argument for allowing Ireland to manage her own affairs so strongly as when I read it in this good Bishop's setting : "England is a rich, industrial, and conquer- ing nation. Ireland is a poor, agricultural, and domesticated nation. England's popula- tion has increased by leaps and bounds; Ire- land's population--since the Union with Eng- land—has dwindled in'a desperate degree. Her revenue has fallen. Her trade has almost vanished. Her sons do not go forth to conquer and to colonise, but as poor emigrants, weep- ing bitterly and loth to go. "What is the antagonism? It is economic. There is nothing here of Celtic hatred for the Saxon, or of Saxon contempt for the Celt. It is the natural, the inevitable antagonism which separates a rich industrial nation from a poor agricultural nation. Unionist politi- 'clans maintain that the wholly antagonistic interests of the two countries can be combined, can be made one. They declare that the British Parliament can budget and legislate for two countries whose interests, talents, and resources are entirely different. They might as well argue that the legislation and the Budgets of Westminster are equally suitable for Denmark or India! How can a rich industrial 3aation legislate and budget for a poor, agricultural nation? Who would not smile if a politician suggested that a rich man should order a poor man to keep house on the same scale as his own? Must not the two houses be separate in finance and management even as they are separate in bricks and mortar? "Let me give you two or three instances of the blunders which came from this discordant union. Take old-age pensions. In England five shillings a week is only just sufficient for the needs of an old person; in Ireland it is too much. In England it is hard to get a cottage under two shillings a week; in Ireland rents are as low as a shilling, ninepence, even sixpence a week. Two old Pe° in England, a man and a wife, with five shillings a week each can manage to live; in Ireland such a ple couple are unnecessarily rich. Not only are commodities cheaper in Ireland, but the man- ner of living is simpler, very much simpler. Our pensions ought to be three-and-sixpence a week at the most. But Ireland has to run pl at the side of galloping England, and we are saddled with your harness and pull at your load."

To add to the Bishop's illustration, not to improve it—that is impossible—l would suggest that the position is like an electric launch that has met a rowing- boat in which the occupants are quite satisfied with oars as methods of pro- pulsion. The Occupants of the launch insist upon attaching the rowing boat and pulling it through the water at twenty knots an hour, to the manifest discomfort of its occupants, whose energies, instead of rowing and steering their own boat, are occupied in keeping out the water that breaks over their bows by being pulled along at a Speed unsuitable both for their boat and themselves, and in a direction they do not want to travel. I suppose that the worthy Bishop, if it came to question of legislation, instead of giving five shillings at the age of seventy would have proposed three shillings and sixpence at the age of sixty, or giving the extra in some better way proportionate to the needs. When we think we realise how different is the condition of an Irish peasant over seventy to that of an English ;workman in an industrial English centre of a like age. The Irishman, if in fair health, is still useful on a farm. I have seen many an Irish peasant over seventy doing the light work, and often the heavy work, on a farm. He is by no means a cipher in regard to the family work. With the English artisan the ' case is altogether different. His chances of ' employment in the industrial market are very few; there is scarce anything he can do at home, ' he has seldom even a garden in which he could grow potatoes. What folly to apply the same laws where conditions so widely differ!
To Keep Their Old People Alive. An amusing account is given by Begbie of his conversation with an rrish doctor. Begbie seems to have the faculty of making friends with

div.head: PARKER.
div.p: PARKER.

everyone, and in a motor ride this doctor startled him by saying Lloyd George was the most infamous man ,in the world. "He has 'made my life a hell. He has made every doc- tor's life a hell. Since his eruption—the Devil take his soul—there is not a doctor in the land whose life, &c." And then it came out that the doctor's outburst, which was half fun, pro- ceeded from the fact that he was sent for at every hour of the night, and called out of his motor at every mile of his way during the day- time, by people anxious and alarmed over noth- ing in the least serious which has happened, or is, they think, about to happen, to grandfather and grandmother. "Where family affection did not exist before, your Chancellor of the Exche- quer has created it; and where it did exist, he has developed and intensified it to a degree which doctors find utterly insupportable. One might almost say," he added, "that a main employment of the peasants newadays is to keep their old people alive." And then the doctor told an amusing story ",I was rung up pretty late one night by a peasant from an outlying village, fifteen miles away. -It was in the days before I had a car. The wind Was blowing horribly, the rain was sweeping against the house, and it was deadly cold. The peasant asked me, rather shame- facedly, if I would come and see his mother. I invited him to collie in; I gave him a glass of whisky. 'Patrick,' I said, 'your mother is a very old woman.' 'I know that, Doctor,' he admitted. 'She's over eighty, Patrick.' 'She is all that, Doctor: And nothing that I could do to-night would be of the smallest use to her? 'Shure, Doctor,' said he, 'I know very well it's the truth you're telling me; but me poor mother, do you see, would have me come and fetch you because she does not want to die a natural death."

But before leaving this chapter let us hear more of the Bishop's wisdom. "At present we are spoon-fed and debilitated with one of England's hands; let, hindered, and obstructed with the other: because our intellect is absorbed by politics; because we have a passion for free- dom; because we cannot rest while we are governed by another; because the form of gov- ernment under which we live has impoverished our industries and drained our population. . . The more you bear our burdens, the more you paralyse our sense of responsibility. We say to you, Set us free; leave us to pursue our own path, to fulfil our own destiny.' We feel that something more than our fortunes are bound up in this plea for self-government; it is our char- acter. You destroy our independence, you paralyse our self-reliance; you take away from us what God gives as a chief blessing to a nation, our sense of responsibility. We tend under the Union to become the parasites of your wealth, the hangers-on of your Imperial great- ness, the sponging toadies of your bounty. That, to us, is more than intolerable, more than perilous; it is fatal to body, soul, and spirit." Seamy Side of Belfast Industrialism.

When Begbie turned his attention to Belfast, in which he appears to have spent some months, the picture alters, and one is saddened by Begbie's descriptions. This suggests a curious problem. Two Warrington Deputations go to Ireland, and when they come to Belfast they find there nothing but causes for congratula- tion. Say they, "We concluded our tour in Belfast and on our arrival we were struck by the appearance of this great city and the evi- dence of prosperity. We were allowed to talk to the workers and in every case we found them contented, industrious, and prosperous." Begbie, who appears to have spent more weeks in Belfast than these Deputations did days, comes to an almost entirely opposite conclusion. We grant that members of the Warrington Deputation are as honest as this writer; both give what they consider a true description of what they saw, both claim to have gone to Ire- land with unbiassed minds. What is the ex- planation of this contradiction? Is it not in this that every mind is influenced by an uncon- scious bias, hence every reader and hearer must jealously guard his own right of judgment. But what is lacking in the Deputation's Report is that the authors appear never to have seen the seamy side of Belfast industrialism, the chief point Begbie observes and graphically depicts. And yet any side turning from the streets illus- trating the civic and industrial splendours would have brought them face to face with the slums, the destitution, and the ugliness of the Orange capital. And this omission is all the more singular because they found ample time to inspect and describe the slums of Dublin. Begbie, seeing both sides, says: "This packed and crowded city is the most depressing, dismal and alarming exhibition of• what competitive industrialism can make of human existence, that I have yet explored." . . . "Fully to realise the conditions of Belfast it is necessary to visit the slum quarters, to enter the kennels of the poor, to examine the wage-books of the home workers, and to make a study of the ragged, barefoot children in the streets. .No honest man who has conducted such an investi- gation can doubt that the condition of Belfast is a disgrace to civilisation and a frightful menace to the health and morals of the next generation."

And then follows a mass of detail, fact& and figures, which, unless they can be successfully challenged, prove Begbie's summary up to the hilt. Begbie not only gives the result of his own investigation, but that of other workers, who have approached the question not from the political but from the social point of view. Perhaps the most important. because coming from such a source it will be scarcely chrillenged, is the quotation given from the report of the Medical Officer of Health for Belfast:—

"It is to be regretted that no improvement has been noted in the rate of payment given to out-workers in the city . . . which is still far too low. In the last week of December, for instance, a woman was observed embroidering small dots on cushion covers; there were 300 dots on each cushion, and for sewing these by hand she received the sum of Id. She said
that for __a day's work of this kind she would

have difficulty in making 6d. "Nor is this an exceptional case. Quite recently our inspector was shown handker- chiefs which were ornamented by a design in dots; these dots were counted, and it was found that the workers had to sew 384 dots for a penny. Comment is needless.

Badly Paid Work. "Among the various kinds of badly paid work noticed may be mentioned "Children's pinafores (flounced and braided), 4id. per dozen; women's chemises, 70. per dozen; women's aprons, 21d. per

dozen; men's shirts, 10d. per dozen." The report gives the number of out-workers from the masters' lists as 3,700, but adds that the real number is considerably more, as em- ployers evade their responsibility br reduciiag temporarily their out-workers at the time when the lists are made out.
Surely these were not the workers our Deputa- tions found "to be contentlkd and prosperous." ,

div.head: GREAT WRECK.
div.p: THE GREAT WRECK.
Warrington Passengers go down with the Empress of Ireland.
TRAGIC MESSAGE ON A POST CARD.

The national calamity through the disaster to the Empress of Ireland, the _great Canadian liner, rammed and sunk in the St. Lawrence last week, has not allowed Warrington to escape, and last night at least two well-known local families were mourning the loss of dear ones. After awaiting a week in hope that their relatives might be amongst the saved, the fami- lies had finally to abandon hope, and yesterday it was made certain that their friends were. amongst the drowned. Usual pathos surrounds the case of each. One, a daughter of Mrs. Nunnerley, Ash-grove, Latchford, after a sojourn of 12 years in Canada, was speeding home to see her sick father when the disaster occurred, and additional tragedy was added by the demise of her parent a few days afterwards. _

The other victim was Mr. William H. Perry, a former employe on " The Examiner," who was paying a surprise visit to his relatives. Writ- ing to a friend, he penned the cryptic yet path- etic message: "It is better to be alive with a dime than to be dead with a thousand." A cablegram received yesterday confirmed that he sailed on the vessel and the relatives have no hesitation in thinking that he is the Perry on the list of drowned.
Mr. Hayes, the second purser, another War- rington man, was amongst the saved, and is expected to give evidence at the inquiry.

div.head: WARRINGTON SURVIVOR'S STORY.
div.p: WARRINGTON SURVIVOR'S STORY.
Praise for the Captain of the Empress of Ireland.
Mr. Ernest Hayes, 22, Fletcher-street, War- rington, one of the assistant pursers on the Empress of Ireland, in an interview at Rimouski, told the story of his escape from death.

Captain Kendall bade him farewell on the bridge when the water was lapping at their feet. The Captain gave up his lifebelt to a Passenger, and then he and Hayes jumped into the river together. Hayes was successful in reaching lifeboat No. 3, which picked him up.

Later that boat discovered the Captain clinging to some wreckage and took him on board. The Captain assumed command of the boat and saved 73 lives, searching for hours for sur- vivors and taking a hand at the oars himself. Hayes is a Chester man by birth. His father, now living retired in Birkenhead, was for many years manager of the Great Western Goods Department at Chester, and lived for a con- siderable period in Cambrian-crescent. Ernest Hayes, who is the youngest son, has been living at Warrington with his brother.

div.head: FATE OF MR. W. H. PERRY.
div.p: FATE OF MR. W. H. PERRY.
Tragic Message on a Post Card.

A well-known family in the Warrington dis- trict is mourning the loss of a relative—one of the victims of the terrible disaster. The one who is supposed to be amongst the loit is Mr. William Henry Perry, a printer's machinist, who served his apprenticeship at the office of "The Examiner." Mr. Perry, who was only 24 years of age, was well-known in the town, but by the name of " Roger " Perry. Twelve months last March he went out to Canada, accompanied by his sister Alice, to " try his luck." At the time it was the inten- tion of both orthem to have at least two years in the Dominion, but some months ago his sister returned home to marry a Mr. Leach, with whom she now resides at Abertillery. At the time " Roger P' was asked to return, but he was strong in his idea to complete the two years, and refused. However, writing honie recently, he said he would be home in June' but what date it would be he did not state, as he "intended to give them a surprise."

div.head: TRAGIC_MESSAGE.
div.p: A TRAGIC_MESSAGE.

Writing to—his aunt, Mrs. Cook, Willow Tree Farm, Burtonwood, he said: "I. shall. I am see you for sure on the 11th June. . . . feeling fine." This was a tragic communication, for it arrived at Burtonwood the day following .the great catastrophe. On a post card to his married sister and her husband he wrote: "Dear Brother and Sister,—l am writing to tell you I am sailing by the Empress of Ireland on May 28th. ram telling no one else but you, so ' mum's ' the word. I lead all others oft the scent."

On the picture side of the card was printed : " It is better to be alive with a dime than to be dead with a thousand." Amongst Mr. Perry's relations in Canada is an unc}e, Mr. W. H. Mather, who lives at Mus- koka, but "Roger" had never met him, and, wanting to break this record, it is understood he made a special journey to Muskoka. Owing to the conflicting of the names in the daily Press, the relatives in England were not sure that he was amongst the passengers, al- though they began to fear the worst when it was announced that a Mr. W. H. Parry was amongst the second-class passengers lost, for his friends noted that he made the journey out by second-class. However, a cablegram received yesterday continued their fears It was sent from Mr. W. 11. Mather, of Muskoka, and read: "Roger sailed and is lost."

PERRY'S CAREER. As a boy, Mr. Perry was educated at Heath- side School, and was a regular attender at the Sunday School, and the services of the Legh- street Primitive Methodists. When he was six or seven years old he lost his father, but lie was adopted by his grandmother (who died two years ago), and by his uncle (Mr. Mather), who now lives at Willow Tree Farm, Burton' wood, with Mr. and Mrs. Cook. As his apprenticeship at "The Examiner' Office was drawing to a close he attempted to Ijoin the Army, but failed. This love of soldiery was probably inherited from his father, a Bristol man, who was in the Army. Finding he could not gain admission into the ranks he travelled about England for some months, and worked successively at Cardiffi Chorley, and Wolverhampton, where his mother is at present engaged as the caretaker of the 'Official Re- ceiver's Offices.

div.head: LATCHFORD LADY LOST.
div.p: LATCHFORD LADY LOST.
Coming Home to See Sick Father.
--- - . One of the daughters of Mr. and Mrs. Nun- nerley, of Ash-grove, Latchford, has also lost her).ife in the disaster.
The deeeased,lady had not paid a visit to Eng- land for twelve years, and was coming over to see her sick father, whose death, we regret to state, has taken place during the week.

div.head: No Pastoral Play..
div.p: No Pastoral Play..
The committee of the Warrington Amateur Shakespearean Players have decided, after care- ful consideration; not to produce a Pastoral Play this year.
Against Closing Order. A poll has been taken of boot and shoe dealers in Warrington, in regard to the proposed closing order. Eleven voted for the order and 14 against, and no order will now be made.

Citizens' Temperance League. The open-air meetings commence next Friday evening at the Farmers' Stores, corner of Bew- sey-street. 'Mr. J. Watkin (Swinton) will be the speaker, and the Rev. T. T. James will preside.

Town Planning. Alderman Bennett, Councillor Pemberton, the Town Clerk and the Surveyor have been " ap- pointed to interview the Local Government Board in regard to the position of the Corpora- tion under the Town Planning Act.

Property for Sale. Messrs. A. 11. Clive and Co. will sell freehold dwelling-houses at Penketh and dwelling-house and shop, 141, Liverpool-road, Warrington, by auction at the Blue Bell Inn on Wednesday, June 17th. They will also sell at an early'date freehold land, cottages, and ground rent in Chapel-road and Doe Green, Penketh, and Lind- ley Green, Great Sankey, respectively, and in various lots. •

Infantile Mortality. The Leather Trade. Trade has Buffeted somewhat owing to the holidays (says the " Leather World "), and buyers have been mostly content with just the smallest quantities needed to complete urgent work, though here and there more import-int orders have been placed for delivery immediately business gets going again. On the whole, there- fore, there was a quiet look about the trade, and the most satisfactory feature was that contracts were not being so generally held back as is usual at this season, and, further, that " waiting order" goods were being rather quickly cleared.

To-night Mr.-Crosfield will occupy the chair at Town's End, and the chairman for Monday at Bridge Foot will be Mr. W. H. Sher- burp. At Ellesmere-stieet on Tuesday, Mr. M. Lleellyn will preside. On Wednesday the final mass meeting will be held at Bridge Foot, when Mr. C. E. Parker will be the chairman. Women Liberals.

The representatives of the Warrington Women's Liberal Association to the annual Council meeting of the Women's Liberal Federa- tion, in London, next week are: Mrs. A. H. Crosfield, Miss Crosfield, Mrs. Osborne, Miss Short, Mrs. J. T. Locker, Mrs. Delaney, Mrs. G. S. Pendlebury and Mrs. T. Bunch. They will be entertained at a reception on Monday by the Countess of Carlile and the Executive Com- mittee at the Portman Rooms; on Tuesday there will be a reception by Mrs. Lloyd George and Mrs. Runciman at 11, Downing-street; and on Thursday the Warrington deputation will be specially entertained by Mrs. Crosfield. Lymm, with its quaint, crooked streets, all nestled amongst the fresh foliage in one of the Prettiest spots of Cheshire, smiled admiringly on her young Queen on Thursday. The old- world streets lend themselves admirably as a backgrouhd to an old-world custom, and on the day of the festival the brilliant rays of the sun completed the "staging" effects. Early in the day the committee and the many helpers were busily engaged decorating the lurries, making the arrangements on the field, and attending to the children; householders were placarding their house fronts with the usual mottoes, " Teas" and "Cycles Stored"; the police was augmented, and the railway staff increased. As the final touches were made the visitors Commenced their influx.
her subjects re-formed into procession, and marching off, passed from sight. In the evening the .dancing programme was repeated, and later the Band (Lymm Subscrip- tion) played for public dancing.
Motor char-a-bancs, cyclists, motorists and rail trippers made Lymm their destination, so that by the time the procession began to move, the narrow streets were crowded.

div.head: BURIED CROSS.
div.p: A BURIED CROSS.

The ancient Cross, with its time-worn steps, could not be seen—it was substituted by a pyramid of cheering women and children. Along Church Green, Booths Hill, and Eagle Brow, walls of humanity lined up, whilst near the old mill the processionists occupied all the road. The procession was equal to any of previous years, and, as usual, nursery rhymes, and his- torical characters were fully represented. The long procession was headed by a troupe of Boy Scouts, whose bugle band heralded the approach of the Queen. Then came Britannia and John Bull, Ring Charles, Duke of Wellington, and a host of other notabilities. "Grace Darling and ' her father ",Made a striking tableau, as also did "Boy Blue" and "80-peep," the latter with her live lamb. Immediately preceding the " royal " carriage were heralds, courtiers, beef- eaters and pageboys, and as the Queen (Miss Dorothy Pearson) herself came in view she re- ceived a loyal and hearty reception. The ap- plause was gracefully acknowledged by a sweet smile and a bow from the " royal " personage. The maids of honour, train-bearer, crown- bearer and sceptre-bearer all proceeded with dignity and conscious of their high positions. The crowd followed the procession to the field. Behind the throne the majesty of the tall trees reminded one of sentinels. Half a dozen chil- dren attired in white Muslin sat on the approach to the throne, and enhanced the picture. Step by step along the crimson carpet the Queen's followers proceeded to bestow the symbols of her office and suddenly, after intermittent ap- plause, the tune of "God save the Queen" broke .the silence. Then applause sprang forth from the throats of the multitude. For the remainder of the afternoon the Queen witnessed the performance given in her hononr. Pretty little girls, daintily dressed, danced around the Maypole. As the applause died down, clever little mites danced on to the plat- form; they were the balloon dancers. Each was attired in a self-coloured dress, and as they hopped about with their balloons in hand, one's thoughts were turned to the fairies to be found in the children's books. The skipping rope dance, executed by a number of older girls, was remarkably well given. An ambulance display was given by a number of Altrincham ambu- lance men and a nurse, and also by a number of Boy Scouts. Competitions -were arranged, and some of the crowd guessed at a hidden treasure in a cake, whilst others attempt- to state the weight of a live sheep, which paraded the enclosure, unconscious of the fate which awaited it at the hands of the successful one. The committee were greatly disappointed that at the last minute the Lancashire Lasses Danc- ing Troupe was unable to be present, but this certainly could not be helped, and the pro- grammeut Queen closed u f thea fwtearsuufiul led s up rpu uoetehdeirußg- isseiheAQt

div.head: FURTHER LOCAL HONOURS.
div.p: FURTHER LOCAL HONOURS.

At the 56th "annual movable delegation" of the Order of Druids Friendly Society, continued on Wednesday at the Royal Victoria Station Hotel, Sheffield, Grand Master Albert Wilde, of Swinton, presiding, Bro. Edwin Allen, Warrington Equalised Dis- trict, was unanimously elevated from the Vice- Grandmastership to the position of Grand- master. It was also resolved that next year's annual movable delegation shall be held at Warrington. These were not the only honours the town received at the hands of the Druids, for Bro. John Bibby was elected a member of the Board of Management. Bros. Allen and Bibby belong to the same Lodge; and it is a source of pride on the part of Warrington that two of -4er , townsmen are on the Board at the same time. Bros. Perdue, J. Bibby, G. Shaw and W. Woods represented the Warrington District at the delegation. Bro. Edwin Allen, who formerly lived in Orford-road, but has recently lived at The Limes, Grappenhall, and is a paint and wall- paper merchant, carrying on business in Buttermarket-street, was one of half-a-dozen friends who founded the " Fearnhead " Lodge in 1898. He was Vice Grand Arch, and thus started ha connection with the Order half-way up the ladder. The " Fearnhead " Lodge was merged into the "Druids' Hope" Lodge in 1906. In 1900 Bro. Allen was, out of five candidates, elected Deputy District Grand Master—before he had been a Druid two years! That is an unequalled record, for no other brother has ever attained so exalted a position after so short a membership. Within a year he assisted in opening the "Sir Gilbert Greenall " Lodge, Walton, initiating no fewer than 100 members on the first night. The following year he rose to the position of District Grand Master, being presented, upon the expiration of his term of office, with a special illuminated address—a dis- tinction hitherto conferred on no other officer. In 1905 he was unanimously appointed district corresponding secretary. During the following • four years the society saved practically £l,OOO, the greatest progress made in any similar period. Honoured many times with the appointment of delegate to the A.M.D.—at Crewe in 1905, Glasgow in 1908, and Newcastle-on-Tyne in 1909 —Bro. Allen was also elected President of the Widows' and Orphans' Fund two years in suc- cession, and has frequently acted as auditor. He
is a member of the Royal Arch Chapter—a higher branch of the Order—and was appointed delegate to the annual meeting (Manchester) in 1906.

A firpa believer in the social side of Friendly Society work, it is natural that, under Bro. Allen's supervision, the "Fearthead " Lodge should have been the first to hold its annual bowling main; and that a most successful social should have been held in 1909, when the grand officers visited Warrington for the purpose of initiating Sir Gilbert Greenall, Mr. Robert Pierpoint, and Councillor Fulton-Smith as hon. members. In fact, Bro. Allen has been the means of making more hon. members than anyone in the district, and in 1900 presented the four principal officers of the district with chains.
These are only some of the many services Bro. Alloll has rendered the Order, which has now conferred its highest honour upon _him._ '

Few members have worked harder in the interests of the Order than Bro. Allen, and the honourable office 'which he is now called upon to fill constitutes a fitting reward for his untir- ing and disinterested labours. BROTHER JOHN BIBBY.

joined the Order in November, 1891, and has assisted his father, Mr. William Bibby, in all his Friendly Society work ever since. He has been assistant secretary to the "Druids' hope" Lodge, the Hope Collecting Society, and the Warrington Medical Association for over 20 years. He is President of the Widows' and Orphans' Fund.

The "sensational, clean, clever and screamingly funny" wire act, as presented by the Cole de Loss.) artistes, is exceptionally smart; and as Hebrew comedians the Bucher Brothers con- vulse the house immediately. Miller and St. Juste present their "two boys and a piano" act in fine style. Sinclair's Three Bluebells appear in a merry dancing and singing act. Joan Deering is a talented vocalist as well as a violinist, and creates quite a sensation in her Gainsboro' hat. div.head: " THE ROSARY" AT THE ROYAL COURT:
div.p: " THE ROSARY" AT THE ROYAL COURT:

A trio of successes belong to the "Rosary." First came the book of that name, then the song, and lastly the play. Those of us who have visited the Royal Court Theatre during the week are assured that the last is not the least of the three; it is to be doubted, in fact, if it will not outlive the other two. Powerfully written,- it brings home recognised truths in a new and convincing fashion, although it pos- sesses no intricate plot, and consists in the main of simple and homely dialogue. The recurring note is one of pathos, but this is happily relieved at intervals by amusing leatures, given in good .style. Every member of Ur, John Glendinning's company is a polished

actor, and consequently the play is produced in a very effective manner. Mr. J. H. Darnley's portrayal of the brawny, though tenderhearted, Father Brian Kelly is an admirably realistic one. His moralising is manly, and is naturally delivered. The sceptic, Bruce Wilton, whose ultimate salvation is wrought by the genial Father Kelly, is imper- sonated sympathetically by Mr. Walter Hunt. Miss Nina Blake Adams presents the sisters Vera Wilton and Alice March in an impressive and creditable manner.

div.head: 1,2 A WEEK FROM POULTRY.
div.p: 1,2 A WEEK FROM POULTRY.

If the way could be clearly indicated how men with a modest capital could realise a clear profit of 40s. per week by poultry keeping, it is not too much to say that tens of thousands would enter upon the Pursuit. Therefore, we do not wonder that this question comes up again and again for discussion. That there are many who do this, and even more, is a fact, but these are either farmers, to whom the fowls are but part of their operations, fanciers, or stock-breeders. It is an altogether different proposition when sale of eggs or chickens for market is concerned. What so many fail to realise, says a writer in a contemporary, is the extent to which operations must be carried on to enable what is here stated to be accomplished, and to leave sufficient mar- gin after the expenses are paid. Here are two faCts which must be kept in mind—the total -value of 50,000 eggs isless than £250, provided production is divided equally over the entire year, and the total value of 1,000 chickens is not more than .2125. Therefore, if anyone managed to do both, his sales would be £.375, out of which food and all other charges have to be met, If these latter were reasonable, the .£2 per week should be in sight, but that is something like the scale necessary for its realisation. To do this, however, the laying and breeding stock mast be 400 to 500.

div.head: BUDGET BENEFITS.
div.p: BUDGET BENEFITS.
What Warrington Guardians will Get Under New Proposals.
SUM OF £2,500 INVOLVED.

How the new Budget proposals will affect the Warrington Board of Guardians was raised at the fortnightly meeting held on Wednesday, the Chairman (Mr. A. J. Jolley) presiding. 'The matter came up in connection with a letter from the Derby Guardians with regard to some of the clauses, and the letter stated inter alia that the object was to transfer the assess- ment for rating from the local authority to a Government department. They asked that the Poor Law Unions Association should keep a close watch upon the proposals. . The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL suggested that they should let the letter from Derby lie upon the table. • The CHAIRMAN: It can be dealt with by the executive of the Association. Mr. G. Mierusa thought it a serious matter. The tendency was to centralise, and that was an attempt to get the matter placed under the con- trol of officials in London. - • 12,500 A YEAR MORE MONEY. Mr. A. BOTTOMLEY (the clerk) said in regard to the proposals in the Budget now objected to, it weld mean, if adopted, that Warrington Union would get £2,500 more money a year. (Hear, hear.) At present they 'got £2,898 per annum in lieu of official salaries. That was fixed in 1888, and it then represented the exact amount paid as official salaries and emoluments. Since that date the amount had never been altered. It was now proposed to pay to the Guardians a sum equal to 60 per cent. of the salaries and emoluments, which would mean an increase to Warrington on the present grant of £l,OOO. In 1888 a sum was fixed for lunatics at the rate of 4s. per head per week. It was now pro- posed to increase that to 6s. per week. Their present claim was about £.2,000 per annum. On the increased rate it would mean about another £l,OOO a year. They had never received a grant in connection with imbecile and epileptic patients, and it was proposed to allow 3s. a week for such patients. SEEKING FOR YEARS. ••

Mr. Miring thought they were expecting a great deal more than they would get. The CHAIRMAN said the Guardians had been striving for years to have the injustice removed. He resented the ided of rejecting the proposals when for years they were seeking to get such an act of justice. The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL thought they ought to feel grateful, especially to that " terrible man Mr. Lloyd George." The CHAIRMAN added it was only a partial remedy for the injustice. The CLERK said petitions had often been sent from other Boards pointing out the injustice that had hitherto existed. Mr. MITCHELL •And you have never had a Chancellor of the Exchequer who responded until the present one. (Hear, hear.) Mr. MATHER : He is the chap who wishes to destroy the Church in Wales. Mr. MITCHELL : He does not wish to destroy the Church at Padgate. (Laughter.) It was agreed to take no action meantime. REGISTER ED CHILDREN.

Several cases v7e-i:ET—re;;;;e—d—W—here women wished to act as foster mothers to the children of other women, and the foster mothers sought to be registered in accordance with the Children's Act. It was stated that one woman desiring registration had gone to the Work- house, the Town Hall, the Health Department, and finally saw the relieving officer. The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL: Why was she sent all round there? The CHAIRMAN : Someone misinformed her. Mr. MITCHELL: The woman had to suffer. The CLERK : It was her fault in not going to the right place. Mr. MITCHELL: She didn't know the right place.

div.head: INSURANCE ACT RELIEF.
div.p: INSURANCE ACT RELIEF.

Mr. G. MATHER moved: "That a sum of £5O be granted to Messrs. W. and A. Ashton, the contractors for the erection of the new dining hall, kitchens, &T., at the Workhouse, in con- sideration of the fact that additional and un- foreseen expenditure was thrown upon them by reason of the National Insurance Act having been passed some time after the signing of the contract."

Mr. MATHER said he had a farm before the Insurance Act came into operation, now paid the insurance money and got no extra value for his goods. (Laughter.) The resolution was adopted. WEALTHY RAILWAYMEN.

Mr. MATHER moved to affix the common seal of the Board to a mortgage in favour of the trus- tees of the National Union of Railwaymen for the sum of .614,500, being the amount of the loan advanced by that Union to defray the ex- penses of the erection of a building to accommo- date the imbecile and epileptio patients at the Union Workhouse, Warrington. The interest is to be at the rate of .£3 17s. 6d. per cent. Mr. Mather said he was glad to see the railwaymen had so much money to spare. The mortgage was signed.

div.head: COUNTY BOUNDARIES.
div.p: COUNTY BOUNDARIES.
Discussion at Warrington Rural District Council.
PROVISION FOR SCARLET FEVER.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural District Council was held on Wednesday after- noon, Mr. William Furness, the chairman, pre- siding. The CHAIRMAN welcomed Mr. Edward Dennett, the recently-elected member for Woolston. He was sure Mr. Dennett, in conjunction with the rest of the Council, would work harmoniously and make the position of the Chairman as easy as possible. DENNETT said he would try to do as the Chairman had suggested. The CLERK reported that a letter had been re- ceived from Mr. Harcourt Clare, enclosing a letter to himself from the Local Government Board, suggesting that the two County Councils should come to some agreement on the boundary question. Mr. Clare's letter suggested a confer- ence at Preston with the Council and the Guardians.

Mr. MATHER said that the Surveyor and he represented the Council at the recent exhaustive inquiry in the boundary dispute, and he would like to say that he had never sat under a more fair inspector. That inspector had since sent out a letter stating that he bad given his award for a certain portion, and the other portion be- tween that and Warrington he suggested ought to come into Lancashire.

_ He (Mr. Mather) hoped that- the question would be amicably arrariged, and that the boundary between Lancashire and Cheshire be the Ship Canal. He thought the conference at Preston was to discuss the financial questions and small details.

Mr. DHNNETT suggested that Councillor Robin- son be appointed on the committee. The CHAIRMAN said the appointment had already been made. Mr. Mather had already been appointed. The Rev. A. M. Mriviim asked if the letter was. a circular letter. _

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 6, 1914.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 6, 1914.
geographical conditions, or the details, and he would like to run round the district with Mr. Robinson.
Mr. Robinson willingly agreed to such a visit.
WINWICK SEWAGE.

The CLERK stated that he had continued cor- respondence re Winwick drainage with Mr. Francomb, and received a reply to his letter dated 7th March, on 21st May, of an explana- tory character and of a conciliatory tone, sug- gestive of a desire for friendly procedure. The letter explained how the foul, crude sewage, shown by the Council's sample, arose, and how a satisfactory remedy had been obtained. He asked that the Council would treat the sewage from Mr. Longton's farm before it entered the Asylum grounds. Mr. MATHER moved that official notice be served on the Eeelesioottioal Commissioners (the owners of Mr. LongtOn's farm) to abate the nuisance.
This was agreed to. PROVISION FOR SCARLET FEVER. _ _.. ._.

__...._—. . —.—..• The MEDICAL OFFICER (Dr. Sephton) reported that there were during the past month 23 births and 39 deaths. There were nine deaths from scarlet fever, all in Penketh, with the exception of one, and he wanted to know if the Council were going to make special provision for such eases.
The Rev. A. M. MrrerreLL: It is :dvisable to make provision for the future.
The MEDICAL OFFICER: The Warrington Cor- poration can only take our cases when they have none of their own. k
Mr. MATHER said ither Warrington Hospital nor any other could take cases when they were full up. The CHAIRMAN: We cannot blame Warrington. _ .

. Mr. MATHER proposed they write to the Earles- town Hospital asking whether they were pre- pared to take the Warrington Rural District Council cases, and upon what terms. The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL: Has not this matter been raised before? Mr. MATHER : Asking them to make provision? The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL: Yes. The CLERK said he was not aware of it. Mr. MATHER : Are there any other places in the neighbourhood we can approach? The DOCTOR: No, unless it be Newton. Mr. Mather's proposal was endorsed. The CLERK said that years ago a certain gen- tleman offered to defray the cost- of building a hospital for that Council and Newton, but it was decided at the time not to accept.

div.head: IN THE COURTS. BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
div.p: IN THE COURTS. BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
MONDAY.

Before Dr. Josepli--(in the chair), Aldermen Bolton, Smethurst and James Evans, Messrs. G. Pilling, W. Furness and C. S. Burgess. Drew Wages and Decamped.—Michael Lyons, marine fireman, 38, New-road, was sent to prison for two months on a charge of running away from Warrington on August 19, 1912, leaving his wife chargeable to the Union. Mr. Basil Shearer, who prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Guardians, stated that prisoner had been em- ployed at Messrs. Crosfield's 'works, and was earning 30s. a week. On the day in question he left home as usual, went to the works and drew his wages. From that time until Saturday morning, when he was apprehended by the police, he had not been seen in Warrington. SATURDAY.

Before Mr. R. T.-Fairclough (in the chair), Alderman Tinnion, and Mr. A. J. Jolley. Attempted Suicide.—Mary Grady, a young domestic servant, who lived with her parents at 3, Pocket-street, was charged with attempting to commit suicide by jumping into the River Mersey the same morning.—The Chief Constable said that about ten minutes to seven that morn- ing Mr. James Bell, 44, Cockhedge-lane, a mil- ler's labourer, employed at the Mersey Flour Mills, was standing on the landing-stage opposite the mill when he saw the prisoner jump into the river. He promptly plunged in after her, got hold of her hair, and succeeded in getting her to the bank, with the assistance of a lock-keeper named Charles Gatley. The woman was handed over to Inspector Stuart and she said she had had some trouble at home with her etep-fatber. She alleged that her clothing had been pawned, and she had told her step-father that she was going to drown herself and he told her to "make a good job of it." The step-father was called and he denied the allegations, and said it had nothing to do with him, to which the prisoner exclaimed: "You are the cause of my doing it." —The Chief Constable: There does not seem much sympathy from the step-father.—The woman's mother said that early that morning, before she got up, she heard prisoner quarrel- ling with her sister over a hat pin and they began to fight. Witness went downstairs and did her best to separate them, and in a mad temper her daughter said she would drown herself. Her step-father was very good to her.— Whilst the Chief Constable was asking if there was any truth in the statement that girl's step- father had told her to make a good job of it, he rose from the body of the Court and said he did not :—The Woman: You did. Don't you con- tradict, you did.—The mother said the girl had been very depressed in her mind for some time and. she sometimes did not know what she was "Mg.—The Chief Constable said he was bound to say that the step-father was well known to the police, but not so far as coming before the Court was concerned. The girl was deserving of a great deal of sympathy.—She was remanded to .the Workhouse for 14 days, preparatory to being found a home.

TUESDAY. Before Councillor 11. Roberts (in the chair). Alderman Bolton, and Messrs. C. Jackson Holmes and C. Sawkins Burgess. Mysterious Boots.—Mary Hill, no settled abode, was charged with stealing or receiving a pair of boots, the property of Benedict Tyrer, of Butterrnarket-street. She pleaded not guilty. Theevidence showed that Mr.Cooper,assistant at Mr. Tyrer's shop, had identified the boots as his master's property. The prisoner made several unsuccessful attempts to pawn the boots, and eventually them. for ls . 9d., she went r et: t the whereshop sh oe se Ails f disposed oci o Jamesf Woods, M I saying that they belonged to her sister, but were too small for both her and her sister. P.C. Green made inquiries and found the woman in the Victoria Vaults, in Mersey. street. She denied all knowledge of the boots when he first questioned her. Eventually she said a man had given them to her.—She was committed to prison for one month. Love in Trouble.—Adam Love, 22, Marbury- street, was charged with being drunk at Bridge Foot on Monday. 'A police-constable .heard a smash and found prisoner had fallen through a window, which belonged to the Warrington Cor- poration, doing damage to the extent of six guineas. A Corporation official said the window was insured.—The Chairman said probably the insurance company would proceed to recover the amount of the damage from Love, who was fined 58.

Cori's Thefts.—Dorothy Rowell (14), 11, Kean- street, pleaded guilty to stealing a piece of silk and a lady's umbrella, the property of Miss Hamilton, 10, Wilderspool-causeway, and was placed on probation for twelve months. The evidence showed that Rowell took the articles whilst her mistress was on a visit to St. Helens. --The Chief Constable said the girl was most untruthful, but the magistrates decided to give her another chance.
THURSDAY. Before Mr. A. J Jolley (in the chair) Alderman —• J. . .•

Tinnion and Mr. W. Roberts. Objectionable Bills.—Thomas Roscoe, who was said to come from Wigan, was fined ss. and pay 10s. 6d. costs for posting objec- tionable to bills in different public places in War- rorderedlgtWar- rington. n

_ Deserted His Family.—Patrick Leonardy, no fixed abode, was charged with deserting his wife and family, who had to go into the Workhouse. It was stated that he had disappeared, and only just returned to Warrington.—Leonardy pleaded for another chance, but he was sent to prison for 14 days.

div.head: GIRL AND BETTING.
div.p: GIRL AND BETTING.
Councillor Roberts's Strong Remarks.
BTJETONWOOD PEOPLE FINED.

Some • exceedingly strong remarks were uttered by Councillor H. Roberts, the chair- man, at the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday, in a betting case. His co- magistrates were Captain G. Crosfield and Mr. Mortimer.

The defendants were Henry Dalton, 4, Win- wick View, Burtonwood, who was summoned for loitering in an entry off Chapel-lane, Bur- tonwood, on May 23rd, for the purpose of bet- ting, and who pleaded guilty; Alice Culshaw, 61, Mercer-street; Thomas Hilton; Green James' Brow; James Tinsley, Mercer-street; Edwlird Tinsley, Jackson-street; and William Penning- ton, Jackson-street, all 6f Burtonwood, who were summoned for aiding and abetting. Cul- shaw pleaded guilty, and the others not guilty. Supt. Foster stated that on the day in ques- tion Police Constables Henderson and Melling were watching the end of the entry in Chapel- lane, opposite the Elm Tree in Burtonwood, from a hiding-place. They were only twenty yards away, and had an uninterrupted view of the defendants. Between 12.40 and 12.55 the officers saw nine men and a girl, including those charged with aiding and abetting, go to the de- fendant Dalton and band him slips of paper and money. He put the money in one pocket and the slips of paper into another. Dalton was going away in the direction of Collins Green, when the constables came out of their hiding-place, and as soon as Dalton saw the constables he bolted into a house, but the police could net get in, because that defendant kept the door closed. A few minutes later the door was opened, and a quantity of papers were burning on the fire. The tenant's wife was upstairs when the man ran in, and she would have told the magistrates, if Dalton had pleaded not guilty, that when she went upstairs there Was no paper on the fire, but when she came down there was a. quantity burning on the fire. Defendant was told he would be reported for street betting, and he said "All right." The police searched him and found .1:3 7s. 7d. in his possession, and an account showing that the preiibus day he had drawn .e 4 and paid out £4 16s. 4d. The other defendants were well known to the police. The girl had admitted the *offence, but the police had the same opportunity. of seeing the others as they had of seeing her. There was a great deal of betting going on in that neighbour- hood.

GIRL QUESTIONED. The Chairman questioned the girl as to who was responsible for sending her with the slip and money, and she replied that she did not know. She saw the slip and the money on the table and she took them to Dalton. The Chairman said he was only asking, because he thought the person who sent her on such an errand ought to be there in her place. They would like to have the opportunity of deal- ing with subh people. ,•• Supt. Foster: The girl's father is in Court. The Chairman: I am not assuming it is the father, but if it was, or a relative of the girl, it is difficult to find language sufficiently strqng to reprimand them. The Father: Can I say a word? The Chairman said that as the father was not concerned in the case he could not be heard. The Father: I was working that day. The Chairman: If you are innocent it does not apply to you. My remarks refer to those, whoever they are, who used this girl for this base and contemptible purpose. I hope it will be a warning. Dalton was fined £5 and costs, and the re- mainder 20s. and costs.

div.head: HOLIDAY TRAGEDY.
div.p: HOLIDAY TRAGEDY.
Three Accidental Deaths ill Warrington.

The finding of a body floating in the River Mersey and two other accidental deaths marred the pleasure of the holiday in Warrington. The Coroner, Mr. S. Brighouse, attended at the Court on Tuesday, when he conducted the in- quests.

div.head: MISSING FOR A WEEK.
div.p: MISSING FOR A WEEK.

....---. _ The first inquest was concerning the death of Thomas James. Smith, whose body was recovered from the Mersey on Saturday night. Harry Appleton, engineer, 34, Orford-avenue, said the deceased was his uncle, and was 36 years of age, and a general labourer, who lived at 2, Ship-yard, Warrington. The last time he saw him alive was four or five months ago.

Joseph Green, of 13, Gas-street, a foreman, employed by the Warrington Corporation Elec- tricity Department, said the deceased worked with him, and was an excellent workman, who never lost any time. He last saw Smith alive about a week ago, when, after refusing to accom- pany witness to the Hippodrome, he said he was going home to bed. The Coroner: Did he appear to have had too much drink ?-lle did not look the worse for drink.
The Coroner; No one saw him after this witness.
Detective-Sergeant Holland: No, sir. The Coroner (to Green: Was the deceased with a womanP—The witness Green: Not when I saw him.

--- Acting-Sergeant Edwards spoke to recovering the body on Saturday. The Coroner, in summing up, said no one saw the man go home, although be was only about 80 yards away when he met Green. That was the last time he was seen alive. The next thing was that his dead body was found in the water a week later. There was no evidence to show how deceased got into the water. An open verdict was returned. KILLED BY MOTOR CAR. The second inquest was relative to the death of Walter Peers, the eight-year-old son of James Peers, a Corporation labourer, 84, Lythgoes. lane, Warrington. The boy was killed by a motor car on Saturday night in Winwick-street. The father said that shortly after 9.30 on Sat- urday night his wife sent deceased to a chemist's shoP in Winwick-street for a syphon of soda water for two children who were at home suffer- ing from measles. Witness heard that a boy had been killed in Winwick-street, but did not know it was his son. Witness returned home about midnight, after a fruitless search for his son, and later he received information that it was his boy who had been killed. He identified the body at the Infirmary. James Bennett, a forge labourer, of 67, Pier- point-street, who witnessed the accident, said the driver did his best to avert an accident. The boy ran in front of the car, and the driver would only be about a yard from deceased when he was first able to see him. Thomas Hartley, the driver, of 39, Dover- street, Chorlton-on-Medlock, Manchester, said lie was only going at about eight miles an hour and had three men as passengers. They had travelled from London and were on their way to Blackpool, where the three gentlemen resided. Ire did. his best to avoid the accident. The boy was taken to the Infirmary. The Coroner: What time did you leave Lon- don ?—About twelve o'clock. That is 185 miles. Why, you were travelling at 20 miles an holt Did you stop anywhere?— At Leicester for tea. Were you sober?—Yes, sir. lam a teetotaler. The Coroner (after a conversation with Detec- tive-Sergeant Holland) said it was only fair to say that the police officer who saw the occupants of the car said all the men were perfectly sober. A Juror said lie witnessed the accident, and was of the opinion that nothing more could pos- sibly have been done by the driver, who pulled up in the length of the car.
