A verdict of " Accidental death" was re- turned, and the Coroner announced that one of the passengers said he would give the father .C 5 for expenses.

FATAL END TO PLAY. At the third inquest a verdict of "Accidental death" was returned. It concerned Maurice, the ten-year-old son of Arthur Jones, insurance agent, 82, Padgate-lane, Warrington. The evidence showed that the boy, along with a number of other boys, was returning home, after wading in a pit. They crossed the Bridge- water Canal at Woolston by a bridge which was not properly in position, and it was supposed that Jones fell off and was drowned. He was at the roar of the company, and the first intima- tion the boys had was hearing the splash. P.C. Kay, of Woolston, spoke to recovering the body.

div.head: DISTRICT NEWS,
div.p: DISTRICT NEWS,
STOCKTON HEATH
TOWNSHIP TITTLE-TATTLE.

With the advent of June Newly-painted trams arrived. This is the way the Tramways Committee Remind us Summer has come. Geraniums have also appeared in I)orders. Their presence makes doubly sure The fact that we are in June, for 'Gardeners will not plant out until The Calendar says the leafy month has come. The Hill Cliffe roads were thronged During the holidays and the visitors found The scenery at its very best. Sprats have been found in the Ship Canal At the Swing Bridge when the tide was up. There are some optimists who sat- 'hat This is a certain sign the waters are becoming purer. They are looking forward to the days when Some of them will be able to catch Salmon at the Swing Bridge pools. , The day may come, but-we will have To wait a long time yet to see it. The holiday visitors behaved so well That the police had only to take charge Of one person, and the tramps during the week Have given the Heath a wide berth.

The Holidays:L. Whitsuntide saw a consider- able exodus amongst the residents of Stockton Heath, the majority going to the seaside. The Welsh resorts were first in favour, but some found their way as far South as Bournemouth and Brighton.

Picnics.—Several parties went for day trips from Stockton Heath during the holidays. The St. Thomas' Men's Class went to Southport: The most important party was composed of members of the St. Thomas' Band of Hope, whose destina- tion was also Southport. They started on Thursday morning and were conveyed from Victoria-square in special tramcars to War- rington. At Southport they spent a merry time, and on return home on Thursday night reportdd that they had had the best day's outing in their lives. The party were in charge of the Vicar, who, in the course of a brief speech, spoke of the very happy time they had. Prizes for an essay, kindly given by Miss Heath, were pre- sented to H. Hughes, M. Goodliffe, M. Hughes, D. Bowden, and R. Haslam. Medals for work done during the session were presented to : Goodliffe, M. Hallows, A. Lythgow, E. Goodliffe, M. Gregory, E. Smith, and D. Jeanne ; boys—R. Haslam and C. Tricket. Mr. Stannard (the secretary) gave an excellent report on the work of the session, and Mr. C. Hallows pro- posed, and Mr. Goodliffe, seconded, a vote of thanks to Mrs. V. Davies, Mrs. Milling, Mrs. Bede', Mrs. Hough, Mrs. Cleaton, Mrs. Oaks, Miss Edgerley and Miss Willett for their kind- ness in providing prizes for the races on the sands.

div.head: MOORE.
div.p: MOORE.

Wesley Guild Devotional Meeting.--on Wed- nesday evening the members of the Wesley Guild met for the monthly devotional meeting, when, in the absence of the Rev. Hugh William- son, an address was given by Mrs. Bray, of Australia, on the work of the Salvation Army in Australia. Mrs. Bray, with her husband, Major Bray, are over in England to attend the conference of the Salvation Army, which is shortly to be held. There was a good average attendance.

Marriage of Miss Eustance.—A very pretty and interesting wedding took place on Thursday afternoon at the Moore Wesleyan Church. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. H. Middle- wood, and a large congregation had assembled to witness the ceremony. The bride, Miss Florence Eustance, is well known and respected in the village, also the bridegroom, Mr. Edward Roberts. The bride looked exceedingly nice in a brown costume, with hat to match, and she carried a bouquet of choice flowers. Her sister (Miss Mary Eustance) acted as bridesmaid, and there were also two small maids in attendance, who carried pretty baskets of flowers. Mr. William Horton, of Warrington, was the groomsman. As the bride and bridegroom left the church they were greeted with a deluge of confetti from friends who had assembled at the gates. The bride has been the recipient of a very pretty tea service from members of the choir and the Young Ladies' Bible Class, both of which she was a member.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

Wesleyan Chapel Choir Trip.—On Bank Holi- day the Chapel Choir, with a few friends, mak- ing up a party of 35, under the care of Mr.. George Carman, choirmaster, paid a visit to Matlock, in Derbyshire. It was an ideal day for such an outing, and everyone took full ad- vantage of it, visiting all the chief places of interest, and enjoying themselves immensely : Before dinner, which was served at Bodo]) Cafe, Crown-square, the party visited the Wish- ing Stone, and commemorated the occasion by a ' few choice wishes of their own. From here a magnificent view of the valley was obtained. After dinner Matlock Bath was invaded, when the party broke up into sections, sorae going over High Tor, first visiting the caverns, where splendid specimens of dog-tooth spar crystals are to be seen. Others looked in at the petri- fying wells, with their varied collection of articles, such as birds' eggs, nests, &c., which have undergone the process of petrifaction. The Lovers' Walk and the River Derwent each claimed its adherents. Tea brought the day to a close. Leaving Matlock at 6.50 p.m., home was reached at 10 o'clock.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.
LINES FROM LYMM.

"Long live the 'queen'!" The three-week preparations for the festival Seemed quite sufficient. It was a hurried event, well done. Ye Olde Village was not lost in bunting. The Cross could not be seen, So many were there who made it a grandstand. A threatening thunderstorm only threatened. The caterers did well. The attendance equalled the average. Statham also made merry. Young and old joined hands And had a happy time. Visitors have poured into the village all the week. Its charms are well knoWn.

Girl in the Canal.—A little girl visitor to Lymm had rather an unpleasant experience on Wednesday, when she fell into the canal. She was speedily rescued, taken to a neighbouring cottage, and placed in bed for a few hours. She was one of the scholars from .St. Bride's, Old Trafford, who were having a picnic.

Church Army Mission.—The members of the Lymm branch of the C.E.M.S. promised at their meeting last Sunday to give every support to a Church Army Mission which is to be held at Statham and Newfield from June 10th to July Ist. The missioner will be Captain Pickersgill, who is very well known in the district, and he will be assisted by Cadet A. Stephens.

Lymm's Missionary Exhibition Representa- tives.—A great missionary exhibition, similar to the one held in Warrington some months ago, is to be held in Altrincham in October of next year. The exhibition is in connection with the Bowdon Deanery, and Lymm's representatives on the Central Committee are Mr. J. T. Milnes and ex-Sergt. Washington.

Lymm's Tribute of Respect.—Out of respect to'the dead—the victims of the terrible disaster to the Empress of Ireland, Chopin's Funeral March was very impressively played at the Lymm Parish Church on Sunday evening by the organist, Mr. Cooke, whilst at the Wesleyan Church special hymns for those at sea were sung.

Men's Society.—There appears to be renewed vitality in the Lymm Men's Society, for on Sunday a most encouraging attendance marked the meeting. The Rector, writing in the Lymm Parish Magazine, says : "A strong central body of earnest-minded men, bound together by the deepest ties of religion, must be an untold bless- ing to any parish, and there is no limit to the good influence that such a band of men can exercise."

Unparliamentary.—At an Occasional Court at the Lymm Police Station on Tuesday, John Wilson, a native of Lymm, but of no 'fixed abode, was charged with using obscene lan- guage.-31r. Wilcox, the landlord of the Fleece Hotel, stated on the previous night he consid- ered prisoner had had enough drink, and when he ordered him out, Wilson became disorderly and made use of very bad language. Sergeant Davies was called and prisoner was taken to the Police Station.—Wilson was fined 108., with the alternative of seven days.

Ex-Postman's I njury.—Mr. Thomas Knowles, of Newfield, Lymm, who was made the recipi- ent of a present from the Lymm Post Office staff on his retirement a few weeks ago, after 37 years' service, is lying at home suffering from the effects of a cycle accident, which befel him on Sunday, as he was riding down Massey Brook UHL Another cyclist, who was accompanying him, rode on in front for some considerable dis- tance, and, missing Mr. Knowles, turned back to see where he was. He was surprised to find him lying in the road unconscious, apparently having fallen from his cycle. A doctor was called, and the injured man was driven home, where he has improved satisfactorily. Upon in- quiry yesterday we were informed that he was steadily recovering.

div.head: RECTOR'S WEDDING.
div.p: THE RECTOR'S WEDDING.
Date Fixed for Next Thursday.

"Let me say at !once how v.ery heartily I appreciate the cordial good wishes that have reached me from all classes and the warm wel- come that is promised on every hand to my future wife," writes the Rector (the Rev. G. B. Thurston) in the June number of the Lymm Parish Magazine. ,‘

so far we can tell at present, are Otour married quietly n London on June a9th, and after a short holiday to come to Lymm bPeln s, i before the end of June. This will give us six weeks of summer weather in which to make acquaintances, settle household arrangements, and wind up parish work before the usual holi- day in August. In this way we think the wel- fare of the parish and our own personal comfort will be least interfered with. I hope to arrange for all the day school children, and for those in our Sunday schools who do not attend the day schools to celebrate our wedding on the day itself. "Other arrangements for receptions after we get back have not yet been completed, but I hope to let you know what these will be before very long. I should like to repeat here what I said when I made the announcement in church, i but what was not reported in the papers, that t is the particular wish of both of us that our marriage should be in no way a financial burden to the parish. I feel I can say this without any fear of being misunderstood."

div.head: FASHIONABLE WEDDING.
div.p: FASHIONABLE WEDDING.
Marriage of Miss D. W. Oliver and
Mr. S. Clark.

A PRETTY CEREMONY. A fashionable wedding took place at the Lymm Parish Church on Wednesday afternoon, when the contracting parties were Miss Doris Winefred Oliver, daughter of Mr. Robert Oliver, West View, Lymm, and Mr. Stanley Ward Clark, son of Mr. John Clark, of Foxley Lodge, Lymm.

The bride, who looked charming in a dress of cream-coloured material, with a train of white satin and a Honiton lace veil, was attended by Miss Phyllis Oliver (sister), Miss Mabel Mills and Miss Cecilia Wilkinson, as bridesmaids; whilst the best man was Mr. Frank Clark. There was a large attendance at the church, where a tastefully decorated archway, composed chiefly of palms, formed the central decoration. The service was taken by the Rector, the Rev. G. B. Thdrston, and the hymns included "The Voice that breathed o'er Eden," and "0 per- fect love," Mr. Cook being the organist. The bride was given away by her father.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 6, 1914.
WARRINGTON WORTHIES.
Philip Carpenter's Efforts After a Sanitary, Sober,

div.head: Sweeter Warrington.
div.p: Sweeter Warrington.
BY ARTHUR MOUNFIELD.

In bestowing recognition upon the efforts of reformers our happiness is often severely tem- pered by the memory of their disappointments. A large share of discouragement waited upon Philip Carpenter's efforts after a Sanitary War- rington. In particular he suffered keen .disap- pointment in his endeavour to bring Warrington under the operation of the Public Health Act. He had formed a Working Men's Health of Towns Association, and at its request the Town Council had petitioned in favour of the Bill. But with the 'Act in force the Council decided to await its working in other places before mak- ing the application which was necessary to bring the town under its operation. The slum owners and 'sellers of intoxicants (in Philip's term "the Drink-and-Dirt Interest") had been busy, and a circular was issued, which asked :

_ " Ratepayers ! Are you going to be gulled by the foolish tracts issued from the Oberlin Press? If not, 'attend the meeting to-night, and vote against the reckless expenditure of X 20,000, which the Public Health Act will inflict upon you." At a public meeting called by the Mayor the opposing' forces were well rallied. Philip described the prevailing feeling as "a violent determination to have no sewers, or anything else that would cost anything ;—except indeed dirt, fever, cholera, consumption, 4e., the tre- mendous cost of which, from their being used to it, they aid not feel or believe." He was shouted down at the meeting, but by the help of the Oberlin Press gave his speech to all who cared to read it. It is a worthy utterance, and his words reveal fine strength and convic- tion:

"When shall we learn," lie asks " how cheap it is to use our money, and how dear to waste it? . . . . Does this meeting mean to tell me that the working-classes do not desire this Act? If it be so, then I say that this is the last evi- dence of their degradation; that .we have left them in such ignorance that they care not for their bodies, much less for their souls;' and that their senses are so blunted with constant expo- sure to the evil, that at last they.have ceased to be sensible of it—like the American negroes, whose greatest mark of degradation is when they know not and desire not freedom. . • • Vote against the Act, • and you support filth, inde- cency, intemperance, misery, irreligion. Vote for it, and you aro preparing the way for true enjoyment, for self-respect, and for the purity of that body .which is the Temple of the Holy Spirit. "You may postpone the Act, but there are those who care for you, more than you care for yaurselves. We are not supported by, popu- larity in our labours; and we shall work on, endeavouring to convince your reason and rouse your better feelings." • It was an enlightened and noble speech, and one is sorry for the town that had so far given way to passion as to refuse to listen to its. author. Though frequently baffled in his public efforts, his work had an educational value, and gave impulses which have lasted to the present hour. Like most other good men, he was to do his most enduring work in the training of others, and in giving inspiration to young men who at another day carried his schemes to success.
one evening, the cost of a Ragged School for a whole year I--Yours,.&c., P. P. CARPENTER.
AS A VEGETARIAN.

For many years philip Carpenter was a con- sistent vegetarian, and the Oberlin Press sent forth tracts which advocated a non-flesh food diet with some earnestness and vigour. Quite naturally he desired that the children in his Sunday school should share his views, and took opportunity from time to time to foster a tender heart towards the animal creation and to en- large upon the cruelty of killing beasts for food. Though very largely successful, his efforts were not entirely so, as the following little " Recol- lection" of oneof his scholars will show :

" On one occasion," wrote one of his pupils, " someone suggested that meat pies should be taken, among other things, for the evening meal on Walking Day. This -rather -shocked Dr. Car- penter, and as the matter was to be decided by the children themselves, he spoke at consider- able length on the cruelty, to say nothing of the sin to his mind, of killing a beast to eat, and wound up by asking if there was any boy or girl who would kill/the sheep to make the mutton pies. Of course, he expected none to offer to do so, and waited a little, when Torn Massam stood up and offered to kill and skin the sheep. This created quite a scene, and ended by the majority voting in favour of fruit instead of meat I know we youngsters enjoyed Tom Massam's offer, because it came within the range of our knowledge, and. though defeated, he was' quite aware of our sympathy for mutton pies. I never remember, however, such- a. question again being submitted- for the decision of the children."

div.head: REAL PHILIP.
div.p: THE REAL PHILIP.

Perhaps in the domestic sphere of his own Church we see him at his best. It is permis- sible to say "domestic sphere," because, leading a beautiful bachelor life, the Church became his home and his all. Organising Christmas trees, teaching the children to sing, :addressing the Barid of Hope, preaching at Town's End and Bridge Foot on Sunday evenings, giving swim- ming lessons at 5 a.m., on Saturday conducting working lads into the country to study Nature, taking his sdiolars away on Walking Day, and pitying the formal marching of the other schools wbile gamboling on the shady lawns of Dun- ham, or seeing the beauties of Chester; in these we see him at his happiest and usefulest and best.

- And then there was his boating crew, who went out upon the river on summer evenings incidentally for the good of their health and to sing temperance songs and glees for the benefit of othei boaters. His Band of hope had a " session " which lasted the year round, and was always interesting, meeting in winter in the schoolroom and in summer in the Cobbs at Stockton Heath. He taught music gratuitously to the members of his congregation, and gave lessons twice a week to the scholars of the British School, known later as the People's Col- lege, printing for them in 1856 "First Notions ofsSinging," and originating the Annual School Concert. And on Saturday evenings there was his " Anti-grog-Shops Concert," held in the Music Hall, as a counter-attraction to the public-house. In 1857 lie induced ten friends—mostly work- ing men—to go with him to Peterborough to witness an eclipse of the sun. He was especially impressed by the uncanny ." darkness that might be felt," and declares that it was felt by each of us with more or less of unaccountable dread. A young man (with so little fear about him that he lately allowed the Warrington drunkards to give him a thorough thrashing sooner than pay his footing) felt cas-if the least thing would have knocked him down.' " Unable-to resist the temptation to pour scorn upon wasteful habits, he concludes, "the whole expense of a journey of nearly 300 miles was less than a month's drinking and smoking to an ordinary working man."
ANTI-WAR, ANTI-DRINK, ANTI-TOBACCO.

His opinions upon War, Temperance Tobacco and Purity were never concealed, and he held to them with entire consistency. ' When some of his friends and pupils joined in the effort to establish the Co-operative Society he gave them the fullest support, but withdrew from the enterprise altogether When it was decided that tobacco be sold. A typical expression of °phi- ;o n and of the energetic language which often flowed from his lips and pen may be found in a published, letter of 1853. The National Militia, after a long suspension, were enrolled in 1852, and the 4th Lancashires were summoned to Warrington for the usual month's drill. He opened Cairo-street School for evening classes to all the men who chose to attend and organised a body of teachers to help him. The efforts of others ran in other directions, and among other events was a dinner given to the officers. This roused his anger, and he wrote: Sir,—As a member of the Executive Commit- tee appointed to make arrangements for enter- taining the .Militia, I beg to say that I have taken no part in the arrangements for the din- Der just held; and for these reasons: • Ist.. I understood that the committee was appointed, and the fund raised, with a view to instruct, or, at any rate, harmlessly amuse, the poor and ignorant Militiamen who might else be idling about the streets or drinking in public- houses; not to feast a number of " gentlemen," who are quite competent to look after them- selves. 2nd. I abhor the trade of man-killing, which I believe to be utterly un-Christian. Therefore, lthoto pay the officers that lar 11 which ahl s willing tnogall men, I think it wrong to show them any respect as officers. On the contrary, if I had opportunity, I should tell them that I thought teaching ignorant men the trade of man-killing was a very wicked employ- ment. 3rd. I should think it wrong to give a dinner at guinea tickets (including wine) to anybody, even if -I wanted to show them the greatest respect. Ido not Care to ask whether any of the persons assembled were drunk, in the com- mon sense of the word. It is enough to know that such expenditure for sensual gratification cannot be reconciled with Christian sobriety. Let the Warrington people who dined the officers at the hotel last Tuesday remember that, to honour those that teach the trade of man-killing, they have guzzled and drunk, in

div.head: AS, A SCIENTIST.
div.p: AS, A SCIENTIST.

Space will not permit. an acconnt of his labours as a specialist in shells. It will be enough to say that this pursuit occupied .much of his time and led to his settlement in America. He purchased in 1858 a fine collection of shells from Mazatlan, HUH of California, which was afterwards presented to the British Museum. About a hundred thousand shells were examined and a catalogue prepared, a task to which he gave long and earnest labour.
The year 1859 and half of 1860 was spent in an American tour, in which science, anti- slavery discussions, and eight-seeing made ex- periences that stood in curious contrast.

The next six years were spent in England, but only for a year and a half of this period was he minister of Cairo-street Chapel. In October,' 1860, at the age of forty, he married Miss Minna .Meyer, of Hamburg, who had re- sided for long in the neighbourhood of War- rington. For the next five years his chief labours were scientific. He prepared a large collection of shells for the American Smith- sonian Institution, using the Warrington Museum as his workroom, and putting in a working day of fifteen hours. His home, for a time, was at Trafford, Man- chester, and then, for a 'space, at Lark Cottage, Lower Walton. It Was a relief to his relatives when his " workshop " at the Museum was required as a Reference Library and his "mountain of shells" must be removed. A life of "enslave- ment to shells" could hardly have been good for the health of either soul or body, and there must have been many who felt like his sister Mary: "How sad that such a tender heart as God Ims.given you should be exiled from human beings, who so much want such love! Scientific work is very vehiable and beautiful, but there are many who can do that; few the other. Do seek a location where the precious gifts God has given you may be'used for His children."

div.head: REMOVAL TO AMERICA.
div.p: REMOVAL TO AMERICA.

- - his mind turned to America. His visit had left him deeply impressed by the need of the great land beyond the sea, and he wrote : " My feeling is that in the present prospect of Ameri- can affairs, there is sure to be any amount of good work to be done by speech, pen and life; with better interest (so to speak) for labour- capital, than is likely to be here; and though I don't doubt I could be usefuranywhere here, I feel more disposed to exert what of working power I still have over there. I have no mis- sion, or call, or definite purpose; but feel as though I wished to ` report at Montreal,' and be ready for orders from the Shepherd." And so to Montreal he went to live twelve use- ful years as schoolmaster, occasional preacher and sanitary reformer.

div.head: LAST VISIT TO WARRINGTON.
div.p: LAST VISIT TO WARRINGTON.

A last visit to Warrington, paid during a short holiday in 1874, brought into evidence much affection, especially on the part of those. who had known him in intimate and brotherly relationships. lie had dreaded meeting his old friends at Warrington, and on paying a visit to his friend, Mr. C. Broadbent, at Latchford, expressed his wish not to give any, lecture, or, if he did so, at Latchford and not at Warrington. But he was announced to speak on "American Life" at Cairo-street Soho°lfoom, and addressed a crowded audience.
This is how Mr. liobson described the occa- sion

--- • " When he paid his last visit to Warrington in 1874, and a large crowd of all classes assem- bled to look once more on their much-loved teacher and friend, and to listen, alas! for the last time, to his well-known voice and to his encouraging and instructive words, the feelings of quite a number of these rough but warm- hearted men, whose association with Dr. Car- penter were mainly in connection with the swimming lessons, found Vent in the utterance of the local name (` Philip ') emphasised as it never was before, and probably never will again by men of this class, who, when bidding him good-bye' and clasping his hand, could find no utterance for their pent-up feelings of gratitude and esteem, beyond the simple ex- clamation, 'Buttermilk Bridge! Buttermilk Bridge!' Aged mothers, too, who had to bless him for what he had 'done for their sons, met him on this memorable evening as he was pro- ceeding to the Schoolroom, and could not re- 'strain their feelings in the public streets, but openly embraced and kissed him. No son re- turning to the home of his childhood could have had a more affectionate reception. Indeed, the proccedings and excitement of that evening formed more than one scene that will not be easily forgotten by those who witnessed them." The end came on May 24th, 1877, when, after an attack of typhoid fever, his heart failed, and he passed away, looking in death "happy and so lovely—as if he were going to utter a bright . thought." lie was laid to rest in the Mount Royal Ceme- tery, and over his grave as a mark of affection some of his former pupils erected a marble

cross. DIRECTIONS FOR HIS FUNERAL. Among his papers, some time after his death, was found an envelope inscribed " Directions for my funeral." It was dated 1843 and read over and approved in 1850. It was a protest against prevailing customs and extravagances at funerals, and gave instruction upon many points. We quote a few passages because of the reflection they give of the writer's mind

• "Let the coffin be the plainest possible, such as very poor people would use. Let there be no handsome palls or other mock finery. Let no mourning of any kind be given away; I should prefer that none be worn. If anything, let flowers be worn, and strewed on the coffin; and let there be signs of gladness. Let a hymn be sung at the grave. Let no intoxicating drinks

And when I'm just so full of play I jump all day, Slelliil Because lit to u laughs she slrannand and dances round with me, Bunderstands, you see!
When I'm so hungry I could cry, And.dinner time is nowhere nigh, She gives me bread and currant jam; She sees exactly how I am!
I don't see what a boy would do Without his mother, all day through, For mothers understand things so, They don't have to be told—they know.

div.head: CUCKOO.
div.p: THE CUCKOO.
As I was listening to the notes of the cuckoo alborauatdtehautPinteresting ltehtitse rmtoor 131,ionug mY mind to write a "Hail, beauteous stranger of the grove! Thou messenger of spring!" bird. _ _

poet's address to the after hearing that cuSekueceh. wiatsenav mg'lealdl-krewfneel welcome note, "Cuckoo,E;ery cuc-koo," for the first timeeone must -feel cheered c m e springno! and inspired by the sweet, warm voice of " spring's harbinger." So enchanting is the cuckoo that the poets doubt its being a bird, and call it "a wandering voice" and "a mystery !" Perhaps the most beloved of all the birds is the cuckoo. It has inspired the great poets to write many beautiful verses. If you haven't seen this bird, do not be dis- appointed when you do if you see a rather dull- looking specimen, and are informed that it is a cuckoo. Its plumage is of a leaden grey colour above, and white, regularly marked with black, underneath, and the ten quills of its tail are prettily patched with white. In spite of its dull plumage it has a very smart appearance if closely seen on a bough. The cuckoo is a migratory bird, or, as J. Logan remarks, "An annual guest in other lands," where it goes "another spring to hail." Although the cuckoo has a rather hawk-like appearance, it cannot be classed as a bird of prey. Its food consists chiefly of insects and a certain kind of caterpillar, of which it is very fond. If examined closely, the beak will show that it is well adapted for catching insects. The cuckoo arrives in this country about the end of April or the beginning- of May—at pres- ent the woods and dales are echoing with its cry—and stays till July,•or, as Wordsworth says, until " the pea puts on the bloom." It is distinguished from all other birds not only by its cry, but also by its peculiar habit of never building a nest for itself. The egg, which is of a brownish tinge, speckled with white, is carried to a nest in the vicinity by the mother bird, and is there placed in the care of the owners of the nest, which often belongs to pipits or wagtails. The behaviour of the young in- truder is not of the most grateful kind. Many of those who study wild birds and their habits, say that the young cuckoo, after a few days, will, without ceremony, 'turn its mates out, and occupy the whole nest and the attention of the foster parents. I don't think the cuckoo can be a very great favourite with other birds, although men praise it so much. Some natur- alists say that the cuckoo sweetens its voice by sucking other birds' eggs, and that is the reason why you will notice some small birds pursuing it. It is very nice indeed to listen to the cuckoo on a calm spring morning or evening, calling his sweet notes from hill to hill. The cry will perhaps be coming from a leafy rowan or ash tree near some stream, where the caller is securely hidden from our searching eyes. It is very difficult to tell the direction from which the sound is coming, and causes us to look in all directions, as Wordsworth says, "in bush and tree and sky." I wonder how the cuckoo would feel if it knew how old and young sing its praises, unit would so gladly change places with him, to be free from the cares of life which hang so heavy over many.

• be used on any account whatever. Let the grave be simple; there need not be a new one set apart for me. I care not whom I lie with; we are all brothers. If wished, let my name and dates, without titles and without character, be engraved on a stone, with a.verse of a hymn or Scripture; but not one which shows Praise to any but God. I should prefer a mound of earth with some flowers (without a stone), a white rose, a pink, and some snowdrops or some lilies of the valley. Let none of my family come from a distance. Let no favourable accounts of character appear in any papers or periodicals." A further paragraph said that if his body could be made serviceable to the ends of science it might be dissected. This idea commended itself the more at a later day, and in his will he Care to be taken that no sermon be preached, or dis- section to t"I direct my yedbieVly stcoholl given for eulogy appear in the papers." But these direc- tions were not known to those who arranged the funeral. Warrington has two memorials to the memory of Philip Carpenter. A drinking fountain in the Park is familiar to most of us. Less familiar is a tablet in Cairo-street Chapel. Its inscrip- tion merits reproduction here:

In Memory of Philip Pearsall Carpenter 8.A., London;, Ph.D., New York. Minister of this Congregation sixteen years. A student of Nature, a servant of God, and a lover of mankind. As a preacher, he was simple, faithful, heart-searching. As a student, untiring, ever learning that he might teach. As a teacher, earnest, loving, and beloved. His heart glowed with all personal affections, And yearned for an ever closer walk with God. He spent himself in the service of man, With a devotion called by some foolishness, But to himself the entrance into life eternal. This tablet Is placed here at the joint expense of many friends, that what he lived for may not be forgotten in the place where some of his worthiest work was done. Born at Bristol, November 4th, 1819. Died at Montreal, Canada, May 24th, 1877.

div.head: WRONGLY NAMED.
div.p: WRONGLY NAMED.

Why is German silver so called? It contains no silver and did not come originally from Ger- many. The Chinese discovered it. Quicksilver likewise contains no silver. Mosaic gold has r.o connection with Moses, and it consists of copper and zinc; blacklead is grey, and is composed entirely of carbon. Whalebone is not bone; dragon's blood is a solid gum obtained from a tree; Burgundy pitch has no connection with Burgundy, nor is it pitch; and galvanised iron, as many Warrington workmen know, is iron coated with zinc, without any galvanic process whatever.
WARRINGTON PHOTOGRAPHIC SOCIETY. Outing to Vale Royal and Pettypool Parks.

On Whit Monday fourteen members took part in this picnic, which was led by the Secretary, in place of Mr. Walker. Arriving at Hartford Station at 1.45, the party walked down to Hart- ford Bridge, and along the river to Vale Royal Locks, whence they turned into the park, and several good snapshots were obtained. The 1 Monkey Lodge of Pettypool is always a favourite subject with photographers, and inside the park tea was taken alfresco. One of the party tried two of the Paget colour plates, one on the meadow strewn with buttercups, the other on a rustic gate backed by rhododendrons, and I have since heard that they are both a distinct suc- cess. .

The party emerged on to the main Chester road at the Tower Lodge, and walked along the great motoring and dusty highway to Hartford Station again, catching the 7 train home. The day was ideal from a photographer's point of view, and many successful negatives are the result.

DEATH OF MR. B. J. EDWARDS. One of the pioneers in dry plate photography passed away on May 24th as the result of a stroke about a month ago, his mental faculties remaining unimpaired until within a few hours of his death. B. J. Edwards is a name known to practically every photographer. He was the first in this country to manufacture orthochro- matic plates under Killer's method, and the quality of these plates, made first at Hackney, and afterwards at Ealing, had a great effect in popularising the use of colour sensitive materials. The intensification of plates by mer- curiciodide was originated by Mr. Edwards. He was the first to make a workable focal plane shutter, and he was one of the pioneers in de- signing what was then a revolution in the photo- graphic world, namely, the instantaneous shut- ter. Later on he applied his genius to improv- ing the Machinery for coating dry plates and papers. A remarkably productive career. Ire is fortunately succeeded by a daughter and two sons, the elder of whom is Mr. Austin Edwards, of Warwick.

SIXTY YEARS OF THE " 8.J." The present year is the sixtieth of continuous publication of the " British Journal of Photo- graphy." Founded in 1854, the "8.d." has wit- nessed the continued progress of the craft and Industry, which it has constantly sought to represent. Its pages have marked /the rise and disappearance of many a process, and it is not exceeding the truth to say that the modern de- velopment of dry-plate photography is most in- timately associated with the "British Journal." The first paper describing a method of making gelatine emulsion appeared in these pages, and during the years when the wet collodion process was in course of being superseded by the gela- tine dry-plate, practically all the information with regard to the improvements in emulsion- making became known through the contribu- tions of experimenters to the "British Journal." It has been decided to mark the completion of sixty years' publication by the issue with the " 8.J." for June 19 next of a twenty-four page supplement, Present." entitled " Photography, Past and

div.head: No Increase in Taxation in This Year's Budget.
div.p: No Increase in Taxation in This Year's Budget.
ELECTRIC LIGHTING FOR CYCLES.

The electric instalment for motors has come, and come to stay, and therefore, it is not sur- prising that the same method of lighting has been introduced for cycles. The surprising thing is that this has not been placed on the market before, since whatever may be said for the oil and the acetylene lamps, they have their failings. Perhaps the cheapness of these two methods of lighting has bad something to do with the matter. I am perfectly willing to own that the initial cost is rather greater with the electric light, but then the running charges are practically nil, being confined to the pur- chase of an occasional bulb. At the present time both magneto and accumulator outfits are on the market, but taking everything into con- sideration I prefer the former. The only draw- back is that when the machine is stationary there is no power and therefore no light. This system of lighting does away with all smell, which is more than can be said for either oil or acetylene. I have used a magneto lamp for some time and have not one word to say against it. My readers will be wise to inspect these in- stalments for themselves.

Cleaning Bearings. Dust and dirt have an unhappy knack of get- ting everywhere, and no matter how well your machine may be made, both will get into the bearings after a time. This is especially the case after runs on muddy or dusty roads, and unless removed the balls become clogged, and the machine requires a large amount of effort to propel it. It is a simple proposition to clean the bearings, and this should be done wherever they require it. The best way I know of accom- plishing this is to suspend the cycle and to pour paraffin oil into the bearings of the wheels and crank axle, making them revolve at the same time. At first the oil will come out very dark coloured, but the cleaning should continue until it is returned in its natural colour. Afterwards lubricating with the usual oil that you use will put the machine in first-class oiler. Do not be afraid to use plenty of pariffin, as this is im- portant, but if of an economical turn of mind you can collect the oil as it runs from the machine, allow the sediment to settle, drain and use a second time. In very bad cases it may be necessary to loosen the bearings, other- wise the oil may not run through. Care should, of course, be taken in tightening them again, so as to ensure easy running.

Weird Cycles. I wonder if any of my readers have seen some of the photographs of the latest American freak cycles that have been published. I have been vastly amused by a number of them, trying to imagine to myself how anyone could be silly enough to spend money on them. That the makers have not made them for exhibition alone is certain, and, therefore, there must be buyers. As far as I can make out, neither science nor utility have been considered, and evidently the manufacturers have only taken into account the gullibility of the general public. Their one aim has been to produce something that is out of the common. They have succeeded. In some cities supplementary curved tubes have been added, with the result of making the cycle heavier, but not one whit stronger or more reliable. One machine I saw the other day had a wheel for steering purposes instead of a handlebar, with what idea I cannot tell. The names of these freak cycles carry out the main idea; for in- stance, I have rend of the mo-bicycle, mo-cycle, I and the auto-cycle. If there are buyers, as there must be in the States, I am glad to say that such machines have not found their way into this country as yet.

The Motorists and Taxation. A would-be motoring friend of mine bas just written to ask for information regarding the taxation be will be subjected to on joining the ranks of the elete. The subject is one of those which everyone supposes everyone else to be quite familiar with, hut the details will bear repetition. First of all, every owner of a car must register it and obtain his distinguishing letter and number; this costs £l. Number plates, of which two are necessary, are the next item, but here there is no absolute standard of expense. The ordinary painted variety only cost a very few shillings, but the more elabor- ate ones which have to be specially made for every car, are naturally far more expensive. A driving licence now costs ss. But worse is to come—within three weeks of taking delivery the motorist must pay at least a ,t 2 2s. licence tax and an annual payment. The latter varies according to the power of the car from the ' moderate sum of £2 2s. to as much as ,t 42 for the owner of the palatial high-powered lemousine. Add to the above the petrol tax of 3d. per gal- lon, and the motorist is faced with a pretty bill! Still the Budget for this year shows no increase in taxation, so we must be satisfied with small mercies.

The Angling Motorist. The Committee of the R.A.C. have recently sanctioned a scheme which will appeal to those members who are interested in fishing. The idea is to form a Fishing Association, confined to members only, on the same lines as the R.A.C. Golfing Society. The scheme will be or- ganised as part of the touring department, but the services of a fishing expert who has had a great deal of experience have been secured, and lie will devote the whole of his time to the in- terests of the R.A.C. Fishing Association. In return for an annual subscription of eel is. any information possible with reference to fishing will be supplied, and not only is it hoped to secure waters later on for the sole use of the members of the Association, but in addition a special register will be maintained of members with private fishing who agree to entertain friendly exchanges on their waters from time to time. Already the Association has the privi- lege of letting a limited number of day tickets on some private trout water in Hampshire, and the tickets issued on this water will be reserved for members of the R.A.C. Fishing Association. I wish the latest innovation of the R.A.C. every possible success, and only wish it could be.ex- tended to angling motorists in general.

Will the Road Hog be Banished
iu Time?
A HOLIDAY ACCIDENIs4
The Editor of the C.T.C. writes

The Cyclists' Touring Club has taken thO keenest interest in the fatality which occurred on the night of Saturday, the 11th April, in which the cyclist, Mr. Henry Tyrrell, was killed and his companion, Miss Wells, seriously injured. The Council of the club has now de, cided to offer a reward of £5O to the first person whose information leads to the arrest and con- viction of the driver of the car who made off after the accident, and who has, up till now, succeeded in baffling the police in their efforts to trace him.

The Cyclists' Touring Club has been success- ful in a case of "driving to the common danger" taken up on behalf of one of its members. The cyclist was run down by the driver of a motor van on Putney Bridge, and had a miraculous escape from death. At the West London Police Court, on the 12th May, the man was fined 13 and Jl ss. costs.

The number of fatal accidents due to motor- ists who have immediately driven off into the darkness was increased by two this last week- end. The road hog has always been with us, even before cycles were heard of, and it mast not be forgotten that in the early days of the bicycle the name was applied to some of our own colleagues, though that cult, I am glad to say, has long ago died a natural death, amongst cyclists at least. No greater offenders were to be found in those days than the drivers of traps, or market carts, and the C.T.C. Gazettes are dotted with many cases (of races generally) that resulted in prison for the criminal convicted of manslaughter. But it was hard for the slow-going vehicles to escape.

Now, however, the motorist who has done what his folly or , wickedness has invited, can get away so easily that the police have a heavy task before them to stop this evil of the road. ' Much has already been done by jotting down the numbers of strange cars as they pass the man on duty, not only to detect offenders, but to put a wholesome fear into the mind of the reck- less cowards, who never know but their route will be traced if any trouble occurs. Yet the condition of the roads, in respect of dangerous driving, improves every year. The superior control over the engines, as well as the greater control over their own desires, generally to show off, is responsible for this, and the increasing number of people who use the roads is in itself a source not of danger, but of security. The fear of being found out has banished the highway man, and it will kill the road hog before many more years have passed.

div.p: WORK-A-DAY WONDERS.
VIII.-ABOUT THE LUCK THAT COMES THROUGH HELPING PEOPLE.

f' Well," said Patty, "if you ask me straight, I DO think Diamond Dyes are lucky. Just you look at the luck they have brought me! First I read about them in the 'Weekly News' and fiaw at once how it was that 1 had spoiled so many things in my past attempts at Home dye- ing. 'lt isn't likely,' 1 said to myself, that a one-packet-for-everything dye CAN be all round successful. If it's best for wool it can't be best for linen; if it's best for linen it can't be best for wool. Everybody knows that the big dye- ing firms separate dyes for different materials.' "Then, if you remember, I bought a sixpenny packet of Diamond Dye for wool and got the Diamond Dye Direction Book, which the grocer or chemist gives away with every packet of dye. And, first. I did my serge skirt—then Mrs. Finch's best blouse, and then I got round that cross-grained' Mrs. Bridges through Diamond- dyeing her linen. After that the luck seemed to come in faster than ever. There was Mrs. Hendry grateful as could be—and the minister's wife—and the old darling that's now next to a mother to me.

"So Diamond Dyes are mixed up somehow with all my luck. Of course, part of it comes of helping people—but then, as John King says, it has to be helping them with a GOOD thing,' and Diamond Dyes are that. "Have I let it out? Well, I don't care if you Do know now—for I shan't be Patty Prue that much longer—and you'll have a job to trace me as Mrs. Patricia King—so there!"

SUFFRAGISTS' HOPES FOR NEXT ELECTION.
That One Party will Include it in their Programme.

Lady Rochdale, speaking at the annual meet- ing of the Rochdale Women's Suffrage Society, said their movement had beeepushed into the background lately by the Irish question. Yet the enfranchisement of women was a far greater question, for it affected the world, while the Irish question, as far as it went, only affected the Empire. It was said by opponents of the movement that there were many women too ignorant to exercise the franchise. "Very well, why not then bring in a Bill to take away the vote from the ignorant men and make the more learned women voters?" she asked. Women wanted the vote because they wanted to make their womanhood of greater importance and of a higher character. The privilege would raise the whole status of women. It would not unsex women; it would help them to fight the battle of life better. It was possible at the next General Election that one of the great political parties would include women's suffrage in their programme, and she appealed to workers to create greater interest locally in the movement, particularly amongst the working men.

The Peebles Hotel Hydro. is a delightful health and pleasure resort in the glorious "land of mountain and of flood." Magnificently fur- nished, finely planned, replete with every com- fort and convenience which the most luxurious could desire, the Hotel-Hydro., near the charm- ing old-world town of l'eehles° and overlooking the beautiful valley of the Tweed, has now taken rank as one of the most successful and Popular resorts in the Kingdom. There are few more glorious views than that from the terrace of the Peebles Hotel-Hydro. itself. Perched high on the north bank of "Tweed's silver stream," 600 feet above sea level, shel- tered from inclement winds, and commanding an unrivalled panoramic view of the bold Pent- lands Hills, the prospect is, one of remarkable beauty. Facing due south, the Hydro. basks all day in the health-renewing rays of the sun, and with its salubrious and recuperative air. The First Woman Aviation Pilot. The first woman to take aviation so seriously as to adopt it as a profession is Mrs. Winifred Buller, who acts as pilot for an important com- pany of aeroplane builders. Although she is an expert in flying, the firm are not anxious that Mrs. Buller Should entei for races, since there is more risk at such times, the number of machines in the air at, one time having a dis- turbing influence on the currents, and thus in- creasing the danger. But Mrs. Buller is never- theless anxious to take part in races. The feat of theyrench lady who ascended strapped to the underpart of a flying machine, and when nearly a thousand feet above the earth, extri- cated herself and descended calmly and serenely —also safely—in a parachute of her husband's invention, has never been paralleled. It was a most daring experiment, and certainly a proof that women are not wanting in courage. Flats with Garden Terraces. _

'Mere are, however, tunics and tunics, and the danger is that the short plump and the tall And lanky woman may choose the model the least adapted to their individual needs. Pro- perly cut and adjusted, the tunic may be trusted to make any woman look graceful, the long, straight model, over a narrow skirt being best iuited to all figures. It may be full on the hips if the fulness is an improvement, or it may be flat and shaped to the figure with a flowing movement near the feet. Every dress has a tunic of some sort, or it has draperies to simulate the tunic effect.

For the River or Country. River frocks are particularly attractive this year, and a skirt of soft pliable pique 'with shirts of mercerised lawn, washing crepe, or any of this season's delightful cotton fabrics, with a. shady hat, make an ideal country or river suit. The shirts should be tailor-made and well cut, loose under the arm, with narrow, hori- zontal yokes reaching the throat, but pointed on the shoulders in the quaint Victorian style that is more suited to the river than an open front. The new combination garment is an ideal one for summer wear, it has so little bulk, yet answers the purpose of camisole and knickers. For evening wear the former can be very easily made of a twelve-inch strip of embroidery ar- ranged fichu fashion and gathered into a cross- way basque about two inches in depth. The under part of the sleeves is of the embroidery, the upper part of white or coloured ribbon; whilst the shoulders have ribbon straps that support the camisole. This little garment is in one piece only.

. The far-famed hanging gardens of Babylon have provided a modern architect with an idea for an improved house. The front of this novel erection, instead of being perpendicular, recedes with each story sufficiently to admit of a broad promenade being constructed on each fiat under- neath. It is claimed that this type of house gets more sun and air than the straight-fronted and that daylight lasts an hour longer in the street where this plan is adopted, besides which it is more economical to build, as greater height can be attained. An experimental terrace of nine flats in each house has been constructed, and as the promenades are in each case made into gardens, the effect is not only curious but refreshing to the eye. Every room in the ex- perimental terrace is sound proof, and there are I no chimneys in the block, a radiator in each room providing uniform and pleasant heat.

Small Print Bibles. The medical department of the Derbyshire Education Committee has been investigating the influence of the type used in school books upon the eyesight of children, and condemns the use la and bulky book, must be in of small print Bibles. The whole Bible, if it is not to he a large small type, but in many public and preparatory schools abbreviated editions are used, not only to the advantage of the students eyesight, but of their appreciation of the "Book of books." The education authorities might well follow this example and issue specially the portions of the Bible required in State schools.

The progress of Esperanto during the last few years has exceeded the anticipations of even the most sanguine, and it is no exaggeration to say that the obstacles which retard its final and universal adoption are one by one breaking down. The many and varied schools of thought are becoming more and more convinced that this wonderful and extremely interesting second lan- guaie for all has justified its existence. Its practicability and fitness to survive can be judged by the fact that during 1913 no fewer' than 14 National Esperanto Congresses were I held; and by the Esperanto days held in connec- tion with the big International Exhibition, particularly at Ghent (Belgium), Breslau (Ger- many), and Kieff (Russia). The crowning effort of the year was the ninth Universal Esperanto Congress held in August at Bern in Switzerland under the hon. presi- dency of Colonel Frey, director of Swiss Tele- graphs, when upwards ,of 1,100 Esperantists from 23 different countries took part in the Congress. At the business meeting a most im- portant decision • was arrived at, viz.: The foundation of an International Association of Esperantist Propaganda Societies, with a cen- tral Bureau at Paris.

A significant feature of these International Congresses is the increasing number of meet- ings of various Specialist Societies, where sci- entists, doctors, social reformers, vegetarians, postal officials, Esperantist policemen, jurists, &c., meet to discuss matters pertaining to their particular interests. On every hand we see a steadily increasing acceptance of Esperanto. Its use has been offi- cially admitted at the International Congresses of the Theosophical, Anti-alcoholic and Red Cross Societies.

In September the Catholic ,Esperantists held a pilgrimage to Rome, where their fourth Con- gress took place. Here the Pope signified his approval and appreciation of Esperanto by giv- ing his special blessing to the Esperantists in the presence of 8,000 pilgrims, and by allowing the Catholic Esperanto hymn to be played by the Vatican orchestra immediately after the ceremony. It was proved conclusively at the great Inter- national Congress of Esperantists doctors, held in London, that discussions are much more use- ful and comprehensive when carried on in Esperanto than in the other Congress languages; the English newspapers also recognised and em- phasised this advantage of Esperanto.

So impressive is the utility of this language that the International Exhibition for Naval Affairs and Marine Hygiene at Genoa and the Universal Exhibition of Book Industries in Leipzig have been induced to use it in making their names and objects known abroad. For some years now Esperanto has been a grant-earning subject in the evening schools, under the Board of Education. • The good ex 7 ample being shown first by France, is now being followed with ever-increasing zeal by Germany. It has been taught as an optional subject in various higher grade and commercial schools in Augsburg for some considerable time, and is 'low being introduced with excellent results into middle grade schools. The Saxon Esperanto In- stitute has, with special Government sanction, established branch Esperanto Schools in Dres- den, Leipzig, Zittau, Chemnitz, Plauen, and Auerbach.

The local Parliament of Rio de Janeiro, in Brazil, passed into law a Bill introduced by the President, providing that, for all public offices open to general competition, preference be given to those who understand Esperanto, and who hold the certificate of the Brazilian Esperanto Association, also that Esperanto be made an optional subject in all ordinary and middle grade schools. Similar provisions have also been made in Sergipe and Sao Paulo. And so one might go on indefinitely, for even in China, Japan, Persia, &c., enthusiastic Esper- antists are to be found. Thus the last strong- hold of objection of many critics who thought that Esperanto would never be grasped by the Orient has been broken down, and truthfully one may speak of the completion of the " Rondo Familia " (family circle). 1111 k

div.head: HINTS ON HEALTH.
div.p: HINTS ON HEALTH.
The Value of Oranges.

Just now, when English-grown fruit is most difficult to get, the orange is distinctly valuable. Few fruits, and certainly no medicines, can com- pare with it for the benefit it confers on those who use it freely. Besides which, it is a most delightful fruit to partake of, and it may be said that the appetite almost grows by what it feeds upon. In cases where the pulp of the fruit is not wanted, the oranges should be squeezed into a glass and the juice drunk (without sugar or water). To invalids and convalescents noth- ing could be more grateful or cooling. It is not too much to say that every organ of the body is helped in the action by a liberal diet of sweet, juicy oranges, such as can now be obtained at Moderate prices. An orange should not need sugar—its own sweetness should be sufficient. It has a wonderfully cleansing effect on the whole digestive tract, gives the blood greater fluidity and brightness, and has a stim- ulating effect upon the whole system. The man who drinks alcohol is being crowded to the wall:: Railroad companies do not want him, mill-owners pass him by, and private em- ployers do not give him a welcome. Even the pub-keeper loses interest in him as soon as his money runs out. The time spent in drinking is a frightful waste of good manhood. Drink brings a harvest of tears and shame, and leaves a ruin of broken homes and heat-crushed women and dhildren.

Ingenious Smuggling Device. A curious discovery is reported from Pfund- stadt, near Frankfort-on-Main, states the Berlin correspondent of the " Chronicle." A merry- go-round arrived there from Switzerland, and on examining it the police made a remarkable discovery. The wooden horses were found to be hollowed out and filled with packets of sacchar- ine. Altogether 20ewt. of saccharine was dis- covered, and, of course, seized. The owner of the merry-go-round has disappeared.

div.head: Sootf all.
div.p: Sootf all.

The sootfall of Pittsburg, as determined from careful measurements during the past year, ranges from 595 to 1,950 tons per square mile per annum. The destructive possibilities of this immense deposit may be illustrated by stat- ing that if an equal amount Of lampblack were ground with oil so as to form black paint it would cover from 17 to 57 square miles with two coats. -Statistics of sootfall at certain places in Great Britain are as follows: Industrial sec- tion of Leeds, 529 tons; centre of London, 426 tons; Glasgow, 820 tons.

div.head: Bermuda's Rain Catch.
div.p: Bermuda's Rain Catch.

The rain catch is a notable incident of the Bermuda landscape. There is no other good water. All that is gained from wells is brabkish. So the people either use their whitewashed roofs as a means to catch rain-water or they build a big open " catch " on the hillside, with a covered cistern at its foot into which the rain, thus col- lected, runs and is stored. The soil is scraped away from a large surface of the white coral rock that underlies all the island. This surface is cemented and whitewashed, and a low wall built on three sides with the reservoir or tank at the 'bottom.

div.head: Unwanted Jan.
div.p: The Unwanted Jan.

" Coming. down the coast, I noticed that you have no population," remarked Mr. Uyematsu, a director of the Mitsu Bishi Shipbuilding Com- pany, Japan, when he arrived in Brisbane re- cently. " That seems strange," he continued, "In Japan you would see houses everywhere. Japan is over-populated, and Australia is under- Populated. Yet you don't want us. Our people are emigrating to Manchuria and Korea. We owe a lot to the British, and we have learned much from them. Our shipyards are manned by Japanese. The European officials whom we employed at one time have retired graduallY, and they have been rePlaced by Japanese."

div.head: Wireless Music for Liners.
div.p: Wireless Music for Liners.

An invention called the audiphone amplifier, for use on board passenger ships, was tested With satisfactory results by a United States fruit compan4'B steamer. It enables a vessel to he supplied with music from the land by wireless. Another development in wireless tele- phony which is now being tried by the Lacka- wanna Railroad Company aims to secure com- munication between stations and moving trains. A considerable degree of success is already reported, but the experiments are in- complete. The Lackawanna Company's officials declare that the perfection of the arrangement, as is hoped will occur shortly, will add vastly to the safety of railway traffic. - •

The Wedding Day of Theii• Majesties lii July the King and Queen will celebrate the twenty-first anniversary of their wedding day. It may be pointed out that Queen Mary has only one predecessor since the Conquest, who as Queen Consort has borne her name, although there have been two Queens Regnant named Mary. The second wife of James 11. was Mary d' Este, an Italian princess, and mother of the Pretender. Although still young, our Queen, if Carmen Sylva be excepted, comes next to the German Empress in seniority. The latter was born in 1858, whilst the Queens of Belgium, Denmark, Greece, Italy 'and the Empress of Russia were all born in the seventies; the Queens of the Netherlands and of Spain dating from the eighties.

div.head: Royal Sisters.
div.p: Royal Sisters.

The affection existing between the Royal Sisters of Denmark—our own beloyed Queen Alexandra and the Dowager Empress of Russia —finds a parallel in the sisterly love borne by the Dowager Queen of the Netherlands—now on a visit to this country—and the Duchess of Albany, to each other. The latter, with her children, was so frequent a visitor to the Court of Holland, before Queen Wilhelmina, came of age, that suites of rooms were reserved for them in all the Royal palaces, and since the Queen- Mother has been relieved of the onerous duties of Regent of the country and guardian of her dafighter, she has paid frequent visits to this country.

div.head: MEMS. FOR MOTHERS. Leading a Child by the Hand.
div.p: MEMS. FOR MOTHERS. Leading a Child by the Hand.

Has it ever occurred to you that a young child suffers a considerable amount of discomfort, fatigue, and even pain by its little arm being held up to meet the hand of the person leading it? Perhaps during a long walk the limb is in this unnatural position for nearly an hour with- out being released, and all that time the blood is prevented having its proper circulation. When it is necessary to hold the child's hand the older person should reach down as far as possible, even at the risk of inconvenience, and the other hand should be frequently taken in change. I have known a child's hand to be icy cold after being held up for a long time, owing to the blood running down from it.

div.head: Cure for Dandruff.
div.p: A Cure for Dandruff.

Dandruff is a very tiresome affection of the scalp, which spoils the health and appearance of the hair. A preparation of one ounce of sul- phur and one quart of water, repeatedly agitated at intervals of a few hours, will in a few weeks remove every trace of dandruff from the scalp, if the head is saturated every morning with the clear liquid. The hair, under this treatment, will become soft and glossy. The burning, irri- tating feeling which always accompanies this trouble is due to the dry state of the skin of the head. _ -

Another treatment of scales recommended is this :—Wash the head once a week, with a good tepid lather, and rub into the scalp thereafter a little glycerine and borax. Each morning rub into the roots of the hair, with a small piece of sponge, a little of this lotion—vinegar of can- tharides, 4 ounce; eau de Cologne, 1 ounco; rose water, 1 ounce. Mix.

Of the comfort and convenience of the Hotel- Hydro. itself it is impossible .to speak too highly. Of out-door recreation there is plenty of variety within the 33 acres of the Hotel-Hydro. grounds. The facilities for golf-putting, tennis, croquet, bowls, &c., are particularly good on the well- kept lawns. Then the golfers are given special terms at the fine 18-hole course which is not far away. The links are particularly " sporting " and the "holes" are very varied. For anglers the Peebles district will be found a Perfect Paradise. The Hydro., however, while making plenty of provision for the hale and hearty, holiday- maker, caters equally for the invalid and those run down in health. The baths are wonderfully complete, and a journey to any of the Contin- ental Spas need not be undertaken when every-. thing to be obtained there can be found just as perfectly at Peebles and at so much less expense. In short, the Hydro. is an ideal place for a delightful holiday, with every possible form of outdoor amusement—golf, tennis, croquet, bowls, motoring, fishing, cycling—amid the most charming scenery; whilst indoors, a spacious ballroom, resident orchestra and all social amusements finish up the evenings well. At the same time it is a fully-equipped Hydro. with all the advantages of a Continental Spa under one roof. All the latest baths and elec- trical treatment—resident physician. A new gymnasium has recently been completed. Their latest brochure, with full details, is sent post free by the Manager, W. A. Thiem, Hotel- Hydro., Peebles.

div.head: COOKERY CORNER.
div.p: COOKERY CORNER.
Recipes for Simple Dishes.

To make rye bread get 21b. of rye flour, which can be got at any grain merchant's, and 11b. of white flour dough (from your baker). You will also require one teaspoonful salt and half a tea- spoonful carraway seeds. Make a sponge of the dough, • half the rye flour, and three half-pint cups of lukewarm water. Set it to rise for three hours, perhaps longer; then add the salt, seeds, and the remainder of the rye flour. Set to rise again till double the original size; make into small loaves, and bake in a moderate oven for about li‘lf an hour.

Soft Gingerbread. Four cups flour; one cup each butter, sugar, syrup, and buttermilk; one tablespoonful each ginger and cinnamon; one teaspoonful soda; four eggs; a little salt. Beat the butter and sugar till well creamed; add the syrup, flour, spices, and the yolks of the eggs; stir the soda into the buttermilk, and add it. Last of all, stir in the whisked whites of the eggs. Bake in a moderate oven for l hour.

div.head: Cucumber Salad.
div.p: Cucumber Salad.

There is sometimes to be found a prejudice against this delicious and cooling vegetable, and I am inclined to think that this prejudice only exists where there is carelessness or ignor- ance in the selection of the cucumber, and also in its preparation. In the first place it must be fresh, and newly cut from the vine;. it must be firm to the touch and very brittle. If it bends it is not fresh. Then some people do not quite understand how to make it into a salad. Remove the peel, cut the cucumber into thin slices, and sprinkle them with salt. In about 20 minutes drain off the liquid. Wash and mince two or three young green onions, and wash, drain and break in small pieces the crisp heart of a lettuce. Put all into the salad bowl, and pour over a simple dressing of oil, vinegar, .salt, and pepper.

From 1500 to 1535 the num- ber of books produced annually averaged only It was not until 1700 that the annual average passed 10,000, and it was not until 1887 that it reacited 100,900. He said be was in expectation of marrying the world's most natural girl. The bridegroom is Mr. Jan van der Blassbalk, aged 40, formerly the owner of a glass factory in Batavia, Java; and to substantiate his claim to artificiality he has a cork leg, a cork arm, a ruler ear, a glass eye, and wears a wig. It appears that while he was experimenting with chemicals an explosion occurred which left him but little of his natural self.

Four Guardians Who Drove to Padgate in Carriage and Pair.
A HUMOROUS DISCUSSION.

The Guardians who are members of the Pad- gate Homes Committee drove there on Tuesday " in style," as the Rev. A. M. Mitchell, at the last meeting of the Guardians, suggested they should do. He complained about one .horse being employed to pull ten Guardians, all per- sons of weight. For the committee meeting at Padgate on Tuesday a carriage and pair was provided, and only four members used the vehicle.

On the minutes of the committee coming before the Guardians meeting on Wednesday, Mr. G. MATHER jocularly said he wished to report that at the meeting of the Padgate Homes Committee on the previous day they had a car- riage and pair, yet a member had referred to the Guardians as an inhumane Board. The Rev. A. M. MITCHELL: I take exception to that—it's not parliamentary. (Laughter.) Mr. MATHER : Ever since they had one horse-- (the Rev. A. M. MrrcnELL : But there were two horses)—to convey the Guardians to Padgate there have been complaints, but on Tuesday they drove up in a chariot and pair, and there were only four members inside. (Laughter.) I think I should report. on that. (Laughter.)

WHY NOT WALK? Mr. DENNETT, a new member, said he would like to add something to the remarks of Mr. Mather. Mr. Mitchell had referred to the cruelty in having one horse, and on Tuesday the four members had two horses. Did that not mean an extra cost to the ratepayers? He thought the four members should pay the extra cost.
Mr. FURNESS : Charge the cost of the extra horse against the member for the Burtonwood parish. (Laughter.)

, Mr. MITCHELL thought it was not fair to charge the members of the Eiggird with being inhumane, as the member for Fearnhead (Mr. Mather) had done. Ire resented that charge,. and he thought that Mr. Mather should prove it. (Laughter.) As regarded Tuesday, the members forgot the fact it was Whit Tuesday, and the majority of the members of the committee had not recovered from the Whit Monday holiday, and that, no doubt, would account for the small attendance. Suppose there were eight or nine members pres- ent, no fault would have been made about hav- ing—two horses. It was • better to have two horses for a light burden than one horse for a heavy burden. In employing two horses on Tuesday they were showing themselves humani- tarians, and Mr. Mather ought to be thoroughly ashamed of himself and covered with confusion for the remark he had made. (Laughter.) The CHAIRMAN (Mr. A. J. Jolley): He would take a great deal before he was covered with confusion. (Laughter.) _
, Mr. MITCHELL ! I know it takes a great deal to cover Mr. Mather with confusion, but I sin- cerely think in this case he ought to be covered with confusion. (Laughter.)

A SALARY OF £l5O A YEAR. Mr. DENNETT said he appreciated ,the Rey.. Mr. Mitchell's sympathy with animals—(laughter)— but he (Mr. Bennett) had no pony, and had to walk to the meetings at the Homes. The War- rington contingent could travel by tram or train and walk from the terminus or station. He had to walk three times that distance. He sug- gested for the benefit of the rates that these members find their own conveyances. (Hear, hear.) Mr. MITCHELL thought the last suggestion was going rather too far. He had to pay between £7 and £8 a year inDorder to fulfil his duties as a Guardian, and he did not think any other Guardian paid so much in fares. He did mit see why he should have to tramp from Bank Quay Station to the Padgate Homes. Of course, he could hire a motor car, but he was not going to do it. (Laughter.) On the other hand, he thought all his ex- penses ought to be paid. (Laughter.) He thought the time had come when they should have a motion brought forward that Guardians be paid £l5O per year. (Laughter and ap- plause.) VOW

FLAVOUR AS IMPORTANT. If it were not for flavour we should not digest our food properly. Epicureanism in eating is the handmaid of good health. Flavour has been called the soul of food. The viands that are most. agreeable to our sense of taste, those we enjoy most, are those we are most likely to digest well and from which we are most likely to derive the maxituum of nourishment. A whole book was devoted to this subject by Henry T. Finck, of New York. He called it "Food and Flavour." In a review of it the " Scientific American" says: "The psychic factor of desire must precede ingestion, or re- sults will be unpropitious. To each cent, spent for nutriment we add five more for flavour. Flavour, in short, has an appetising value, a health value, a commercial value. The evolu- tion of a discriminating appetite and the educa- tion of the cook must go hand in hand. But your glutton is never an epicure. Rational mastication must accompany the highest enjoy- ment of food, and in this enjoyment lie perfect assimilation and health. It is flavour that stimulates the flow of the digestive juices; it is the digestive juices that prepare the food for the extraction of nutriment."

KING EDWARD AT HOMBURG. "On the Track of the Great," by Aubrey Stanhope, shows that very varied experiences, indeed, have brought Mr. Stanhope into touch with many interesting personalities. In dealing with the various Monarchs he has met with, he adds one more to the many portraits which have appeared of King Edward. Mr. Stanhope met the late King, then Prince of Wales, at Hom- burg. He describes the highly. managed and regularised life of the Prince. "It was quite surprising," he says, "to see how simply he lived in Homburg. A small sitting-room, a little writing bureau, a very modest bedroom, with a couple of small rooms at the back, one to serve as office for the equerry, and that was all. . He was always in good spirits, and laughad constantly, making a peculiar sort of chuckling sound as he did so, and giving himself up heart and soul to the pleasure of the moment." A whole chapter is devoted to anecdotes con- cerning King Edward in " those jolly Homburg days," as Mr. Stanhope describes the time. Here is just a little picture which is quite charming : With a great number of the local people the Prince of Wales was on very friendly terms. Each time lie arrived for the first visit to the Elisabeth Spring he would go up to where the flower-stands were, and there shake hands cordially with Frau Zeininger, his :favourite flower saleswoman. And as Frau Zeininger had much to do with roses, her hands were rough and torn with the thorns.

THE LIFE OF GEORGE OF GREECE. As the brother of Queen Alexandra, as one who had for a long series of years laboured seriously and well for the country of his adop- tion, King George of Greece has long been an

div.head: :Wilk 'NO I. %ilk VIM Wilk NEM %Mk VW law
div.p: :Wilk 'NO I. %ilk VIM Wilk NEM %Mk VW law

interesting figure to English people, and many should welcome this admirable and sympath- etic presentation of his character and story of his life. In the introductory chapter the author, Cap- tain Walter Christmas, descrihes the way in which he first ;net King George. He was at the Lime but "a little ship's boy," doing his work as an officer's servant--such work being then the preliminary part of a Danish naval cadet's duties; his vessel was in the Pirmus, and the King of Greece came on board and invited two of the boys to be his visitors at the Palace. It reads like some bit of one of Hans Ander- sen's stories, the account of "those seven weeks of splendour and delight" in the lives of the young sailors, and it forms a capital introduc- tion to the story of King George's half-century as ruler of Greece, for we see the simplicity and dignity, the intimate home life, of the Danish' Prince to whom it fell to play an important part in the regeneration of Greece. Prince William of Denmark became King George of Greece at the age of 18, and, with the confident spirit of youth, entered upon a task which might well have seemed an impossible one in the face of the recent history of his new kingdom. The Danish youth had to prove that, as ruler of a nation which contemporary sceptics condemned to a hopeless decadence, he could lead his kingdom through the trials of re- birth, through crises and perils to new life in the path of development and progress. How well he proved it is shown in the history of Greece during the past half-century, a his- tory which, despite sets-back and difficulties, has assuredly been one of remarkable progress. The King was, indeed, an astute, practical man; it was largely owing to his initiative that Greece built up a considerable mercantile marine, and during his many journeys about Europe--" I am my, own Ambassador" is said to have been his favourite dictum—he was ever ready to think of what he could do to benefit his people.

div.head: RUNCORN POLICEMAN'S LONG WATCH.
div.p: RUNCORN POLICEMAN'S LONG WATCH.

Richard Matthew Jones, a native of Widnes, was committed to gaol by the Runcorn magis- trates on Tuesday for 14 days' hard labour for loitering with intent in Penketh-lane the pre- vious evening. The prisoner, by his movements on the Fair Ground, aroused thp suspicions of Constable Tudor, who had him under observa- tion for two hours and a half. He was seen to follow young girls about, and when questioned by the officer he said, "I have not been- picking Pockets."—Prisoner said he went to Runcorn early in the day for pleasure. lie had no inten- tion of doing anything wrong.—Superintendent Owen .said he had made inquiries. The prisoner had given them a false address. He was a man separated from his wife, and lived in common lodging-liouses. lie had one previous conviction.

A letter complaining that the music of a Territorial Band which marched past a Carnar- von church on Sunday morning disturbed the service has been sent to the Commanding Officer by the Pastor. Letters of protest were also sent to the police authorities and the Town Council.
