There was a -striking c—oarast between the win by five points of the Junior Conservatives and that of 73 by Bull's Head. The Juniors won all the games at Warrington and they needed every point, too, for at Earlestown Bate had gone down 4-21, Melbourne 9-21, Black- ledge and Armitage 10-21, and Gatley and Holbrook had only won by majorities of two and three. At Warrington it was always the Juniors' game, and they sent the Earlestown men home beaten by 60 points. The Crosfield's contingent was no match for the Bull's Head men at Church-street, for they went down by 64 points. On their own green, however, Crosfield's only lost by nixie points, and that is not bad when one considers the men included in the Bull's Head team. VICTORIOUS WHITECROSS.

The matches between Fearnhead and White- cross were keenly contested, although on their own green Whitecross were successful in win- ning by 56 points, which was just as much again as the Fearnhead majority at home. Jos. Weston and J. Appleton played a good game, the former only winning by the odd point in 29 ends, after his opponent had led 19-18. At Whitecross the victors did not return one los- ing card, and only one of the opposition ran up a score of 17, all the others being under that number.
The third round will be played to-day, and the first round in the Consolation Competition should be commenced.

majorities that could leave no doubt as to which were the better teams. The railwaymen and the Union Tanneries were 48 points each better than Longford (No. 2) and Whitecross .(No. 1). In the former match Cheshire Lines had a bene- fit in the handicap, and only lost four out of the twelve games, and these by no large majorities. Longford (No. 3) men had a certain amount of hard luck to lose by 24 points, for several of their men only lost by a few points, two by one point, six by two points, two by three, and one by five. However, it must be said that only one of their players had a start of less than six points. A. Richardson (7) and E. Llewellyn (7) put up a good game, although the latter, who led 14-9 at the eighth end, was always consid- ered the winner. Several of the other games were full of exciting incidents. Although they played a brilliant match, the Whitecross men found the opposition handicap too big, and although they started off in fine style, winning three out of the first four matches, they ultimately lost by close upon 56 points. Amongst the best games were those played by J. Gregory (5) and T. Edgington (3), A. Warburton (1) and P. PiHingham (5), J. Spilsbury (3) and S. Baker (7), and J. Horton (2) and E. Lloyd (7). The Tanneries have everything in their favour, and if they main- tain Saturday's form on such a huge handicap they should go a long way.

JOINERS v. TANNERS. Whilst no one hardly expected such a result in the match between Crosfield's Joiners and Fenketh Tannery, one cannot help commenting on the fact that the Joiners were rather patron- isingly treated by fate. Of course, no one would be so unjust as to say that it was a fluky win; the only thing that can be said is that they had more luck than their opponents. There were some good men on each side and a typical game was that between T. Jackson (1) and J. Bowyer (2). The latter player started off in promising fashion, running up to 13-7 in fourteen ends. But here Jackson found a good length and stuck to the jack up to the finish, when he recorded a two points win. W. Shave (5) and If. Wilcocks (6) fought hard, but here again Wilcocks broke down, after having led 13-8 and never scored • again. GREENING'S BEATEN. Rylands' (No. 3) team are a good set of trund- lers and one of the best matches of the after- noon was witnessed when they beat Greening's by nine points. A. Littlewood (4) and A. Gil- bert (6) were a well-matched couple, and after having kept very close together in the scores, there was only three points difference at the completion of 14 ends. L. Bate (5), the Rylands' captain, looked like being hopelessly beaten by H. Hughes (7), for he was in arrears 8-14 at the eighth end. Here he got the jack and ran to within one of his opponent in three ends, when he finally lost the jack and—the game. An even game was played between J. Hankinson (6) and 11. Houghton (5), tne forme/ only winning by a couple after 10-10 and 1:1-13 had been recorded.

div.p: TUBE MEN'S SUCCESS.

. _ The men from the Tube Department at Monks, Hall's Works feel very pleased with themselves now that they have entered the third round at the expense of Thewlis and Griffiths (No. 1). Each man played a hard game, A. Molyneux (5), only being beaten by C. Tranter (6), 15-14, after having peeled at 6,8, 9, 11 and 14. W. Thomason (2) gave F. Molyneux (5), a good run for his money, or, rather, his one point victory, for the game ex- tended over 21 ends. Thomason had every chance of winning when he led 14-11 at the 16th end. His opponent bowled a better wood and then ran to game with a double and two singles. Another good day's sport is promised for to-day. COCO AMATEUR GAMES. •
Warrington and District Association.

Eight home-and-home matches in the second round of the Club Championship Competition in connection with the above association were decided on Saturday, and some fine matches are reported. Rylands' (No. 1) made themselves felt both at home and at Woolston, winning by a total majority of 42 points. The best indi- vidual games were played at Woolston, where A. Stringer, one of the two beaten men from Warrington, lost to J. Houghton by three points. The Warrington man had the best of the game at the outset, but at the 21st end Houghton pulled up and ran to 18-18. Stringer only registered two more singles, although he played hard to win. G. Monks had a struggle with J. Hepherd, who, although he was 12-19 in arrears, did not give up, but pegged away, to come to within two points of Monks at the finish. James Hepherd also lost in a similar game with I. Newton, although the Warrington man had led 20-17. At Gorsey-lane the Lang- lays did not come up to expectations, for two of them lost their games. J. Langley, however, made short work of his opponent by defeating him 21-11.

CEMETERY BEATEN. This was a great match, for the teams—the Cemetery Hotel and the Senior Conservatives— were the finalists last year, and are always keen rivals. At the Cemetery Hotel the homesters won by 24, winning all but two games, but at Sankey-street only two of their men managed to win. T. Ellison, however, had nothing to give against J. Jennings, for that player compiled 20 in a commendable fashion. R. F. Ander4on was just the one point better than T. Bolton, but H. P. Turner had nothing to do to beat A. Foster 21-5. The Seniors should go well in the competition now that their most feared opponents are vanquished.

BREWERY TEAM LOSE. Though losing to King and Queen, Walker's Brewery have no need to be ashamed, for they put up a genuinely good game at Arpley, to win by nine points, but at the King and Queen they could not keep defeat away, but they minimised the majority better than was expected. J. Dagnall set a good example by beating J. War- burton 21-15, but G. Bates went under to the next Padgate-lane man by eight points. A. Glover won his game against J. Brown by two points, after a strenuous game had been played.

div.head: TIE.
div.p: A TIE.

Croft and Walton both sent the right men to the right place, for the players came home with a 14 points' win to their credit, which makes the game a tied one. At Croft F. Shaw and T. Fazackerley opened the game in promising style, for when they left the green there was only two points between them. W. Onions and H. Shaw played a similar game at Falton, where the former lost by three points only, although at the 23rd end the Croft man was leading 20-11.

LIBERAL CLUB AT EARLESTOWN. The Liberal Club were defeated at Earlestown. The players found it very difficult indeed to get the proper land, and although at home they won by a comfortable majority, on the two matches they lost by seven points. At Earlestown M. Tobin, F. Walker and the two Broadhursts were not beaten so badly, only a matter of a couple of points or so separating them from their opponents. At Warrington, J. Bridge and T. Davies played a game worth witnessing, for the Liberal only lost by three points in 33 ends. The final issue could never be forecasted with any degree of certainty, for at the 31st end Davies was only 18-19 in arrears. Joe Benion might have made his majority over T. NOTICE. We shall be pleased to receive from Secretaries scores and details of bowling in matches played in this locality. Out of the way feats with bat or ball, or in the field, will be specially welcomed, and will be used as NOTES. Particulars should reach "The Examiner" Office as early in the week as possible.

div.head: WARRINGTON'S TWO DRAWS. Games Left Unfinished.
div.p: WARRINGTON'S TWO DRAWS. Games Left Unfinished.

Warrington celebrated the holidays by playing two m'atches, each of which ended in a draw. They were at Prescot on Saturday, and the local team knocked up 180 at the cost of four wickets, when they declared, leaving Warrington not very much time, and the result was that the Arpley men had only compiled 124 for eight wickets when the game ended. On the Warrington side T. Wright batted remarkably well and had the honour of regis- tering his half-century, when he put up a rather soft ball, which was promptly caught by Mercer. W. Richardson, who seems to be batting consistently, made a nice 25, but soon after, through a misunderstanding, had the mis- fortune to be run out.

The Warrington howling .was not as deadly as it has been in some previous matches this season. W. Bennett came out on top of the analysis with three wickets for 54 runs, got in 22 °vers. Hannam bowled 24 overs, and lost 62 runs for one wicket. The three other trundlers I failed te take a wicket

div.head: DRAW AT •NORTHWICH.
div.p: DRAW AT •NORTHWICH.

In the match played at Northwich on Whit- Tuesday the home side made 166 before they were disposed of, Hilditch, with 43, proving their top scorer. Warrington replied with 58 for the loss of four wickets. W. Richardson maintained his steady form and made a carefully played 37. There was an improvement in the bowling of the Warrington trundlers. W. Bennett, in 21.2 overs, took eight wickets at the cost of 60 runs. S. Partridge had two wickets for 34 runs.

CAIRO-STREET STILL WINNING. Cairo-street met Widnes St. Ambrose'. Both teams had unbeaten certificates, and after an exciting game the Unitarians ran out winners by 8 runs. At one period things were anything but rosy for Cairo-street, as they had 8 wickets down for 16 runs, but thanks to a nice stand by Forbes (12) and Wright (5 not out) they pulled the game off. Ellsmore (7 for 11) and Mather (3 for 10) were the destructive agents for the visitors. For Widnes, Oliver (6 for 17) and Cleworth (2 for 10) did the damage. Cairo-street Unitarians 2nd beat Emmanuel 2nd at Arpley on Whit Monday, and so main- tained their unbeaten certificate. For the win- ners Mather and Ellsmore bowled well, taking 6 wickets for 10 runs and 4 for 12 respectively. Oakes was in fine form for the losers, taking 5 wickets for 14 runs. The only batsman to show any resistance against the bowling was T. Knight, who really batted well for a few runs.

div.head: LOCAL DERBY.
div.p: A LOCAL DERBY.

There will be a local Derby match to-day be- tween Working Men's Mission and Cairo-street Unitarian 2nd. The following will represent the Unitarians: W. llankinson (capt.), J. Bailey, A. Ellsmore, C. Harvey-Cook, A. H. Mather, A. Forbes, S. Wright, F. Ellsmore, F. McKie, P. Hill, J. Hallam. Reserves J. Whit- taker, R. 11111 and J. Moore.

div.head: EMMANUEL'S FINE WIN.
div.p: EMMANUEL'S FINE WIN.

_ Emmanuel added another win to their un- beaten record this season by defeating Golborne- street C.C. on Saturday. C. Harrison carried out his bat with 15 to his credit, anctS. Hughes took 6 wickets for 10 runs. Emmanuel Juniors met 01....ir0-street Juniors in a friendly match on Monday, and were de- feated by 10 runs. A. Oakes bowled well for the losers, and W. Eaton made a fair stand for his 7.
STOCKTON HEATH _BEAT RYLANDS'
RECS. 2ND.

Stockton Heath entertained Rylands' Recs. 2nd on Saturday, at Appleton, and were successful in beating the Rees' team by 33 runs, the score being 103 to 70. For Stockton Heath, the Brothers Harold and Fred Moors batted excep- tionally well, their scores being 30 and 37 re- spectively. While they were at the wicket they made very few mistakes, and if they bat in such form throughout the season, Stockton Heath will come out with a very good record. For Rylands' Recs., Hicks took 3 wickets for 12. Smalley batted well for Rylands', scoring 25 not out, and Warren was unlucky in being run ouT when he had made 19. Knight again bowled well for Stockton Heath, taking 3 wickets for 10 runs.

WINWICK'S FOURTH DEFEAT. Winwick Asylum met with their fourth de- feat on Saturday by 25 runs. The visitors were Eccleston, and they owed their victory to brilliant fielding, and particularly to the catches in the long field. The highest scorers were R. King (30) and J. Parr (25) for Becleston, and W. R. Walker (23), J. Walsh (16), and A. Simpson (13), for Winwick. R. Grundy (Eccleston) took three wickets for three runs, and J. Palin four for 31. P. Hilton (Winwick), had five for 32, and C. Cunningham, four for 38. ELMWOOD-AVENUE JUST DEFEATED. Playing on their own ground on Saturday, the Congregationalists sustained another defeat. Padgate Wesleyans did this. Batting first, the Congregationalists were dismissed for 34, whilst Padgate surpassed this by three runs. Hollows was in fine form with the ball for the visitors, securing seven wickets for 14 runs.

div.head: MYSTERY OF A HUSBAND.
div.p: MYSTERY OF A HUSBAND.

The extraordinary story about .an alleged irregular marriage in Scotland, which was com- menced in the Warrington Police Court last week, was yesterday carried into the second chapter and will reach a third chapter, as the magistrates adjourned the case for a week to see if further evidence can be produced to help them.unraveksthe.tangle._ •

Last week Sarah Speed, or Platt, 96, Knuts- ford-road, sought an order in respect of two children against William Speed, a Corporation tram driver, of 35, Wash-lane, Knutsford-road. Her story was that, believing she was a widow through the death of her husband, named Platt, in:the loss of the Drummond Castle, 19 years ago, she left Hebdea Bridge, Yorkshire, with Speed," who was a former sweetheart, went to Glasgow, and went through what she took to be a. marriage ceremony according. to Scottish cus- tom. She lived with him for over 18 years as his wife. She had been told that Platt lost his life in the sinking of the Drummond Castle, and thought that she was at liberty to marry Speed. After hearing the evidence the magistrates thought she was married to Speed and declined lf,o make the desired order. •

FRESH DEVELOPMENTS. Yesterday the woman, sought a separation order against her husband, William Speed, on the ground of persistent cruelty, and she asked for an allowance of ms. per week. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the woman, and Mr. T. S. Steel represented the defendant. Dr. Joseph was the presiding magistrate, and others on the Bench were:_ Aldermen Bolton, Smethurst, Pier- point, and James Evans; Messrs. S. Wright, G. Pilling, and A. J. Jolley. Mr. Browne said he had hoped better counsels would have prevailed, and that they would not again be troubled by that lamentable case. As defendant had failed to do anything for the woman it was necessary to press the case to a final isene. The man had treated the woman cruelly and had ordered her to leave the house. As she was very' mild' afraid of what he might *do, she and their two children left. Speed was earning 355. a Week and a bonus, and the woman asked for 15s. a week.

div.head: WOMAN'S STORY.
div.p: THE WOMAN'S STORY.

Sarah Speed, answering Mr. Browne, laid she honestly believed that- Platt, her former hus- band, went down with the Drummond Castle, and that she was free to marry Speed, who had courted her in Yorkshire before her first mar- riage. Speed and she left Hebden Bridge for Glasgow.

What did he say to you there?—He said I was his wife for all time, and for so long sboth of us lived. He then gave me a. ring and intro- duced me to his Glasgow friends as his wife. I have had four children since.
Who registered the birth of your children ? That man! I have now living with me two chil- dren.
Did you complain to the Chief Constable about Speed's conduct towards you?—Yes; and he re- ferred me to Mr. Laws, the Police Court Mis- sionary.

You daughter was drowned two years ago?— Witness (crying bitterly) : Yes, sir; and he charged me with being the cause of it. He used to write objectionable letters to me, put them in the letter-box or fix them to the wall. Has he struckyou and thrown things at you? —Yes, a jug and its contents. The jug just missed my face. How many times have you been kept out• of the house?--Scores of times. I have had to get through the cellar window.

div.head: "BLUE MURDER."
div.p: "BLUE MURDER."
On 25th April did he come home drunk?—Yea. We were locked in the bedroom, and he broke in and turned upon me. He ordered me to go out, and find a dog that had strayed from the house that afternoon.

Did he get hold of you by the throat?—He tried to, but the boys helped me and we got him outside. He then took the lock off the bedroom door. He told me to fetch the dog in or clear out. The next morning he said: • If you are here when I come home I'll kill you all." You were afraid he would do it?—Yes, and the whole of the neighbours said there would be "blue murder" in our street. Did he leave this letter against the bedroom wall?
"Read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest all this envelope contains. There is plenty of beer at I hope I shall be there to-morrow about 11 o'clock, lunch time." Witness (sobbing) : Yes, he left that.
THE CROSS-EXAMINATION. Mr. Steel (cross-exarnining): You knew Speed before you married Platt P—l kept company with him.
--Were you in a certain condition when you married Platt?—Yes.
Was it in consequence of that Speed gave you up p—Oh, dear! No.

Did you obtain an order against your husband, Platt ?—Yes, and he went to the Transvaal. I heard later he went down in the Drummond Castle. Later I heard he was killed in a skirmish in the Boer War. Did you ever see a paper containing an ac- count of the excitement in Hebden Bridge through your going away with Speed ?—Yes, but what it said was 'hot true. I went away with him because I believed I was a single woman. You were posing as man and wife before you left F—No; I thought when we got across the Border we would be man and wife. Did you rely on him saying in Scotland that you were his wife ?—Yes; I believed every word he said. He said it was as good a marriage as if it was held in the drawing-room or the church. Did you get any document from a registrar?— No.
Has the marriage been confirmed by register? —I do not know.
Have you been told that your husband Platt has been seen three times since then in Hebden Bridge?—l have not seen-hfin.

div.head: CABMAN'S STORY.
div.p: A CABMAN'S STORY.

- - Joe Sunderland, cab driver, Hebden Bridge, said he knew Platt, the woman and the defend- ant all his life. He remembered Platt's depar- ture, but never heard that he was supposed to have been on the Drummond Castle. He thought Platt went on a ship named Crete. He sailed about 18 or 19 years ago. Mr. Steel: How many times have you seen him since?—l have seen him three times when he came to Hebden Bridge. I met him in several public-houses and he seemed to know about his wife living with Speed..

When did you s'ee him first P—About 13 or 14 years ago. He then talked about Speed run- ning away with his wife. He stayed at Hebden Bridge about six months while on that visit. When did you see him again?—About 10 years ago, and when he went away I drove him to the station.

And again?—l saw him in March, 1908. He then came to take his two daughters .out with him to Sim Francisco and stayed only a short time. You could not mistake him?—No: There was no mistaking him, as he had the mark bf a horse shoe on his face, which was done through a horse kicking him when we were boys.

div.head: CASE ADJOURNED.
div.p: CASE ADJOURNED.
The magistrates Wirtrif ic:i.—s—oine time and on their return Dr. Joseph said:

The Bench makes no decision and adjourns the case for a week for the production of any further evidence it may be possible to bring. We do not consider the present evidence is suffi- cient to form a judgment. Mr. Browne asked for costs, but that question was adjourned.

div.head: ST. HELENS ELECTRICITY PROFITS.
div.p: ST. HELENS ELECTRICITY PROFITS.

The •St. Helens Corporation Electricity Works show an income for last year of £28,557, against an expenditure of £27,458, and the committee have decided that the credit balance of £1,099 shall be carried to the reserve fund. The new St. Helens Tramways Company have asked the Corporation for an extension of theig lease of the tramways for a period of 21 years from the pre- sent time. The present lease does not expire for about five years. The Parliamentary Committee have instructed the Trathways Sub-Committee to make inquiries as to the running of trackless trams and motor 'buses.

div.head: ANGLING.
div.p: ANGLING.
'Warrington Workingmen's Associa-
N.A. CENTRE.

As we predicted, angling has somewhat wakened up after the long rest. Many anglers have turned out at the Gowy and the Walton Reservoir. Although trout have not been caught in great quantities, some fair specimens, have been taken.
THE GOWY. A fair muster visited the Gowy, with indiffer- ent sport. Three fair trout were taken by re member; another took a roach about 11b. with the worm. stream. It was carefully returned to the

Pe THE WALTON RESERVOIR. This grand stretch of water has been added to the list of the Warrington Working Men's Asso- ciation, through the kind Gilbert Greenall, who has been a patron of the above society for a number of years. As all funds received from this fishery go to permission of Sir the Warrington Infirmary, members of the asso- ciation will feel that they are doing some little somewhere, besides their own club. The charge from the society for a day ticket is 6d., and when a member has taken out four 6d. tickets he is entitled to free fishing upon application for a day ticket at any time during a season, and as he has subscribed Es. the officials think be has paid his fair snare towards the upkeep of the fishery. Mr. P. Fallon was responsible for two fair trout on the first day of issuing tickets; 141 in. and 14in. respectively. Mr. T. Singleton lost a beauty through being inexperienced in trout fishing, as di Mr. E. Wales, His rod would not stand the strain of the tug-of-war, which is not necessary. . Mr. Falions played his fish in a splendid manner, with tackle that is quite within the limit of match angling.

ROSES. All rose trees must now be given manurial assistance. Many varieties are now showing flower buds, and it is at this juncture that feed- ing is most required. Waterings with weak liquid manure will give both size and colour to the blooms. In place of the manure liquid light sprinklings with nitrate of soda, sulphate of ammonia, or guano will be helpful.

LOCAL WEDDINGS. NISBET AND DOBSON. A pretty wedding was celebrated at St. James' Church, Latchford, on Saturday. . The bride was Miss J. Nisbet, of High-street, Haddington, Scotland, and the bridegroom was Mr. James Dobson. The bride, who was becomingly attired in grey, was given away by Mr. E. Davies (organist). Mr. Robinson acted as best man, and the Rev. H. B. Firth (vicar) performed the ceremony. Suitable music was played by Mr. B. Davies, and as the happy pair left the chureh he played Mendelssohn's Wedding march. The honeymoon is being spent at Llandudno. The bridegroom has been connected with St. James' Church practically all his life. He has been continuously in St. James' Choir since he was nine years of age. He is also a Sunday School teacher. BOOTH-LEAH. A pretty wedding was solemnised at the Grap- penhall Parish Church on Whit-Monday morn- ing. The contracting parties were Miss Sarah Booth, the youngest daughter of Mr. and Mrs. J. Booth, The Cottage, Cliff-lane, Grappenhall, and Mr. G. A. Leah, son of Mr. and Mrs. J. Leah, of Cherry-lane, Lymm. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. H. V. Pigot. The bride, who was neatly attired in a grey costume, was given away by her father, and was attended by Miss Ada Horsfall (cousin of the bride), whilst Mr. T. Booth acted as best man. A reception was afterwards held at the home of the bride's parents, after which the hp.ppy pair departed for Llandudno, where the honey- moon is being spent. As evidence of the high esteem in which the parties are held in their respective localities, they were the recipients of a large number of useful presents.
